THE OLD YEAR. The year is old, feeble; Upon his aged brow Cares of human toll and strife Have all but vanished now. Hi; early- dawn we welcomed. We hailed him with delight— llop?d that happiness might te Attendant on his Tght. How have we used the blessing; He brought us day by day? How uged the corrective woe That erring ways must pay? Have we improved the moments That ne'er again may be ? Welcomed the boo they bore us Upon life's changing sea? For passing hours bring with thorn The fruits of seeds lc ng sown ; And years shall bear us surely To death's dark state trokn-,wn. But when the year is dying, " When night ani morning rnEet," The world from time etei-nal A glad new ye or snail greet : Warrington, Dec. 23th, 1832. B. KENYON.

CHRISM... 9 WAITS.—WAttI parade the streets at mil.- night about the time o: Christmas, pa rticalerly on Christ- mas Eve, playing and sioging at the doors of the princ ioal inhabitants. At the conclusion of their serenade, they offer the congratulations of the season, and next day solicit gra- taitiese lu olden times the waits were a kind of watchmen, and the word is apparently derived from the Mceso-Geth wahts, vigilia, excutdeo ; ii old French, aecording to Cot. rare, gicette, a watchman. Hone, in his "Every-day Book," remarks :—" In London, the Waits are the remains of the musicians attached to the Corporation of the City." Miss Baker, in her "Glossary," relates that the Corporation of Narthamoton, within the memory of her inforrealt, had a band of musicians called the Corperation waits, who used to meet the judges at the entrance Into the town, at the time of the assizes. They were four in number, attired in long black gowns, two playing on violins, one on the hautboy, aed the other on a whip and club, or tabor and pipe. A Wreereet Pecenue.—lt is afternoon which in winter -is evening. The sward of the down is dry under foot, but hard, and does not lift the instep with the springy feel of summer. The sky Is gone, it is not clouded, it is swathed In gloom. Upwards the still air thickens, and there.is no ern or vault of heaven. Formless and vague, it seems some vast shadow descending. The sun has disappeared, eted the light there still is, is left in the atmosphere en- eeeed by the gloorey mist as, pools are left by a receding tide. 'Through the sand the water slips, and through the Inlet the light gllees awl,. Nearer comes the formless abaiow, and the visible earth grows tanner. The path has Laded, and there are no means on the open downs of know- in; whether the direction pursued is right or wrong, till a boaer (which is a lardmark) is perceived. Thence the Wia- 13 down the slope, the last and limit of the hills there. It is a rough descent, the paths worn by sheep may at any moment cause a stumble. At the foot is a waggon track beside a low hedge, enclosing the firet arable field. The hedee is a guide, but the rats are deep, and It still neede Blow- and careful walking. " Wes-ah-wee !" Up from the daiey Surface of the arable field springs a plover, and the notes are immediately repeated by another. They can just be seen as darker bodies against the shadow as they fly over- head. " Wee-ah-wee !" The sound grows fainter as they fetch a longer circle in the gloom.—" Haunts of the Lap- wing," L 2/ Richard Jefferi?3, in" Good Words" for January. LET THE HEART }tEST.—I was able to convey a consider- -able amount of conviction to an intelligent friend of mine a little time ago by a simple experiment. I was in his house, ant he was extolling wine and singing its praise. He sing— Life is chequered o'er with woe. Bid the ruddy bumper flow, Wines' the soul of man below. He sing that to me every morning, In order, as he said, to rain my digging spirits. I said, "You sing that song well. Why not begin with wine at breakfast and give it to your servants?" "My dear friend," he said, "I couldn't get Arough a day. I should be as seedy as possible. I eemiefdt ; and as for my servants, if I gave it to them I den't Sinew lama: 'mild happen." "Then when do you take ?'' I asked. "When ;he ;area of the cl5l are over, then's the time for a few glum of wine and a nightcap." "Will .you," I said," be good enough to feel my pulse as I stand ' here ?" He did. "Count it carefully. What does it say ?" "Your pulse says 74." I then sat down in a chair. "You count it now." Your pulse has gone down. It is now 70," I then laid myself down on the conch and said," Will you take It again? What is it?" "It is 64; what an ex- traordinary thing. What is the effect of position on the 1 foible ?" "When you lie down at night that is the way I ,nature gives your heart rest. You know nothing about it, tut that beating organ is resting to that extent, and if you reckon it up it is a great deal of reat, because in laying • down my heart is doing terr strokes less per minute. Multi- ply that by 60, and it is 600. Multiply eight hours, and within a fraction that is 5,000 strokes different, and as my I heart is throwing up six ounces of blood at every stroke, it • me'see a difference of 30,000 ounces in lifting during the night." "That is a calorie fact; but what has it to do wife me?" "When I lie down at night without the alcohol that is the rest my heart gets; but when you take your wine or grog you do not allow yours to rest, for the influence of alcohol is to increase the number of strokes, and instead of getting this rest you put something like 15,000 extra strokes, and the result is you rise up very 'seedy,' as you yourself have said, with the result of a restless night, and unfit the next day for work until you have taken a little of the wine Which fills the ready bumper, and which you say is the soul of man below." His wife said, "That its perfectly true. The night is attended with a degree of unrest and broken eleep which I can hardly describe and which gives me very I much anxiety." That conversation had an influence. He began to reckon up those figures acd thirk what it meant, I slitting up an ounce so many thousand times, and in the I result he became a total abstainer, with every benefit to his health, and, as he admits?, to his happiness.

NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, froßri- CULTURE, &c. SCDIAN DEATH IN THr UNDERLEY HERD.—We are sorry to record that Earl Bective has lost his famous bull, Duke of Underley. On the morning of December 6he was found dead in his box. He had been ailing somewhat for a few days previous, but hls illness was not deemed serious, and simply attributed to his age. His death brings up an epoch in shorthorn history that will long be remembered by shorthorn breeders—namely, the New York Mills sale in Amerdca. In reference to this sue, the quidnuncs had a great deal to say, and Earl Bective's purchase of three anmele, at the price of a little over £ll,OOO, received a lot of animadversion. We do not care to recall the flattering (!) adjectives used by the "knowing ones," but as the proof of the pudding is in the eating, the death of Duke of Un- derley Trey form an occasion on which we may aek, were : the faalt•findera justified in their etrictures? One of the animals then bought was Dachees of Geneva 10th, and, after her arrival in England, she gave birth, at Underley, to Duke of Underley (33,745). His sire was rtir. Campbell's I (U. 3. Duke of Oneida 2ad (33,702), and we venture to say I that, looking to the good he has done in the Underlay herd, and in the principel herds of the United Kingdom, he alone would have repaid Earl Bective for his outlay on the lot. He was a model of a shorthorn sire, and his birth dates from j January 18, 1874, so that he is a month short of his eighth j year. Briefly we may state further that from the sale of I direct descendants of Earl Bective'e New York Mills nut- : chaos, between £13,000 and £14,000 hive been realised. iDuchess of Lencaster, a daughter of Duchess of Geneva j 10th' fe still at Underley, as also Duchess of Letecieteee I son, Duke of Uatlerley 6th. Stock by Dike of Uncieriey hive been sold from the herd for about £6,000, and there are from fifteen to twenty descendants, fernelce, now in the herd. Seeing also that his services have been in :inch re- vest in the leading herds of the kingdom, we think we have said enough to show that Earl Bective's investment at New York Mills has proved the reverse of unprofitable for himself, or licking in utility to the breeders of shorthores generally.-eR . in Agriculture, Gazette. REMOVING WORN-OUT FRUIT TREES.—In Tinny gardens and homesteads there are fruit trees, old, eankered, insect. eaten and exhausted beycnd renovation. These are not only unsiehtly, but worse, as they occupy space that might be profitably utilised. The winter is the time for clearing away and uprooting such trees, as at no time can this work be so cleanly and expeditiously done as when the ground is hand, a layer of snow being no real obstacle. If the worth- less, barred trees were removed front the gardens and orchards of this country, and young trees of superior varie• ties planted, American cultivators would have to keep their 1 e fruit at home; as it is, their produce from young orchards is superior to oars from ancient jilted 'trees of inferior varieties, and thus they have the advantage. This is a matter that has been systematically overlooked during the past hilt century by owners of land and trees in this coun- try, and there should be no more delay in the removal of old trees that never bar fruit of marketable quality. The winter is the precise time for lieerating the ground from such profitless occupants so that healthy trees of superior varieties can be established, as it is obvious a barren tree of a worthless sort takis up as much room as a fruitful tree of the most superior variety. In one case the ground is wasted, and in the other it is utilised, and no great depth of reason- ing which is the batter method to adopt. The subject needs thinking about; but as a reminder is often needed to direct thought into a certain channel, such a reminder is now given at a time when it may be of practical value. FamenY Jeas.—lt is well known amongst his more im- mediate friends that to his knowledge of dairy farming Pro- fessor Sheldon unites it considerable affection for old china, and probably few men are better acquainted with the old curiosity shops in various parts of the country than he. At his quaint home amongst the Derbyshire hills, he has an array of the brittle ware of which any collector might well be proud, but even in the beat regulated collections the fragility of the fabric will occasionally betray itself in frac- ture. This bring so, it occurred to the Professor during his visit to the recent Smithfield Show that it might be worth his while to call in at the bazaar and provide himself with a bottle of coaguline, with which to heal the sores that had here and there cast a blemish upon the frail components of his collection. Jest as he was approaching the stall, it so happened that the young lady whose lot in life it is to dis- pense the adhesive fluid to the British public was extolling the virtue of the sticky material, and remarked, in passing. "that it would join almost any two articles together." Thereupon, our professional friend, who seldom misses an opportunity for a joke, Inquired: "Now, would it, for ex- am ole, join two persons together in holy matrimony ?" "No, sir," replied the demoiselle, "but it is Avarranted to mend all family jars." He bought a bottle and departed.

SEASONILBLE Um.—Winter has set in with a venge wce, but, although sel3onabl9 and very enjoyable to those who are in perfect health, it brings additional respon- sibilitias, especially to those who have pets in their care. Tender pet dogs and puppies will be injured by the cold, unless measures are taken to prevent it. The former re- quire to he kept warm and comfortable, but, at the same time, to have an amount of exercise or their blond will stagnate. This exercise must be sharp and quickly over, nor must there be any loitering, or a fine bred and tender dog will very soon get cold. Poppies must be kept as warm as possible at night, and have plenty of good wheat straw bedding on their benches. If the kennels be very cold, a tire mxy be lit

tit, either in an op.. we spoke of in our lest paragraph a week ago, bat, which- ever is used, a wire guard must be placed in front, to pre- vent the dogs getting too near, and, perhaps, dragging some of their bedding with them. Such a fire will only need to be lit in an afternoon and kept up until night, as the dogs are generally romping about in the morning and thus keep themselves warm. Clothing should be pat on such dogs as require it, and it will be advisable to bring small and delicate ones into the house. Fox terriers often suffer from cold in winter, as their coats are very thin. In the winter season dogs are vary apt to have swellings come on their legs, causing them to go lame. A good dose of cestor oil as soon as the lameness is perceived is the best treetm nt, but at the same time if dogs are well fed, kept in kennels free from draught, and have plenty of exercise, they will he less liable to be attacked by kennel lameness. All dogs should now be induced to corns off their benches 4or exerciee several times a day. Kennel doors should no longer be set open, but a small oblong hole, half circular at top, should be cut out of the aide of the door to admit of dogs going into their yards, and a slide fitted thereon so as to close up this means of egress when required. Care must be taken ti see that this hole is high enough, or It is apt to cause a crouching carriage. There are many comelaints which trouble small dogs that are caused by in- correct feedine. It must be remembered that whilst a dog is naturally a flesh eater, too much is very apt to bring on mange and other skin diseases. This is one extreme, and the other is to give the dogs no flesh at all, consequent upon which the blood becomes poor, which causes the skin to be- come dry and scaly. wed the hair to fall off. Small dogs should have a email quantity of boiled meat, mixed with, such vegetables as turnips, cabbage, and potatoes. And as for the larger dogs, they must, at this time of the year, have an increased supply of fresh meat, to make up for the extra absorption of their bodily heat by the cold weather. Cars—MANGE —Badly kept cate are sometimes troubled with a form of skin disease which is commonly called the mange, but it is lot the same as mange in the dog. It may also be caught by contact with other cats, and this must be blamed if the cat is properly attended to at home. The first thing is to pay strict attention to diet, seeing that it is nourishing, not overheating, and moderate in quantity. The cat should also have plenty of exercise and have free acme to grase which, as is well known, is eaten by the cats as a medicine. When the eruption is found on the skin mix one pert of carbolic acid to seventy parts of water, and apply as a loti in, which muat be washed off two or three hours after- wards. Then apply an ointment of sulphur and hellebore, which any chemist will mix, and give some liquor arseni- cals internally, say six drops to an ounce of water; a tea- spoonful of this to be given twice a day in milk. This treatment should be continued for a fortnight, when it should be suspended for a few days', and then resumed until the cat is better and the hair begins to grow again. Great care must be taken in mixing the carbolic acid not to make the lotion stronger than we have stated, or It will be too powerful. PIGEONSOITT-DOOII LOFTS FOR FLYERS.—!fI Fulton' Book of Pigeons an illustration is shown of a capital out- door loft for flying pigeons, very suitable where there is no other accommodation for the birds. Upon this the author remarks :—For pigeons which are allowed their liberty, or are "flown" as it is called, less care is needed as regards the internal arrangements of the loft, the birds being stronger and hardier and passing much of their time in the open air. The breeding places for such birds are similar to those we have already spoken of, and it Is only needful to mention the arrangements for giving the birds ingress and egress In all pigeon lofts these consist of some kind of wire cage, called an "area," fixed at its open side to an aperture in the loft, and furnished round the other sides and end, or some- times only on one side, with hinged doors, which can either be lowered like drawbridges to form a landing or closed. Such an area is perhaps found in its greatest perfection of arrangement in what is known as the Spitalfields dormer, and of which any number may be seen, with slight media- cations, in that celebrated pigeon-flying locality. All round are the trap-doors, which in the blpitalfields affairs are con- nected together, so that they can be closed instantaneously by one pull at a string; and if a stray pigeon lights on any one of these doors he is a "gone" bird—for the truth must be told, that the object of many (we do not say or mean all) of these Spitalfields contrivances is as much pigeon °etch- ing as pigeon flying. On each side of the trap-door in front of this area will be observed what are called bolting wires. They are simply little swing doors composed of a few wires fixed into the little roller which serves as a 1 hinge. The bottoms of these wires, or of the door, rest I against the inside of the frame of the area, or of a small Strip of wood, so that the door will open inwards, but not o'eterards. The need for such an arrangemelt is obvious; , without it the owner must either stay on the watch till all 1 his birds have returned or some of the last must be shut out, able fall a prey to thieves or cats; but these bolting wires ,n- -fastragglers to come in after all is shut up for the night, I while they do not allow any pigeons to leave in the morning till the owner pleases. The loft already spoken of is built of wood, and can be erected in any place, say at the bottom of a garden, without any great expense. It should be about six or eight feet square, with a door and window in front, and be about seven or eight feet high. On the two sides wire pens are fitted, which will serve as breeding pens when the doors to them are left open, while they give the power of confining any bird if desired, or shelves may be fitted up on one side and wire pens on the other. Any one handy with tools Can make such a house at a very small cost, and it will be quite as comfortable and effective as more elaborate ones.

CAGE BIRDS.—GE.RMAN PASTE.—German paste has been highly recommended as a soft food for canaries, either by itself or mixed with bread crumbs. &c. We therefore give a couple of receipts for making it, for, though it Can be pur- chased in the shops, we prefer to have it fresh and wade in our own way :—Take 21bs. of pea reeal,l!b. of lard and eggs. The eggs and lard to be gradually rubbed amongst the pea meal, then gently baked in the oven or over the fire in a pen; when cold crusil Ana, and It i then rearly for use, , Cats Toast be taken that it is not over-cooked or ieuret, au it ehould be put in a cannister, where it will keep for a long time. To this can be added ants' eggs, hemp and maw seed. currants, &en and upon it, whether with or without thus extras larks, thruhes, and, in fact, most British birds will do well. Another recipe is 31bs. of pea meal, lib. of scotch oatmeal, lb. of moist sugar, lb. beef dripping, -!1.). honey, 1 pint crushed hemp seed, and 1 pint of maw seed. The deipeing and heney to be melted together in a saucepan, and the melt and sugar well rubbed in, so that no lumps are left; then add the crushed hemp and maw teed, and when cool pnt the whole in an air-tight jar, add keep it there.‘ MANAGEMENT OF FOREIGN BIRDS.—The importations of the smeller varieties of foreign birds have been simply enor- mous during the past few years and the demand for them appears to be on the increame. At years, very strange ideas were held as to the weer they shoted be managed, end though mere corrcel w 43 a have dsene tbroagh txparlance, thete ere etiii tenie which need to he altered. A curious idea exists among many laiperters of theta birds, that they do not drink water, and very often from the time they leave Australia uneil they:arrive in Londor, they never obtain a taste of this grateful beverage. This shows their wonderful powers of abstention in this direction, and what may be accomplished under exceptional circumstances. They do not drink much, it is true, and it is as equally as true that there attest be something more than solids in the seeds on which tbey are nourished, but those who have them any length of thne know that, if they remove their drinking vessels for an hour or two, on their being returned the birds will run to the water, just al canaries or any other finches will do under like circumstances. Betides, they like an occasional bath. Canary seed ought to form their staple food; it is always well, when purchased, to sift it in a fine sieve, as there is too often a large Quantity of dust mixed with it. The Bpenieh is the largest in the grain, and decidedly the best, and when it can be had none other should be taken. Along with this millet seed should be given, either by way of a change, or in the shape of a treat. It can now be generally purchaeed in the ear, and if given in this way the paroquet3 will evince much delight in shelling it foe themselves ; indeed, nothing appears to give them greeter pleasure. A little bit of sponge cake will do no harm, but so long as they keep in good health on the necessaries of life, the less given of luxuries the better.

shire. The eighth went into Holy'Orders, and became a Prebendary of Carlisle. The ninth became a Colonel in the Army, and Equerry to the late Duchess of Kent. If we put aside the Sparkes and Norths and Pretvrnans it would, perhaps, be difficult to find a more striking instance of the abuse of Church patronage than this. Yet by some, no doubt, I shall be accused of holding up the Church itself to contempt, even as Milton was when he denounced "the hireling wo:ves whose gospel is their maw." But it was only a few days ago that I read in the columns of a leading Con- servative journal a pitiful complaint from one who gave the clerical history of several fellow-students of high attain- ments for whom the richest Church in Christendom had barely provided a piece of bread. It is true that the worst scandals Of Plurillism belong to a past generation, but it is equal!y irua that the church of England is still largely tlegraded into a system of out door relief Lr the younger sons of the territorial aristocracy. It is commonly repor ed that there is a strong disposition on the part of some mem- bers of the Royal Commission to palter with the great evilA, of patronage; it is all the more necessary, therefore, that they sho aid be constantly kept before pubHQ

able a proportion of their princely revenues in the encour- agement of the highest contemporary art and the patronage of the most eminent art-workers the world contains, without respect to their nationality. The Orangery is another fine gallery, 108 ft. in length and 27ft. in width; and the Ball Room or Banquetting Room is of corresponding proportions, being 81ft. long by 30ft. wide. The Basement Storey of the Mansion contains the Duke's private suite of rooms, Lord Hartington's private rooms, and other apartments on the west front. The Chapel is at the south-west angle of the Mansion, and is 47ft. 4in. long by 231 t. 10in. wide ; and in height is equal to two entire storeys. It has a wainscot of cedar wood, and is rich with the most elan-rate wt car 7:: ing. There are still numerous important not named, such as the West Libra,— looms that we have the Leather Room, Szc.; but the reader may form .4n idea from the statement we have given of some of. and their the chief apartments, halls, and galleries, uunensions, of the extent of the palace as a whole, b'fino• in mind that the kitchens and all the rooms con- ! necteZwith the domestic establishment, which are not so much as mentioned, must be numbered by scores. We can- not pretend to begin to describe the grounds, gardens, and park of Chatsworth, a few of the most noteworthy features of which are the numerous pieces of statuary in the gardens the French Garden, with its cluster of nillars sur- mounted by busts ; fIIC Great Conservatory; the breat Cas- cade ; the Emperor Fountain, Willow Tree Fountain, and other fountains; the Temple, the Alcove, the Rockeries, the Royal Memorial Trees, Queen Mary's Bower, the Victoria Recr°ia House, the Hunting Tower, &c. All them! "wonders" of Chatsworth must be .seen to be appreciated. The visitor usually completes his day at Chatsworth by going to see the "model village" of Edensor, consisting of picturesquely grouped miniature villas and cottages of really architec- tural designs, the homes of the enviable upper servants upon the Chatsworth estate. The new Church in Edensor, the burial-place of the Cavendishes, is a perfect example of Gothic church architecture on a minor scale, with its tall, graceful tower and spire. The Chatsworth Hotel at Edensor stands just outside the park gates, and there the visitor who has spent the morning in a promenade through the palace and grounds may order the lunch or dinner for which he will be quite ready by the tima he reaches that privileged and well-directed hostelry.

div.head: "OUR OLD NOBILITY,
div.p: "OUR OLD NOBILITY,
[Publishod bp Mr. E. J. Kibblewhitc, 31, Tavistock-street London, IF.C., and reprinted by permission] THE HARCOURTS.

rit the time of the marriage of the Princess Louise, Sir William Vernon Harcourt excited some ridicule by alluding to his distant connection with royalty. Ido not know why he should have been laughed at; he might, had he chosen, have claimed some connection more or less remote with almost half the great families of England, and with a few in France beside. The very names are indicative of Norman descent. Both Harcourt and Vernon are in Normandy, the latter on the direct line from Dieppe to Paris. We will take the Vernons first, Harcourt being but a name assumed by a younger son of the house on coming into possession of the Harcourt estates, which descended through his mother, a Harcourt heiress. The Vernons came into England with the Conqueror, and acquired great estates in Derbyshire. Sir George Vernon of Haddon Hall died leaving two daughters, one married to a Stanley, the other to a Manners, by whom the extensive Vernon property was inherited. But the house had already thrown off several branches. One of the Vernons married a Staffordshire heiress; later on another Vernon married the heiress of that property ; later still another Vernon married another Vernon heiress of Haslington, in Cheshire. Yet another married the sister of Sir Peter Venables, also a Cheshire heiress ; and he, in 1762, was created Lord Vernon. The second wife of this nobleman wag the sister of the first Earl Harcourt; by. her he had a numerous family, of whom more hereafter. More recently a Lord Vernon married into the Warren family, an ancient Cheshire house which had, since. the days of the Plantagenets, been seated in that county, on lands which are rich in coal. Thus by successive marriages the Vernons have been able to acquire a moderate estate of 9,801 acres in all, in Derbyshire, Cheshire, and Staffordshire; lam only surprised that it is not larger. There is little notable in their history beyond mere marrying and giving in marriage. I turn now to the Harcourts, whose story is of far greater interest. _ _ _

The-Harcourt3 are said to have been descended from a Saxon Prince, who lived in Denmark, and accompanied Rollo on his piratical expedition to Normandy. There were two branches of the family who came over with the Con- queror to England. In the reign of Henry I. the repre- sentative of the e'.der line was Earl of Leicester, but .his . . .

Mantled- the Norman archers at Hastings. Frcai him, according to one antiquary, the Scotch Hamiltons and the French Montmorencies are descended. His grandson hr.d considerable grants of English land from the Crown. In the reign of Richard I. a. Harcourt became possessed, in right of his wife, a Norman heiress, of Stanton Harcourt, in Ox- fordshire, which for centuries was the seat of the family. Henceforth the Harcourts played a not inglorious part in English history. One of them fought with Simon, the patriot Earl of Leicester, at Evesham ; another, a Yorkist, was slain in the Wars of the Roses ; another, a Lancastrian, bore the standard of Henry VII., at Bosworth; another fought at the Battle of the Spurs; another was associated with Raleigh in his offorts to colonise America; another was in Sir Horace Vera's. campaigns in tile Low Countries and was killed in the Irish War in 1613. The son of this last suffered much in estate by his steady Royalism during the Civil War, for which he obtaioed no compensation from Charles 11. beyond the barren honour of a knighthood. His son was destined to play a prominent, but yet a somewhat timid and inglorious part in the reigns of William 111., Anne, and George I. Simon Harcourt was by education and conviction not only a Tory but a Jacobite. Onslow describes birn as "a man very able, but without shame." He conducted the impeach- ment of the illustrious Lord Somers, and defended the worthless Sacheverel, but his greatest dishonour was his conduct of the prosecution of Defoe for writing "The Shortest Way with Dissenters," in which he displayed a savage vindictiveness, and, in Defoe's belief, a bad faith, which will be remembered as long as the name of the man whom he persecuted. In the reign of Anne Harcourt be- came successively Solicitor and Attorney-General. Lord Keeper and Lord Chancellor. He was leagued with Boling- broke in the plot to procure the restoration of James at the Queen's death; but the prompt and decisive action of the Whig nobles disconcerted the conspirators, and, finding himself overmatched, Lord Harcourt not only took the oaths to George 1., but himself administered them to the Council. Ho was, however, dismissed from office; but, though his Jacobite opinions were well known he had been too prudent to compromise himself as Bolingbroke had done, and so escaped a prosecution. During the Jacobite Rebellion of 1715 he cautiously sat on the fence, waiting to jump till it was quite safe, and so escaped once more. In his later years he contracted a friendship with Sir Robert Walpole, who induced him at length to accept the Hanoverian Succession as a fait accompli. Out of his official emoluments he saved sufficient to purchase considerable additions to his ancestral estates, particularly Naneham Courtenay where his grand- son and successor, who was crekated Earl Harcourt, built a mansion, and laid out an extensive park. This Harcourt line died out in 1830. The last Lord Harcourt having left his property to his wife's family on condition that they shouhl assume his name. The present head of the Hat, court family is Mr. J. S. Chandos Harcourt, of Ankerwycke Priory.

We must return' now to the first Lord Vernon, who, as I said, married as his second wife the sister of the first Earl Harcourt. His eldest son by this marriage ultimately in- herited the Vernon title and estates. The next son, Edward, who married a daughter of the first Marquis of Stafford in 1830, inherited the Harcourt estates, consisting of 5;720 acres in Oxfordshire. He went into Holy Orders, and when quite a young man was made a Canon of Christ Church; at the age of thirty-four he obtained the Bishopric of Carlisle ; not long after he was translated to the richer See of Salis- bury; and a few years after he became Archbishop of York. This was in 1807, and he lived on till 1847. In the course of his lifetime, Archbishop Harcourt must have received from the Church considerably over half a million of money —three-quarters, I think, would be nearer the mark—And taking residences and offices into account, he and his reverend sons must have had altogether about a million from that source. The Archbishop had quite a patriarchal family, no less than ten sons and four daughters. The family motto is Ver non saver inret7The spring does not always flourish—which he inferentially translated into "Make hay while the sun shines." With a princely revenue, to say nothing of the Harcourt estates, he might have provided for his family himself; but what need was there to do so when the rich much cows of Church and State were ready to hand? Of his ten sons no less than eight were provided for in the Church, the Army, and the Navy. The eldest son, being heir to the Harcourt estates, of course had no need to choose a profession. The second son was Rector of Rothbury (£1,106 and a house), and Rector of Kirkby-in-Cleveland (£6OO and a house), a sinecure; like- wise Chancellor and Commissary; also Prebendary of York. He afterwards became Canon of Carlisle (£l,OOO and a house). The third son was Vicar of Bisbopsthorp (£3OO and a house) and Rector of Etton (£7OO and a house) ; also Canon of York. By the way, nearly all the preferments of the clerical Vernon-Harcourts were given them by their father, or obtained through his influence. The eldest son of Canon Vernon-Harcourt has succeeded to the Harcourt estates, and is a member for Oxfordshire; his brother Sir William, the Liberal member for Derby, who not 10. go reminded his Sheffield audience that he was a Yorkshire- man. The fourth son of the Archbishop was an Admiral in the Navy. The fifth was a Colonel in the Army. The sixth becAme Chancellor of the Diocese of York, mad I married an heiress who brought him the mansion of Grove Hall, in Nottinghamshire. The seventh, an Admiral in the Navy, married the widow of Mr. W. Danby, of Swinton Park, who had begeathed her for life 11,441 acres in Yorl:.•

div.head: OUR ALAIANAC ILLUSTRATIONS.
div.p: OUR ALAIANAC ILLUSTRATIONS.
TIIE DUKE OF DEVONSHIRE.

With the large Sheet Almanac given to every pur- chaser of this day's Examiner we present a Portrait of his Grace the Duke of Devonshire, and a picture of the most celebrated of his Grace's numerous re- sidences —Chatsworth, It may be information to c,pi,p if we name all the Duke of Devonshire's houses dig." eat. His London residence is Devonshire House, Piccadilly; and in England his Grace has extensive estates in four counties, upon each of which is a mansion, occupied during some portion of the year, whilst in Derbyshire the Duke has two houses. These are Chatsworth Palace and Hard- wicke Hall; in Sussex, Compton Place, Eastbourne; in Yorkshire, Bolton Abbey, Wharfedale; in Lanca- shire, llolker Hall, in Furness. In Ireland the Duke ha a great estate, upon which Lismore Castle, Co. Waterford, a noble pile of buildings, is the residen- , tial mansion. It is hard to say which of these country houses of the Duke of Devonshire is the most delightfully situated. The _scenery around all of them is of exceptional beauty; and two of the English seats are near the sea coast, and enjoy beautiful sea views—we refer to llolker Hall, in front of which Morecambe Bay expands finely, and to the Duke's house at Eastbourne, on the coast of Sussex, with a pleasant outlook upon the English Channel. But Chatsworth has an eclipsing glory as the concentration of beauty in art as well as in nature, as a vast and stately store-house of whatever is best and most wonderful in all the branches of fine art. It is a shrine for every lover of the beautiful in art to perform a pilgrimage unto, and as such it is the object of universal interest amongst the_cul- tured in this and other lands. CHATSWORTH PALACE,

Of which we present in our Sheet Almanac an engraved View, would occupy many columns of the newspaper were we to enter into a detailed description of the world- renow nel " Palace of the Peak," as Chatsworth has been not very accurately designated, seeing that its delight- ful natural situation in ;he vale of Derwent is some miles distant from the rugged mountain region of the Peak of Derbyshire. The objects of beauty both without and within the walls of this magnificent patrician home are simply countless; and our descriptive power would fail us in the effort to characterise even a limited portion of those treasures of art and charms of nature in its highest state of cultivation. One visual glimpse of such a scene and place is worth a hundred verbal delineations, and we are glad to know that, thanks to the most generous and considerate courtesy of the lord of that fair palace and domain, which admits the humblest to wander freely through its galleries and state rooms, and amidst its gardens, terraces, and sylvan avenues, some thousands of our readers, and hundreds of thousands of our countryfolk, have on one occasion or another visited Chatsworth, and have beheld its loveliness and grandeur. Such a place, once visited, is never for- gotten, but the vivid memories of it are as sweet as the im- mediate vision, for "a thing of beauty is a joy for ever." Chatsworth Park is an extensive enclosure, through the midst of which, for several miles, flows the clear current of the Derwent, The Park is entered by either of four lodges, the Baelow and Beeley lodges on the east side of the river, and the Edensor and Edensor Mill lodges on the west side. Visitors proceeding from the Railway- station at Rowsley usually enter by the Beeley lodge gates, I whence a carriage drive conducts to the palace; but the grand entrance-lodge is at Saslow. In the engraving, the 'great square block of building on the right, with classic ; façade, is the older portion of the existing mansion, and was built to replace the Old Hall (a massive castle-like quadran- gular structure), by the third Earl of Devonshire, between I the years 1687 and 1700. Sir Christopher VVren was con- sulting architect for a main portion of the works. This , stately pile stood alone, with the exception of some small ; attached buildings in the rear, until about sixty years since. In 1820, the late Duke "commenced some great Improve- ; ments at Chatsworth by erecting, from the designs of Sir Jeffrey Wyatt, the North Wing, containing, with all the domestic offices, a number of other apartments, as well as j the dining-room, sculpture gallery, orangery, banqueting- , room, and pavilion; and by altering and re-arranging seve- ral other rooms." This North Wing, with its adjuncts, is the fabric on the left of our picture of lower elevation than the older block, but terminating at the north-western corner with an imposing structure three storeys in height, finished with bold angle-turrets. The entrance-gates are immediately adjacent to this lofty projection of the North Wing. Mr. Jewitt, who is our best-informed guide to Chatsworth, enumerates as follows, in the order in which they are seen, the principal apartments of the palace thrown open to the inspection of visitors :-1. The Sub-Hall, a spacious apartment, the ceiling of which is enriched by a copy of Guido's "Aurora," painted by Miss Curzon. From this hall the visitor next enters the North Cor- ridor, and, turning to his left, passes along its ex- quisitely inlaid marble floor, to the Great Hall. 2. The Great Hall, a noble room, 60 feet in length by 27 feet in width, and of the full height of the two principal storeys of the mansion. The floor is of polished marble, and in the centre stands an immense table of Derbyshire marble. At the south end is the Grand Staircase, leading to the State Apartments. In the hallethe walls and ceiling of which are covered with paintings illustrating great events in ancient history, are two fine busts placed on pedestals, and a hand- some canoe, given by the Sultan to the late Duke, An in- scription in Latin on a marble tablet over the tire-place is thus Englished. :—" These well-loved ancestral halls begun in the year of English Freedom, 1688; William halls, Duke of Devonshire, inherited in 1811, and completed in the year of sorrow, 1840." The allusion to the year of comple- tion as a " year of sorrow" refers to the death in that year of the Countess of Burlington, the highly-gifted wife of the present Duke. The Grand Staircase leads up to suites or apartments on the Library and State Room storeys, and beneath the staircase are the passages to the Grotto Room and the rooms on the Ground Floor. 3. The State Apart- ments (entered from the Sketch Gallery) consist of a splen- did suite of rooms, occupying the whole length of the main building. One of the most important of these is the State Dressing Room, with a covered ceiling beautifully painted, and enriched by exquisite groups of wood carving. In similar style are the Old State Bedrooms, in which, besides many handsome cabinets, dec., is a noble and ancient em- broidered Canopy and State Chair, the work of Christiana,l Countess of Devonshire, the wife of the second Earl of Devonshire. The Canopy is of crimson velvet, exquisitely covered with needlework in gold and colours. The back of the Canopy, above the Chair, bears the arms of Cavendish impaling those of Bruce of Binloss. Next is the State Music Room, the walls hung with embossed leather, richly gilt and brightened with blue. The State Drawing-room which succeeds is a most elegantly furnished apartment, whose walls are hung with tapestry after Raffaelle's cartoons, and its ceiling painted with allegorical subjects. The State Dining-reom is perhaps the grandest apartment of the suite; the ceiling richly painted by Verrio ; the wall- carvings "are of matchless character, and hung in a profu- lesion that is almost bewildering." In this room are busts in marble (by Chantrey, Nollekens,and others) of the Emperor Nicholas of Russia (who some forty years ago was a guest at Chatsworth) and his Empress ; of Fox, Canning, Francis Duke of Bedford, Lord G. H. Cavendish, (Ix. Resides cabinets of rare old china, and a central table covered with rare objects, the visitor will not fail to observe the splendid lClock, encased in polished malachite, presented to the late Duke by the Emperor Nicholas. Another suite of apart- ' ments on this floor, contains the rooms known as "Mary Queen of Scots' Rooms," with suites of state bedrooms, in- cluding the room with bed and bedroom suite used by the Queen when visiting at Chatsworth. These rooms are not shown to visitors. Also on the same storey is the "Sabine I Room," containing the painting of the "Rape of the Sabines." The Middle or Library Storey occupies the foul- sides of the quadrangle of the principal block, and also Oettends the whole length of the North Wing. The other p•eat apartments include the Gallery of Paintings, occupy- ing two sides of the quadrangle; the billiard or Music ROOM and the Grand Drawing Rooms, containing an unrivalled collection of works of art. To the Library we have already referred in the personal sketch of the noble owner of Chatsworth. I.lt is a very impressive apart- ment; its prolonged vista flanked by the handsome book- presses, in which are preserved the gems of British and of foreign Literature. We have yet to come to the Dining-room, a very spacious and striking room, lit by five windows, having two beautifully carved mantel-pieces in white marble, each flanked with two life-sized statues; containing also six side tables of polished hornblende, Liberian jasper, and porphyritic sienite ; and upon its walls, a highly inter- esting series of family portrait% most of them painted by Vandyke. Respecting the famous Sculpture Gallery, itself well worth a journey to Chatsworth in order to see, our authority furnishes particulars. It is 103 feet in length and 30 in width, and lighted from the roof. Amongst its statues and busts are some of the most celebrated works of Canova Thorwaldsen, Chantrey, Schadoxv, FinellieTrenta- nove, Kessels, Tadolini, Albacini, Pozzi Tenerani, Gibson, Wyatt, Gott, Westrnacott, Bartolini' Barruzzi, Prosalendi, Campbell, Rinaldi, Rennie, Ranch, Wickmann, Nollekens, Bonelli, and Dantan Jeune. What expenditure of money do all these costly works of the seulptors' art represent ! But the art-value is more to be considered than even the money value, and how fortunate is it that England's richest nobles are, in some instances at any rate, like the late and I present Dukes of Devonshire, willing to bestow so consider-

div.head: TIIEJUTF, OF IRELAND
div.p: TIIEJUTF, OF IRELAND

Westgate, the m3n who accused himself of being con- cerned in the Phcenix Park assassinations, was on Tuesday brought up at the Dublin Police Court and discharged, it hiving been proved to the satisfaction of the counsel for the Crown that the man nmst have left Dublin before the murders took place. There was an affray between soldiers and civilians in one of the streets of Limerick on Sunday night. The soldiers, who were first attacked, effectively defended themselves with their belts far some time, but as the civilians were con- stantly increasing in numbers, the military combatants were being severely handled when the police came and put an end to the affray.

The Dub-lin Gazette of Tuesday night containel a pro- clamation renewing the offer of the reward for the discovery of the Phcenix Park murderers, namely, £lO,OOO for the arrest and conviction of the murderers; £5,000 and a free pardon to other than the actual murderers who will give the necessary information; £I,COO for private Information; and £5OO upon the conviction of any one harbouring the murderers.

One of the London papers says a strong belief is now held in usually well-informed business quarters that Ireland is rapidly and permanently recovering prosperity. Railway and bankinc, affairs in the sister kingdom certainly show Apart from opposite political views on the sub- ject of the remedial legislation which has been applied, it is possible to take a purely business view of the position, and to congratulate those concerned on the improvement in Irish business prospects with which the year is ending. THE CASTLEISLAND MURDEIL—The second trial of Poff and Barrett for the audacious murder near Castleisland, has resulted in a conviction, and the two men have been sen- tenced to be hanged on the 23rd January. Both protested their innocence. The evidence against them, however, was of the most complete kind, and one of them, apparently over- - whelmed by the knowledge of the fact, had sought to save his own life by turning "approver." The wisdom of the refusal of the prosecution to accept the offices of the would. be informer is now made manifest, a jury having adjudged both the accused to be deserving of the punishment of death.

A singular arrest is reported from Clontarf, near Dublin. Three men were seen furiously driving a c tr towards Dolly- mount, and the police, having in mind the manner in which the Phoenix Park assassins and the assailants of Mr. Field made their escape, stopped the car, and as the men refused or could not give a satisfactory - account of themselves, arrested them. The owner of the car was then found, but he was as uncommunicative as the men who were driving it, and for a time refused to prosecute them. At length, however, he consented to do this, and was bound over to appear on Monday for that purposs. THE IRISH ATTORNEY-GENERAL APPOINTED A JUDGE TIIE REPRESENTATION OF MALLOW.—The Attorney-General for Ireland (Mr. W. Johnson, M.P.) announced at Mallow, on Wednesday, that he had accepted the vacant judgeship. The announcement caused some surprise. It is stated that Mr. Naish, Q.C. (Law adviser to the Castle) will be the Go- vernment candidate, and the Conservatives also intend to start a candidate, feeling that they may hays some chance betw_e_en,Mr. Naieh on Lilo one, hand and-Mr. O'Brien, United Irelan(l, on the other.

TM,: PROSECUTION OF Mn. BIGGAR, M.P.—Mr. Biggar, , M.P. was, on Tuesday, served with a summons at Butters- , town, near Waterford, where he is staving, calling upon him to answer why he should not be called upon to give security ' for his appearance at the forthcoming aseizes to answer the , charge of having, in his speech at Waterford, endeavoured ,to bring the Lord Lieutenant, the courts of justice, the jurors of Dublin, and the administration of the law in Ire- land into contempt. The summons calls upon Mr. Biggar to appear before a special petty sessions at Waterford on 1 Tuesday, the 2nd of January, to answer these charges. Mr. : Biggar authorised a Belfast newspaper, on Wednesday night, to state that "he regards the whole affair as a joke." i SEIZURE OF A NEWSPAPER.—For a specially ferocious . attack upon the Irish Government in the matter of the trial of the Lough Mask murderers and the execution of the as- sassins of the Joyce family, last week's issue of the United Ireland was seized and its. sale forbidden. It is stated i too, probably on good information, that the editor of the ! paper, Mr. Wm. O'Brien, is to be summoned to answer for the publication of the article. Without any qualification, the article alleges that "both as to the tribunal and as to , the evidence the proceedings against these men bear an in. delible taint of foul play," and declares that " packed juries and bribed witnesses were the all-sufficient implements of , justice." It speaks of tribunals carefully concocted to "convict murderers by hook or crook," and calls rather for the abolition of the jury system than the " white terror" . that has been set uji.' Mr. William 'O'Brien, the editor of United Ireland, appeared at Dublin Police Court, on Wed- nesday, to answer to a summons charging him with having published in his paper "a false and malicious libel " in an ; article entitled "Accusing Spirits." The article, it will be ; remembered, commented in what may safely be described as very disgraceful terms on the recent murder trials in Dublin. The defendant requested the adjournment 6f the case on the ground that he had had no time to engage counsel. , The prosecution assented, and Monday next was fixed for , the hearing. It is said that Mr. A. M. Sullivan will pro- bably defend Mr. O'Brien,. who was on Wednesday accom- ! panied in court by Mr. Healy, M.P., Mr. Sexton, M.P., aeld Mr. Patrick Egan.

div.head: RECONSTRUCTED CABINET.
div.p: THE RECONSTRUCTED CABINET.

Now that the reconstruction of the Cabinet is complete, a few facts relating to its composition may be noted. They are of a character to reassure those Conservatives (if any such there really be) who dread an approaching era of con- fiscation, revolution, and other dreadful things with biz; names. In the first place, the 14 gentlemen to whom the government of the British Empire is more or less confided are all middle-aged, and a fair proportion of them may even claim the respect due to the old. The average age of mem- bers of the present Cabinet is between 56 and 57. The first in years, as in position, is Mr. Gladstone, who will be 73 on the 29th of this month. The youngest is Sir Charles Dilke, who has not yet completed his 40th year. Seven ate peers, one is heir-apparent to a dukedom, another a baronet, another in the succession to a baronetcy; yet another is a bishop's son-in-law. Lords Spencer, Carlingford, Granville, Derby, Hartington, and Kimberley, and Sir William Har- court, belong to families which, according to Mr. Bateman, have held land in the same county in unbroken male suc- cession since the days of Henry VII. The united rent-rolls of Mr. Gladstone, Lords Spencer, Carlingford, Derby, Kim- berley, and Northbrook, and Mr. Dodson are reckoned in the modern Domesday Book at £289,330, and represent the ownership of 140,416 acres. Lord Hartington's father is proprietor of 198,665 acres, yielding a rental of £180,990. Lord Carlingford, it may be mentioned, is also heir pre- sumptive to his brother, Lord Clermont, who owns 21,027 acres, from which he draws an income of £15,784. Again, all the Cabinet Ministers, with the exception of Mr. Chamberlain, are University men. Seven have been at Oxford, and six at Christ Church; six at Cambridge, and five at Trinity. Sir Charles Dilke's college waa Trinity Hall. Six are public school men, the P,remier, the Indian Secretary, and the new Chancellor of the Duchy being Etonians, and the President of the Council and Harrovian. The Chancellor was educated both at Rugby and Win- chester; the Colonial Secretary at Eton and Rugby.—London Echo. '

AN Rasa ELOPEMENT IN HIGH LIFE.—A Coleraine cor. respondent, telegraphing on Wednesday night, says a rumour which has since been confirmed was current in Coleraine on Tuesday that Lady Macnaghten, wife of Sir Francis Edmund Workman Macnaghten' of Dundaraye, Bushmills, county Antrim, had eloped with a young gentleman named Thornhill, agent for the Macartney estate, and for several other properties in the north of Ireland. The parties were traced by Sir Francis to Dublin, where they were found at an hotel. Arrangements were at once made to obtain a divorce. Lady Macnaghten, who is a daughter of Dr. W. H. Russell, and was married to Sir Francis in, 18613, has left several children behind her. Sir Francis, who is 54 years of age, served in the Crimea and the Indian mutiny. He is chief of the Clan Macnaghten, and his family is of great antiprity in the Western Highlands. The occurrence has created a great sensation. The Rev. J. G. Rogers writes to a London contemporary: —"Sir,—l am not so ignorant of the true relations of ' Church parties as to suppose that a Nonconformist, and especially a member of the Liberation Society, has a right to an opinion as to the .appointment of an Archbishop of Canterbury. But the Bishop of Truro has so recently made a slanderous charge against the society, and made it in a manner so deliberate, that the announcement of his eleva- . li4ll. to the Primacy can hardly be.received by us in silence. 1I haYP °WPM met with a more offensive statement than that of the Bishop at his Diocesan Conference held only a few weeks ago : 'When I see the crafty forgeries and miles of printed falsities which are rolled out and about by our self-appointed would-be deliverers, it is time we spoke out.' Such language requires no eminent. It may be that it 'a as spoken in haste, and as the speaker is now raised from the superintendence of one of the newest and most obscui-e sees in the kingdam to the Primacy, he may think it desirable to retract a statement which is unworthy even of an agent of the Church Defence Society. The liberal Archbishop who has just 'crone to his rest did his utmost to ' ,n-peigee kindly relations between Churchmen and Noncon- formist Unless his good work is to be interruptel, these s. words must be e.4lier recalled or proved. They might have been treated with coml;:ratlys indifference so long as the speaker was nothing more thi:.7 aßt shop of Truro. They assume an entirely different charactt: if endorsed with the authority of the Primate. It would be muj.h to be regretted if his administration were to begin in contrOs7ersn but unless the imputation be withdrawn those against who it it is directed will be forced to vindicate themselves. The sooner the new Archbishop recognises that there is a real distinction of principle between us, and that the cause of which he is so able a champion will not be advanced by the substitution of reckless and unfounded stsetnents for solid arguments, the better for his own peace, for the security of his own Church, and what is of more importance to all of us, the interests of our common Christianity.—Yours, J. Kains Jackson writes to the Tinos-The cereal harvest of the year 1832 in the mitt.] Kinatinm ha hann orrrowti over an- "a-Fre-age of-wheat, 3,004,000; barley, i 2,255,000; oats, 2,833,000. These areas, compared with those of 1881, are about 9 per cent. increase wheat, 7.7 de- crease barley, 2 3 decrease oats. The English wheat area is cultivated very irregularly over the several counties-a fact I wish to show to indicate the relative importance of differ- ent districts and in older to make it the basis for forming an estimate of an average yield. The 40 cOunties of Eng- land may be conveniently grouped into four divisions, each grewing, roughly reckonire• a fourth of the total yield. Group 1: Three counties %aye probably 32 bushels per acre-Lincoln, 279,000 acres; York, 230,000 acres; Norfolk, 180000 acres-total 880,000 acres, yielding 2,720,000 qrs. Group 2: Six counties I put as yielding but 23 bushels through the low average yield of Devon- Essex, 162,000 acres; Suffolk, 140,000 acres; Cambs., 119,000 acres; Devon, 110,000 acres; Hampshire, 95,000 acres; Kent, 90,000 acres-total, 716,000 acres, yielding 2,501,000 quarters; Group 3: Tea counties grow a fourth, and may be estimated as yielding 30 bushels per acre- Sussex, 85,000 acres; Wilts, 84,000 acres ; Gloucester, 80,000 acres; Salop, 70,000 acres; Northampton, 70,000 acres; Notts, 64,000 acres; Warwick, 60,000 acres; Somerset, 60,000 acres; Hertford, 60,000 acres; Berks, 55,000 acres- total, 688,000 acres, yielding 2,580,000 quarters. Group 4: Twenty-one counties grow the last fourth-Oxford, 55,000 acres ; Worcester, 54,000 acres •, Berks, 51,000 acres; Here- ford, 50,000 acres; Beds, 48,000 acres; Staffordshire 44,000 acres; Huntingdon, 44,000 acres; Cornwall, 43,000 acres; Dorset, 41,000 acres; Leicester, 35,000 acres; Surrey, 32,000 acres; Northumberland, 26,000 acres; Lancashire, 25,000 acres; Cheshire, 20,000 acres • Derby, 22,000 acres; Durham 20,000 acres; Monmouth, 16,000 acres • Cumberland, 15,000 acres; Rutland, 18,000 acres ; Middlesex, 3,000 acres ; Westmoreland, 1,000 acres-total, 704,000 acres; should yield 28 bushels per acre; yielding, say, 2,4o4,oooquarters. Gross English crop yields 10,268,000 quarters. Ireland 155,000 acres, Wales 90,000, Scotland 85,000, total 330,000 acres-do not form a group, being only one-tenth of the wheat area, and, estimating the produce at 23 bushels per acre, the yield would be 1,145,000 quarters. Grand total, 11,412,000 quarters. But here, while crediting the areas above as growing an average crop generally, yet the charac- ter of the season has been such over about half a million acres of either poor clay land or soils unsuited for growing wheat, and from the effects of the great storm on April 29 in the southern counties, that probably a sack per acre deficiency must be allowed off the average totals, making a reduction of 250,000 quarters, while the requirements for seed may be put at 750,000 quarters; leaving a total production for bread mak- ing, &c., of 10,412,000 quarters. As regards barley, about half the, production is grown in eight counties-York, 232,050 ; Norfolk, 204,000; Lincoln, 195,000; Suffolk, 152 000 ; Essex, 124,000; Devon, 68,000; Hunts, 62,000; Wilts, 68,000; total, 1,103 000 acres; which I estimate as growing 36 bushels, say 5,000,000 quarters. The other 32 counties, 32 bushels per acre on 1,152,000 acres, including Scotland, which has an acreage rather superior to Yorkshire, and produces barley of fine quality, 4,600,000 quarters. From the Irish acreage of about 190,000 acres the yield should be 800,000 quarters. Total available for malting distilling, and feeding, seed, 10,400000 quarters. The oat crop is grown in three divisions. Group 1- England and Wales, acreage about 1,800,000 acres, of which 13 counties counties contain nearly half the area- York, Lincoln, Devon, Northumberland, Cumberland, Hants, Sussex, Kent, Lancashire, Cheshire Durham, Essex, and Cambrideshire ; the other half divided among 27 counties and Wales; I estimate the yield 48 bushels per acre, say 10,400,000 quarters. Group 2-Ireland, 1,400,000 acres, may be nut as five quarters per acre; 7,000,000 quarters. Group 3-Scotland, 1,000,000 acres, six quarters; 6,000,000 quarters. For home consumption and seed, 23,400,000 quarters.

MYSTERIOUS DEATH AT WEDNESBURY. Two Royal Engineers, when surveying some land at the Delves, Wed- nesbury, the other day, discovered the dead body of a man unknown in a field. The deceased was respectably attired, and about forty years of age. There were several bruises on his head and face. It is supposed the body has been lying in the field for several days. The coroner has directed a post mortem examination to be made on the body. A decision of considerable importance to farmers has been given in the Edinburgh Court of Session. The case was popularly known as "the Aberdeenshire rabbit case," and the chief point of contention was whether a place where rabbits have scraped below a wire fer.ce in order to pass from the one side of it to the other is a "rabbit-hole " under the meaning of the Ground Game Act of 1880. By.the casting vote of Lord A dam this has been decided in the negative, and accordingly farmers are not entitled to use traps in such places, section 6 of the Act restraining them from setting traps elsewhere than in rabbit holes. On Saturday, shortly before midnight, the body of a man, at present unidentified, was found with the head cut off and Otherwise mutilated, in Otterspool Tunnel, on the Cheshire Lines Railway. We (Daily Neics) have reason to believe that Sir Henry 13rand does not contemplate retirement from the Speakership during the present Parliament, still less in the course of the eneuing session. On Saturday night and Monclay-aight the streets of Aber- deen were lighted by electricity, the "Brush" lamp being 1 • used. The experiment is not regarded favourably, but a : bright moon light interfered with a fair test. On the arrival of the two p.m. train at Havant on rriday it was found that a gentleman, mane unknown, had blown his brains out in a second-chaos carriage. He had a ticket from London-bridge Station for Portsmouth. The Birmingham magistrates on Friday committed for • trial a hairdresser named Henry White on a charge of hav- ing received human. hair (if the value of 220 "mowing the . same to have been stolen ;sand two other local hairdressers Were remanded on a like charge. Medals were distributed on Saturday at Chelsea Barracks . to about 500 soldiers eef the 2nd Bettalien Coldstream Guards, I who were engaged in the Egyptian campaign. The Duke .of Connaught, Who was expected, was unable to attend, and the distribution was made by Col. C. J.Wigram, . Who commanded the battalion in Egypt. FOUR Coeseents KM:ED.—An acmdent occurred on Satur- day at the Cannock Chase Company's Colliery, Brownhills. Staffordshire. Three men were descending one tf the shafts when /he rope broke, and they fell to the bottom and were killed. A miner named Themes King was at work at Bradley Ledge Colliery, near Bilston, the previous night, when the roof fell 4n and injured him so much that he has since died. The Lord Advocate, in a letter to the Sheriff of Inverness cn the disturbed condition of the Island of Skye, states that tie Government: 'neve come to the conclusion that they ought not to sanction the employment of a military force under existing circumstances, but that the county authori- ties should provide or obtain the services of such a force of police as they may consider necessary for preserving the peace and executing the law within the county. THE RESIDENTIARY CANOFRY OF YoRK MiNsTER:— The Archbishop of York has conferred the residentiary canonry in York Minster, vacant by the death of the 'ken. Archdeacon Hay, upon the Von. Richard Frederick Lefevre Blunt, D.D. Archdeacon Blunt has been vicar of Scar- borough since l'iL64, and prebendary of York since 1871. In 1873 he was appointed archdeacon of the East Riding, and last year was nominated one of Her Majesty's honorary chaplains. A DISHONECT ACCOUNTANT.—An accountant named *Godolphin Osborne was charged at Westminster, on Satur- day, with converting to his own use valuable securities Which had been entrusted to him by a servant girl named Bose. It was alleged that he realised upwards of £lO9 by selling shares she left with him, and when, after some diffi- culty, she obtained a settlement, he represented her to be in debt to him •1. He was committed for trial. VISIT OF THE QUEEN TO NETLEY HOSPITAL. oThe queen, following up her recent visit to Netley Hospital, Went on Saturday to the hospital at Hasler, and showed a deep interest in the sick and wounded soldiers who are still confined there after their sufferings in Egypt. Her Majesty teas shown some of the relics of the war, and pinned meda4s On the breasts of a number of the convalescent soldiers; but What touched the men most was her sympathetic and kindly inquiries as to their wounds. FALL OF DURRAM.CASTLE WALL.—Early on Saturday Morning theofficials of Durham Castle were greatly alarmed by loud reports, and for some time it was feared that a threat made about Btu months ago by a student to blow up the cathedral and castle was being carried into execution. •On making an examination it was found that about .60 yards of the enter terrace wall of the castle had given way and fallen into the river. The crash was heard miles off. A HYDROPMEIA PANlC.—Great alarm continues to exist in Radnorshire in consequence of canine madness etill, being Prevalent in the district. Some dogs have been killed at Knighton during the past week, and, as far as can at present be ascertained, them appears to be very little, if any., abate- -Meat of the disease in the county. Special sessions have been held by the magistrates at Penybont to consider a resolution of the Llanbadarnfawr School Board praying for More stringent orders to be made respecting the dogs. ESCAPE vetotts GAOL.—A man named John Tierney has just effected his escape front Leicester Gaol, and all the 'efforts of the police to recapture him have proved fruitless, Tierney was convicted of robbery from a dwelling-house, -and was undergoing three months' imprisonment, but while at work in the front garden he cleverly effected his escape 13,1 bolting through a little door into a side street which tied accidently been left open for a moment. He was seen in one of the principal thoroughfares in gaol clothes. THE VICAR OF PONt‘EFRACT AND THE TITRE QUESTION. --Considerable surprise has been caused in Pontefract by some 100 County Court summonses having been served nPon prominent residents demanding payment of the vicar's tithes. It seems that the date Rev. Dr. Bissett had a private income, and did not enforce payment of the tithes for 13 or .14 years, and now the ratepayers demur considerably and intend to oppose the claim of the vicar. The Rev. J. J. Christie has appointed Mr. \W. R. Wilkinson, accountant, of Pontefract. his agent to collect the tithe. M/E.ITARY RIOT AT CAIRTERBuRY.—A Canterbury cor- respondent reports that a serious collision took place on Monday between the men of the Inniskillings and the Buffs, quartered there. Nearly 200 men were for an hour engaged in a fierce encounter, with belts and bayonets. Many were injured, and one man in the Inniskillings had his head laid open. The riot warequelled by some non-com- rnissioned cacers rushing into the ?wide just as one excited fellow had gone to the assistance cf his comrades with a axed bayonet. Extra guards were mounted, all men being Confined to barracks. THE RAILWAY RATES BETWEEN LIVERPOOL AND OLD- If-AM.—The various railway companies carrying between Liverpool and Oldham intend to reduce the rates of carriage ,25 per cent. This reduction will make a difference to ,u.ldham of between £40,000 and £50,000 a year. It is be- lieved that this is being done to counteract the popularity '4 the proposed .ship canal, but the announcement has, nevertheless, been received with much satisfaction in Old- Liam.
