div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, IiECE

Four dwelling houaes at Tunbridge were on Wednesday destroyed by fire. His Eminence Cardinal Newman is confined to his room at the Oratory, Birmingham, through an attack of brochitis. Frederick Ripley is in custody at Taunton on the charge of baying murdered a ycung woman named Rowsell cutting her throat. A potted-meat manufacturer, named Wm. Henry Whllc., was charged before the magistrates at Aston, Birmingham on Wednesday, with being in possersion of meat unfit Tor food. A sentence cc six months' hard labour, withont the eption of a fine, SCI.S passed. The lieutenant's naval peasion of £5O a year, vacant by the death of Retired Comets:eider J. Hollingworth on December sth instant, has been conferred on Retired Com- mander John s'Arcy Irvine from this date. Mr. H. Kains Jackson says in a letter that the cereal harvest of 1t.82 in the United Kingdom was grown over an acreage of—wheat, 3,0000; barley, 2,255,000; oats, 2,833,000. The Eerl of Derby weites to a Welsh correspondent I conceive that representatives in Parliament should be chosen , with a view to their, general efficiency and fitness rather than Ire-persons pledged to defend the interests of one class in particular. I have more than once expressed myself in I public as favourable to the assimilation of the borough and county franchises." PAL-PERS AND TI:EIR BEER.—The Devonshire magistrates have come to an important decision with regard to the maintenance of the eight hundred pauper lunatics now in , the County Asylum at Exeter, the visiting justices having decided that with the end of this year the (hilly supply of beer that has hitherto been given the patients shall be -entirely discontinued, and that in future neither beer nor -spirits shall be given except under medical order. DEATH FRCPM EXCITEMENT.—A painful affair was in- ,mstigated at Croydon' a village near Royston, on Tuesday. Two labourers, named Hagger and G-arman, had a dispute at a public-house. A fight ensued, and Garman was felled by a violent blow on the head, death ensuing almost im- mediately. At the inquest, on Tuesday, the medical evidence showed that the deceased was suffering from ex- tensive heart disease, and that the violent exertion, and not the blows, caused his sudden death. The jury returned a verdict accordingly, and Haggar was afterwards released from custody. THE MURDER OF PROFESSOR PALMER.—The Secretary of the Admiralty announces that a telegram has been te- ceived from Captain Stephenson, of H.M.S. Carysfort, dated December 20, from Suez, stating that Shedide reports from the Desert that he has captured Ali Showeyer Tens- bin, who shot Professor Palmer; also Salim Abu Telhaida. Colonel Warren has left for Nackl to examine these mur- derers, and will b 3 away some days, but he does not think that Shedide will get the remainder of the people for at least a fortnight, but will in time get all. Shedide has taken possession of all the waters, but the rains -enabled the Bedouins to show fight from the mountains. The sheikhs of Terebin have bound themselves in writing to assist in capturing all implicated. FATAL FeGerr.—At three o'clock on Sunday afternoon a fatal fight occurred between two men in Hopkine's lodging- house, Dumple-street, Scarborough. The men's names were —Elarcroft Booth, bricklayer, 34, native of Selby, and Joseph Lumley, labourer, of Stacton, near Scarborough. They agreed to fight, and went out in the back yard. Lumley was very drunk, besides being far advanced in con- sumption. When he went into the yard he fell down, and on rislng leaned against the wall. Booth struck him violently on the side of the haad, knocking him against the wall. Lumley fell, and expired soon afterwards. Booth was apprehended, charged with the manslaughter. FIRE IN BURNLEY Towx HALL.—On Wednesday even- ing afire, which had it not been almost instantly discovered, would probably have been a most disastrous one, occurred in the Corporation buildings. About seven o'clock the Water Committee were holding a meeting in the Town Clerk's office, when they noticed a strong smelt, followed by the appearance of flames in the floor of one corner of the room. An alarm was given, the fire brigade were speedily on the spot, and jets were applied to the flames, which originated in one of the baths under the Council chamber. The books and documents were removed out of the learning building, and the fire was got under in about half an hour, though not before considerable damage had been done. MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND WORKING-CLASS REPRBSENTA- .TivEs.—Mr. Chamberlain, M.P., writes to a Welsh cor- respondent :—" It is the earnest hope of the Government that the present Parliament will not separate without hav• • ing dealt with the question of the assimilation of the borough and county franchise. As to labour representation in Parliament, the answer must depend more upon the character of the men sent than the class from which they are taken. Ido not doubt the advantages to the working classes of the presence in Parliament of such men as Mr. Burt and Mr. Broadhurst, who would do honour to any constituency. If there are any more men of the same stamp willing to undertake parliamentary duties, I sincerely hope their presence in the House of Commons may be quickly assured."

ALARMING ACCIDENT AT THE LIVERPOOL CENTRAL STAnorr.—On Wednesday morning, about one o'clock, a stretch of wall nearly 50 yards long and 10ft, high, forming the bumsdary of the Cheshire Lines station, tame down with a great crash just as the last train had left the station. The result was that both the station and the line were covered with debris, but apart from the piling np of a large quantity of 'bricks and stones no damage was done. Imme- diately a gang of navvies were got together, and by running trains on the cingle line as far as the Brunswick Dock 'station Bank Holiday traffic was not interfered with. In eroler to guard against further accident the engineer has placed supportsagainat the remainder of the Fan, vfoth ia some 40ft. higher than the permanent way.. The collapse is attributable to the recent rains.

A CANDIDATE ,rOR A "RESPONSIBLE SITI7ATION."—The following is from the Warehonseman and Drapers' Trade Jcitr,;*al:—A gentleman advertised the other day for a per- son .qualified to occupy a responsible situation. Among the replie.3 received was one asking for further particulars, and enclosing the following paragraph :—" Those who have to any eztent undergone the ordeal in part, in little heathen England,' of being morn or less permanently and needlessly injured in mind, body, or estate,' because of the tricks and tactics of deceased mente:ars, voleurs, legal serfs of ceremony and sham, the leper and the liar, &c., (57.3., know by queer experience thrust on them that there has been long needed in most parishes free and fit central baths, libraries, rests, sanatoria, museums, studies, laboratories, velocipedes, boats, observatories, restitution, coin transit, dm., pro bow; apart from doubt, deism, diabolical intrigue, force, fraud, fury, facetious mendaeity, pomp, plague, plundering, blundering, ignorant insolence, or unique, heretical, 'unruly vulgarity, and the awkward defects and indifference of ism,' didn't, and wouldn't!" SERIOUS AFFRAY NEAR TAILS rocK : POLICE, OVER- POWERED BY NAVVIES.—A Tavistock correspondent reports that while Sergeant Richards, of Tavistock, was on Wednes- day conveying a prisoner from PrinCetown to Tavistock pike station, several navvies mode an attack on him, seiz- ing the conveyance and overpowering the police-sergeant ! and driver with clubs, &c. The mob rescued the prisoner, ' who was got away. .Forty navvies afterwards made their way to Horrabridge, to interc3pt any police who might be sent for. All the police in the district were summoned, and twelve of the warders at the convict establishment, by per- mission of the governor, volunteered their services. Fire- , arms were served out to them, and to a large force of police. The riot arose out of an assault on Police-constable Van- I &tone, made on the previous evening on his apprehending an escaped prisoner. Vanstone had his nose almost bitten ' off, and Richards was severely cut about the head and face. I MR. COWEN, M.P., ON THE HOUSE OF COMMQNS.—Re- plying on Wednesday night to the toast of the House of Commons, at the annuli dinner of the Newcastle Clerks' i Association, Mr. Joseph Cowen, M.P., contended that the 1 existing House compared favourably with former ones, and for those who were sceptical on that point he prescribed a course of Hansard. Let them dig deep, and they would soon ' find a sample of some buried debates which would modify their judgment. They would find that the language used in , past times was not only etrong; but even coarse and some- , times vulgar. The manners of the present House of Com- mons might not be faultless, but they were a vast improve- !Tient 911 Ivh2.i. they Onee were. As to the terrible offence of i obstruction, what was it but the tactics of Fabius applied to 1 legislation ?—the effort of the weaker party to secure the, defeat of objectionable measures by delay? It was a prac- tice that every party had resorted to, sometimes justifiably and sometimes unjustifiably, and as long as politicians con- tinued to be moved by the common motives of mankind, as lung as a strip of parliamentary fighting ground remained, it would be utilised by the minority to postpone proposals 1 of which they disapproved. The majority would call that opposition factioßs ; the minority would call it patriotic; and this had been and would continue to be the case till we reached that period of political beatitude when none are for a pay blt fill for the state, a period that none present wefe likely to live to see. ExTtieoRDINArtY SWINDLER! 44 THREE LADIES."—About three mouths ago "three ladies" (one pretending to be an invalid l made arrangements to rent a lodging-house near Abergele for a term of three months. The three " ladies" also requested the landlady, who lived close by, to engage two servants for them, which she did, the females inform- ing her that they would " settle" with her every quarter, as they were in receipt of some money every three months. It was further agreed that the landlady should allow the ladies the use of the horse and carriage, and that they should be supplied with farm products. The ladies were also introduced by the landlady to some of the " best " local shopkeepers, who supplied them with the necessaries of life —such as meat, provisions, groceries, em.—on conditions similar t 2 those agreed upon between the "ladies" and herseff—viz., three months' credit. On Monday last the quarter expired, and, seeing that the time Co " settle " matters was drawing nigh, the three females booked several hampers, boxes, &c., full of different goods, to Abergele, which upon arriving there, were re-booked to various places. The" ladies" also subsequently left, informing the landlady that they would return with the evening train, and directing her to order a carriage to Meet them at the station. The servants, who had had a merry time of it since the ladies bad "left home," pos- sessing some suspicion that they had been deserted, /rent into the ladies' rooms and found that everything, with the exception of a box which was screwed to the floor, had , been taken away. On Monday one of the servants received a letter bearing the postmark " Manchester," in which she and the other servant were ordered to clear the house and go home. On Tuesday a meeting of the duped shopkeepers L was held, and it was decided to report the freaks of the lady swindlers to the police, who are now making every investi- -1 gation into the matter.

Mr. Fa;veett?'s condition continues to be in every %fay satisfactory. It stat 'officially announced on Tuesday that t,in Bishop of Trey° had accepted the Archbishopric of Canterbury. Mr. Dodson, who has retired from the head of the Local CiLuvernment Board, where he will be succeeded by Sir Chas. Diike, has been appointed Chancellor of the Duchy of Lan- raster. The Right Hon. John Bright has now defini ely agreed to deliver his Rectorial address to the students of the Glas- gow University on Thursday the 22ad of March. It is pro- bable that he will also address a public meeting in Glasgow ou the following evening, but with regard to this nothing has yet been quite decided upon. Another great fire has occurred in London at a shop belonging to Mr. Whiteley, whose great establishment in Westbourne Grove was seriously injured by tire a few weeks ago. The shop burned on Tuesday was in Bayswater, and the damage is estimated at about £20,000. A MilssiNG TUTOR.—Nearly a week ago a tutor, named Heazle, of Wesley College, Sheffield, quitted the town to pass his holidays with some friends in London. He never reached his destination, and his relatives and the police authorities are making most anxious inquiries, fearing that some harm has befallen him. He had a large sum of money on him when he left Sheffield. _ _

INDISPOSITION OF Mn. GLADSTONE.—Mr. Gladstone has had a slight attack of lumbago, through which he was con- fined to his room during the greater part of Wednesday. On Tuesday afternoon he spent some time in felling a tree in Hawarden Park. and, as it was a very inclement day, it is believed that he contracted a chill through injudicious exposure. His condition has since much improved. Mn. OSCAR WILDE.—Mr. Oscar Wilde sailed for England by the Bothnia on Wednesday. The correspondent of the Daily News states that Mr. Wilde left sorrowfully. He says his mission to reform the tastes and dress of the Americans has been a failure; he has been in New York a month and has been entirely neglected. He never was, the correspondent adds, regarded seriously in any part of ' the country. The public got as much fun out of him as possible, and then dropped him. The Potteries stipendiary magistrate at Tunstall, on Thursday, sent an Irishman, named Patrick Carroll, to prison for one month's hard -labour for committing a terrible assault on a pudler, named E. Cooper, at the Ravensdale Ironworks, Tunstall. The prisoner worked for prosecutor at a puddling furnace, and on being provoked he struck him on the face with a pair of -hot tongs, inflicting a shocking gash over one eye and laying open the cheek to the bone. The death of a boy named Thomas Wainwright, the son of a publican in Wolverhampton, has just occurred under shocking circumstances. On Christmas Day he went to look at a pudding which had just been lifted off the kitchen fire in a pot of boiling water and placed upon the floor. Whilst stooping he fell into the boiling liquid, and was so frightfully scalded that he died on Thursday morning.

_ RAILWAY RATES FROM 'LIVERPOOL TO OLDHAM. Last week the announcement was made that the rates of carriage for cotton between Liverpool ard Oldham had been reduced to the extent of 25 percent. This, we are informed, is an exaggeration. The cotton spinners of Oldham and the district have received an intimation from the Lanca- shire and Yorkshire Railway Company that on and after the Ist of January the rate for cotton, which is now lls, per ton, will be reduced to 10s. The cartage rate, both in I iverpaol and Oldham, remains the same as hitherto, so that the actual reduction to be made upon existing rates from the let of January will be a fraction over 9 per cent.

The London and North-Western Railway Cotnpany's em- ployes who v,,orit the 'Shropshire lieion Canal are busi:y en• gaged at Beeston, Cheshire, endeavouring to avert a serious disaster. The .-canal, close to where the Liverpool.cater mains are intended to cross, passes over an immense bed of quicksand, which is evidently on the move. When maling the canal the eneineers were compelled to -sink massive iron plates and girders,and it is these that are being shaken. IProps hays been hurriprily thrown aerna2 tho is to promo,i- a total collapse, and-the ground has sunk a foot round tha locks. The sides of the canal are evidently bulging in. Traffic is carried on to the dangerous part, and goods are then put on the London and North-Western Railwag, which fortunately passes near the snot. The learne3 jndge (Euddleston) concluded his summing up in the Belt Libel ease shortly after half-past twelve o'clock on Thursday. The jury immediately retired to consider their verdict. The verdict was in favour of the plaintiff; damages £5,00. The result was received with cheering in the crowded court. Mr. Webster applied, en behalf of -the defendant, to have execution staved. Baron Huddleston : Certainly not. Sir Hardinge Giffard, on behalf of the plaintiff; asked his lordship to certify for special jury, which was agreed to, as was also an application by the same counsel for the shorthand writers' notes in the cases of Belt lieFsus Lawes and Mr. and Mrs. Verheyden. Judgment was then entered with costs for plaintiff. MIIIMER AT Ihnnow.—Thoreas Postlethwaite, joiner, 11, Arthur-street, Barrow, about 47 years of age, an intem- perate man, is in the custody of the Barrow police on a charge of murdering his wife. On Saturday night he went home drunk about eight o'clock and went to bed. His wife, who was also of intemperate habits, went home afterwards, when prisoner got up and asked her for some money. and as he did not get a satisfactory reply he pulled her upstairs by the hair of the head, and there brutally assaulted her. She received one severe cut ever the eye, and other evidences of violence present themselves, but it is not known in which way the assault was committed. Information was given to ' the police, and medical aid was called, but the woman died at one o'clock on Tuesday morning. Prisoner was appre- hended at the Model Lodging House, Barrow, where he gave the name of Mount.

ROMAN CATHOLICS IN ENGLAND. According to the Boman Catholic Directo:y, sshich is" published by the authority of the Cardinal Archbishop and the (Roman Catholic) Bishops of England," the total clergy of that religion in England and Wales amounts to 2,112 priests and 17 bishops, who serve 1,188 churches, chapels, and mis- sionary stations. Beside these, in Scotland. there are six bishops and 300 priests, whose ministrations are distributed over 295 chapels. For England and Wales there is one archbishop with 14 suffragans and two auxiliary bishops, and two archbishops for Scotland with four suffragans. These numbers are about double those which figured in the same Directory a little before the constitution of the Hierarchy in 1850. There are 20 Roman Catholic peers who have seats in the House of Lords; there are four 'Roman Catholic Privy Councillors; there are 47 Roman Catholic baronets, the premier being the " Infant " Sir Henry Alfred Doughty Tichborne, and the last in rank Sir Maurice O'Connell, Much excitement prevails respecting the mysterious disappearance of a cabman named Wm. Thayer, who drove from Cardiff to Pontypridd on Tuesday night with two fares, and has not since been heard of. The occupants of the cab, a jeweller named Phillipini, and his assistant, named Marrelli, state that there was some dispute at the turnpike beyond Cardiff about fares, and that Thayer' I offered to fight Pbillipini, who ref cud. Eventually the matter was settled by Phillipini paying the extra sixpence asked, and all three men had some drink. On the journey Thayer appeared overcome, although he had only had a small quantity, and Marrelli took the reins. On reaching their clf:stination they pai4 Thayer, and SAW no more of him. It appears that a horse and cab were found near the river on the following morning, but Thayer was missing, and all the efforts of the pp:ice to discover his whereabouts have, up to the present, been without result. Thayer, it is stated, was sober when he left Cardiff, and had live pounds in his possession. He was the owner of several cabs besides the one he was driving. Mr. Phillipini is a trademan of high character, and relates his story in a very straightfor- ward manner. The affair has created a great sensation both in Cardiff and Pontypridd. The United Ireland, published for the first time in Dub- lin after the seizure, appeared on Thursday with a cartoon entitled "Christmas at the Castle." It predicts the Lord Lieutenant presiding at the dinner table laden with Christ- mas fare marked "Inspected and found correct.". Crown officials round him are drinking "Long life to the Inquisi- tion," while Lord Spencer is waving off a spectre represent- ing Famine. In a leading note on the various Clown prosecutions, the editor asks: "Is it in order to stimulate' outrage that the Castle officials exasperate the people by prosecuting every man they trust in all over the country ?" Referring to the seizure of last week, United Ireland also says: "For the first time the Government have dared to bring to issue the truth or falsehood of the statements which, to the interests of the Irish people, have been printed in these columns. We shall, as a perfect godsend, avail ourselves of the opportunity which Dublin Castle pro- poses to offer to test once for all the fairness and honesty of the prccess of trial by jury in Green-street Court House. The seizure and summons are accepted by us as another instance of the blending of the wondrous policy of gentleness and firmness of which, since the arrival of Messrs Trevelyan and Spencer, so much has been heard." HREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
EGYPT. ThE DECTR MITION OF ARABI AND HIS ACCOMPLICES.

The public degradation of Arabi and the other chief prisoners was carried out en Monday afternoon in one of the inner yards of the Kasrelink Barracks. Two battalions of the new Egyptian army were drawn up on the spot where the proceedings were held, but only a few Europeans and about one hundred natives were present, the event not having been publicly announced beforehand. The prisonets, Arabi Abdellah, Ali Fehmy Toulba, Mahmoud Fehruy, Mahmoud Sami,anci Yakoub Simi, were brought in, dressed in plain clothes, and the Under Secretary of State for War read the Khedive's decree of degradation, whereupon the prisoners were removed.

div.head: INTERVIEW WITH THE EGYPTIAN EXILES.
div.p: INTERVIEW WITH THE EGYPTIAN EXILES.

A special correspondent telegraphs :—I have returned from an interview with Arabi and the principal prisoners. Most of them professed pleasure at having, before their departure from Egypt, and for the first time in the course of their confinement, an opportunity of expressing, through a newspaper correspondent, their gratitude to the British public for the interest it has taken in their fate. " Tel-el- Kebir (said Arabi) was the end of my career, but I care nothing for that, because I hope ihe cause I have fought for will survive that day. The English," he added, "are morally—bound to encourage the cause of Egyptian freedom. They will find my country grateul. All Egypt is with me." He reiterated, and with a sarcastic air averred that what he had beard in prison regarding the popular reluc- tance to serve in the new army contrasted greatly with the readiness of thousands to vo'unteer into the army of rebel- lion. About one hundred prisoners will be released imme- diately, twenty of whom will be allowed to retire to their -own estates. Thirty will be simply exiled for five years, and six to specified places in Egyptian territory. A con- siderable number, including the Gagazin prisoners, will be free during good behaviour; but Shemshi gives bail in £5,000, and Abaza in £2,000. Eight of this category were members of the National Chamber. Mahmoud &any is the only prisoner with property. His own wives and four of the other prisoners were downed by Ismail Pasha, of whose harem they once were inmates.
According to a report from Madrid, Ex-Marshal Bazaine is dying; but the rumour requires confirmation.
Arabi .snl his fellow-exiles were taken from Cairo to Suez on Tuesday. All of them "seemed comparatively cheerful."

Another raid has been made on gambling houses in Berlin, and several arrests made. It is stated that the stakes played for in the " clubs" entered by the police were exceptionally high. Six of the 51 persons who have been tried at Prague on the charge of Socialism were acquitted on Saturday ;on was sentenced to two years' hard labour, and 44 others to terms of imprisonment varying from six months to fourteen days.

For the year 1883 the Academy of Medicine, PAris, offer' 17 prizes, the total amount of money being over -80.000 franc. The largest prize is one of 25,000 francs (X 1,000 which will be given to any one who, in the lodgment of the academy, has found a remedy against diphtheria. Loss OF A BARQUE AND THREE OF THE CREW. - Ac- cording to a New York telegram, the barque Goodell, from Liverpool, has been lost. Three of her crew, including the second officer, were drowned. The Allan line steamer Mora- vian, which for the last month has been ashore at-Yarmouth, has now become a total wreck. ANOTHER SUICIDE AT MONTE CARLO. —The Monte Carlo gaming tables are responsible for another suicide. A shop- keeper at Nice lately went to them with 15,000 f. not belong- in e to himself, lost it all, and committed suicide, leaving a letter to his wife explaining what had led him to commit the act. Much -sympathy is felt at Nice for his widow and children, mingled-with indignation against this scandalous institution. It should be mentioned that Monte Carlo pro- fesses to exclude inhabitants of Nice from its tables.

The Tonquin question has entered upon a new phase. On Saturday the Trench Ministers discussed the -expeditionary proposal, and it was determined that the departure of the Chinese troops had rendered an expedition, properly so called, unnecessary. The troops at present in Tonquin are to be slightly reinforced, and if it should be focnd when the Chambers reassemble in January that this force is not suffi- cient the Government is to demand from the Chambers means to canoe the Treaty of 1874 to be respected. STOPPAGE -OF A SWIGS BAWL—A painftil sensation has been caused at'lnterlaken by the failure of the Comntoir d'Escompte cf that place, and the absconding of the manager, Herr Burke, to whose defalcations the failure is said to be due. The capital of the concern wa-s not large; but as it enjoyed excellent credit and bed a large aggregate of small deposits, its suspension will entail severe losses and much suffering on the peasantry of the Bernese Ober- land.

THE ARREST or A PRlNCE.—Prince Krapotkint's arrest is understood to:have led to ,the discovery of some,very im- portant papers, which show that the conspiracyln which he was involved included amongst its members a relative of the Czar and a well-known diplomatist who filled the post of Ambassador at Paris. Whether this gentleman was the Russian Ambassador is not stated, but the papers are re- garded as additional proof of the extensive ramifications of the conspiracy.

The derm;n Government has under consideration a ;pro- posal for rai9ing a licence tax on the manufacture and ,sale of tobacco, which would bring in a net annual revenue of about 031 millions of marks. This sale license tax would I vary from 30 te 00 marks per ar_num, according to sir— sunny ..d rvietgu proaucts wilt oe sus- : ject to a scale of dues. :It is not thought probable, the I Berlin correspondent of the Times gays, that Parliament, :which rejected the tobacco monopoly scheme, will approve this substitute for it.

THE PELTZER TRIAL.—The great Peltzer murder trial lin Brussels came to an end on Friday night, when the two prisoners, Leon and Armand Peltzer, were found guilty, and •sentenced to death. It will be remembered that the victim wac an Antwerp barrister, named Bernays, and the prosecu- tion contended that Armand, being the lover of Madame Bernays, determined to make away with the husband. Possessing great influence over Leon, his brother, he induced him to commit the crime. Leon, it was contended, assumed a series of skilful disguises, and thest, under a fictitious came, wrote to M. Bernays to visit hint for con- sultation at his house in Brussels. Here Leon was declared to have wilfully shot him. The defence, on the other hand, utteely denied that Armand had any other relations with Bernays and his wife, who lived on very bad terms, than that of an intimate friend very solicitous to promote domestic peace. The shooting by Leon was represented to be a pure accident, and the suspicious movements by the brothers after the event were attributed to extreme alarm at what had occurred. The case excited the keenest interest both in Belgium and France, and the evidence was most conflicting. The prosecution, however, succeeded in establishing a case, which was very little shaken by the very clever efforts of the representatives of the prisoners, and it is difficult to see how any other result than conviction could have been arrived at.

div.head: TRAP E NOTES.
div.p: TRAP E NOTES.

At Cinderfurd a mass meeting of the Forest of Dean col- liers pledged themselves to carry out the resolution's adopted by the Leeds conference. It is stated that the miners of South Wales have resolved "not in any case to sanction artificial means for the regula- tion of the coal market," despite the resolution come to by the recent conference at Leeds.

The colliery firemen in the Rhondda, Aberdare, and Merthyr valleys held a delegate meeting at Pontyprid on Saturday to consider the wages question. It was decided that an immediate demand for an advance should be made, it being represented that the men had only been recouped 71 per cent. of the 15 per cent, reduction to which they pre- viously submitted. The disirese among the South Wales tinplate workers continues, and families are still suffering from want of food. The relief committee which has been formed has afforded some aid at one or two places, and Earl Jersey hat aeted with munificence, but the general subscriptions come in slowly, and much more substantial aid is required in order to afford the necessary relief. In celebration of the twentieth anniversary of the forma- tion of the Northumberland Miners' Mutual Association a demonstration was held at Blyth on Moeday. Mr. Burt, M.P., was one of the speakers, and he remarked that he had always endeavoured to avoid strikes, knowing the misery which was Inseparable from such conflicts, and since this Union had been established there had been but one general strike, and that was owing to the refusal of the masters to submit the matter in dispute to arbitration. A Liverpool correspondent says the shipbuilding trade on the Mersey has been very brisk during the year, and the re- turns show an increase of work done both in construction and repair. Messrs, LairSl Pr9tbers, cf Nirklnhead, have launched nine Vessels ofall classes, with an aggregate ton- nage of about 16,000, and an engine power of 2,500 nominal. Messrs. Thomas Royden and Sons have launched vessels with nearly 16,000 aggregate tonnage. Messrs. W. H. Potter and Son launched and completed seven vessels of an aggregate tonnage of 14.280. Other firms have been well occupied, and the prospects of the trade for the coming year are reported to be promising. PRESENTATION TO A TRADE UNION OFFICIAL. At Darlington, on Tuesday night, Mr. Edward Trow, general secretary to the Ironworkers' Association of Great Britain, and one of the joint secretaries of the Arbitration Board of the North of England Iron Trade, was presented with an illuminated address, a marble clock, and a purse of gold raised by subscription among the operative ironworkers and some of the employers. Mr. David Dale, late president of the Board, remarked fifteen years ago a meeting at which employers of labour were present to do honour to a trade unionist would have been impossible. Mr. William Whit- well, of Stockton, chairman, and Mr. Cullen, of Sunderland, vice-chairman of the Arbitration Board, also addressed the gathering. FAILURES AND BILLS OF SALE.—The number of failures in England and Wales gazetted during the week ending Saturday, December 23, was 196. The number in the cor- responding week of last year was 230, showing a decrease of 54, being a net decrease in 1882, to date, of 967. The number of bills of sale published in England and Wales for the week ending December 23, was 273. The number in the corresponding week of last year was 1,130, howing a decrease of 857, being a net decrease in 1882, to date, of 8,422. The number published in Ireland for the same week was 18. The number in the corresponding week of last year was 21, showing a decrease of 3, being a net decrease in 1882, to (We, of 394.—Kemp's Mercantile Gazette.

div.head: BER 30, 1882.
div.p: THE LANCASHIRE COAL AND IRON TRADES: MAN- CHESTER, WEDNESDAY.—Business in the coal trade has naturally to some extent been interrupted during the past week by the holidays, but with the exception of Christmas day there has been no actual er.ra stoppage of work at the pit. Although business has been somewhat of a broken character there is a fair demand coming forward, and the recent improvement noticeable has been well maintained up to the holidays. In the Manchester district prices ara steady at full rates, and generally there is no alteration from late quotations, best coal at the pit mouth remaining at lOs to 10s 6d ; seconds, is 6,1 to 8s Gd; commom house fire coal, 6s 6d to 7s; steam and forge coal, 63 to 63 6d; burgy, 4s 9d to 5s 31; and good ordinary slack, 3s 6d to 4s. The improvement in trade does not appear to have a suffi- ciently established character as to give any general con- fidence with regard to the future. After the hopeful ten- dency towards improvement in the iron trade which had been shown up to the commencement of the holidays, a somewhat depressing effect was produced by the less favourable reports from Glasgow. There was, however, nothing doing to at all test prices, but these were still quoted at 48s to 49s for forge and foundary Lancashire pig iron, 47s 61 to 48s 6d for Lincolnshire, and 49s to 50s for good brands of Derbyshire, less 2A. per cent., delivered equal .o Manchester. None of the local finished iron makers were prlsent-on 'Change, and in the absence of inquiries in the market quotations for bars delivered into the Manchester district can only be said to remain nominally on the basis of £6 103 per ton.

Sr. JAM :S'S (2ND) V. GOLBORNE (2ND).—This match was played at Golborne on Saturday, and resulted in a draw each side scoring a goal. RUSHOLME V. WIDNES.—This match was played on Saturday last, at Widnes, and resulted in a draw in favour of Rusholme by two minor points to nil. OVER WANDERERS (2ND TEAM) T. MIDDLEWICH (A TEAM).—The above clubs met on the ground of the former on Saturday last. The game resulted in a victory for Middlewich by three goals to one. , ST. JAMES'S (HAYDOCK) V. GOLBORNE : IST TEAMS.—The return match between these clubs was played, on Saturday, on the ground of the former, and after a well-contested game resulted in a draw, neither side scoring. BOLTON WANDERERS V. NORTHWICH VICTORTIS.—On Saturday the Northwich club, the preaent holders of the Cheshire challenge cup, made their first appearance in Bol- ton this season, when they met the Wanderers. The Wanderers won by eight goals to nothing. CARLTON V. WIDNES TRUE BLUE (2ND TEAM). This match was played on the ground of the formr, on Saturday, and resulted, after a fast game, in a victory for the Carlton by a goal and a try to nothing. The trios were obtained by C. W. Williams and W. A. Morgan, the latter also kicking tie goal. FALLOWFIELD V. KNUTSFORD (13).—These clubs met at Fallowfield on Saturday last. The visitors brought but nine men, several of their best players being absent, though they obtained useful assistance in four good substitutes. Clarke, Holbrooke, Newton, and Ridgway were absentees on the home side. Knutsford played pluckily in face of their serious disadvantages, especially during the second half. Gregory and Burch were especially brilliant for the winners, each scoring once, the latter also placing a goal.; Faulkner, Swaine (2), Vernon, and W. Worthington each gained tries also, the first-named dropping a neat gaol besides. A pleasant game ended in Fallowfield's faveur with 2 goals, 8 tries, and 6 touchdowns to nil.

RUNCORN (13) V. ST. HELENS RECREAMON (15).—This fixture was played off on Saturday at St. Helens, when a strongly-contested match was played, which ended in a draw. Runcorn, however, laboured under a great disadvan- tage, playing two men abort; also Mason, after a few minutes' play, had to retire, leaving but 12 men to fight out the struggle. Hughes started the oval, which, after a few quick exchanges, rested in touch. Hughes was first in a smart attempt to score, Green tackling him in time. Tight scrimmaging lasted some time in the Recreation's half, and then Cuncliffe, getting hold, made a splendid effort to work his way round, but was soon in the arms of Broady, who stopped further progress. Andrews essayed to get away, but was, after a smart ran, collared by Cuncliffe. The latter player then picked up. Andrews, how- ever, landed him in touch. Soon after the visitors touched down. On the ball being restarted, Gatlevwas to the fore in a fine dribble, getting within an ace of the Recrea- tion's goal line. Pennington, however, saved, punting back. The home team removed the action to the centre field Half-time was then called. On change of ends, fast play was witnessed, Wright defending his goal admirably, the ball travelling all over the .field. Broady, Hughes, and Andrews were frequently conspicuous for the smart runs they made, which proved-ef great service. Play still con- tinued in the home half. Cuncliffe and Gregsen successively attempted to get away, but the sure collaring of the Run. corn forwards, Page, Atherton. and Pownall, made their efforts futile. ' Gatley was again seen dribbling along the field fiaely, and again seemed dangerous; the ball, however, was carried back into neutral ground. Ura to call of time play was seen in the home 25. A pleasant game ended in a draw, St. Helens scoring 3 minor points., Runcorn nil. Teams—Runcorn: Wright, full back; Broady and Jackson three-quarter backs; Andrews and 11 Hughes (captain), Mason, Page, Atherton, Gatley, Mullaney, C Pownall, Lewis and Ainsworth forwards. St. Helens: Pennington and Taylor backs ; Ross and Gregson three-quarter backs; Taylor and Cuncliffe half-backs; forwards: Green, Fernley, Farr, Roberts, Finn, Forster, Rankin, Slater, and McLoughlin.

div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.
ASHTON.

SUDDEN DEATH OF AN INFANT: INQUEST--On Wednes- day afternoon an inquest was held at the Robin Hood Hotel, Asliton, on the body of Catherine Wilding, one month old, daughter of Thomas Wilding, residing in Chapel-street, who died very suddenly on Sunday morning last. The inquest was held before Mr. J. B. Edge, coroner, of INianchester, who has been conducting similar enquiries in this district since the resignation of Mr. Driffield. The evidence showed that the child had enjoyed good health since birth, and continued to do so up to Saturday last. On being taken to bed at night the child appeared in its usual condition, but early on Sun- day morning it gave the appearance of being unwell, and it was taken to the surgery of Dr. Latham. About two hours afterwards the child suddenly expired as if in a fit of con- vulsions.—The jury returned a verdict of "death from natural causes—probably convulsions."

ASHTON CONGREGATIONAL SCROOL : TEA MEETING AND PRESENTATION.—The annual tea meeting in connection with the Ashton Congregational Church Schools was held on Christmas Day, in the afternoon of which day also the juvenile scholars were treated with coffee, buns, and Onnges. About five o'clock a large number of the parents and friends set down to a most excellent tea, after which Mr. C. Latham presided. A programme of songs, recitations, dz.c., was ex- cellently gone through, several anthems by the choir being greatly appreciated. A pleasing feature of the evening's proceedings was the presentation of a handsome and splendid portrait album to Mrs. Wilson, wife of the esteemed pastor, the Rev. H. Wilson. The presentation was made by the chairman on behalf of the members of Mrs. Wilson's class, and he alluded to the respect La which she was held by her scholars. Mrs. Wilson was taken by surprise at the gift, and briefly acknowledged her thanks, being much affected. Throughout the meeting was an enjoyable and interesting one, and an address by the Rev. H. Wilson, on the duty parents owed to their children in looking after them and their welfare whilst away from school, was very attentively listened to. The customary votes of thanks brought the proceedings to a close.

ANNUAL EXAMINATION OF SCHOLARS AT THE CHURCH ASSOCIATION SUNDAY SCHOOLS.—The annual examination of scholars in religious education and the annual distribu- tion of prizes to meritorious scholars in connection with the Ashton Church Association Sunday Schools took place in the upper room of the Protestant Institute, Heath-lane, cn Monday last (Christmas Day). A large number of parents and friends were present, and manifested the utmost interest, which appears to increase each year, in the proceedings. At two o'clock in the afternoon the scholars were marshalled

into processional order and proceeded to the Lecture Hall, where they were received by Mr. C. Hodgkinson, one of the teachers, who had arranged for them to occupy one side of the room, and the parents and friends the other. The hymn "Hark the glad sound "was then sung, after which were the usual school prayers. Mr. C. Hodgkinson then gave a brief address, and on behalf of the committee and teachers gave all present a hearty welcome and wished them a truly happy Christmas. The scholars in each class were afterwards put through an examination in order to show the success of the past year in instilling into the minds of the children a knowledge of scripture, divine truth, and Bible Protestantism. The examination was conducted by the teachers, and the answers from the children were most satisfactory, shGwing that they were thoroughly acquainted with the teachings of the Bible, the 39 Articles of the Church of England. the Ten Commandments, Reformation History, and the Church Catechism. The 118th Psalm, "This day is God's," was then sung, after which a number of book prizes were dis- tributed by Mr. C. Hodgkinson to the meritorious scholars. Mrs. Marsh then gave each of the scholars a mince pie, over 150 books, cards, and pies being thus presented. In addition, Mrs. Marsh also very kindly gave to each person in the room a mince pie, which by alt was greatly enjoyed. The proceedings were of a very harmonious and enjoyable character from ;beginning to end, an everything passed off as successful as was anticipated. The meeting was brought to a close with the singing of the hymn "Glory to Thee my God this night."

div.p: ALTRINCHAM.

1 RUNCORI: SprwaNT. .1,........,,...-- --____ —A closely-contested match was played at Runcorn on Saturday between these clubs. The Wanderers set the ball going, Larkin cleverly returned past the centre flag, the ball going into touch. On the throw out, J. Pownall and HelsbV indulged in long punts, play being carried on for some time in neutral ground, and effective passings took place between W. Pownall and H. Speakman. Andrews, who then gat close to the Wanderers' lines before he was stopped, did some good service. Boardman and Matthews moved in the other direction, Bunbavand and Clarke collaring smartly, thus confining action some time in the Wanderers' 25; after which Davies and Unsworth broke away with the dribble and matters began to look serious. The home full back, missing his kick, a scrimmage ensued on the home line. Stubbs and Larkin removed the struggle to mid field, and packed scrimmages were of frequent occurrence. Dunbavand came through the pack grandly, and got well on the "go " before he was brought down. Boardman and Bolton showed good form in smart runs which proved of good service. Larkin from a pass by W. Pownall compelled Wanderers to touch down. After the oval was again in play Clarke, Cox, and Dunbavand were to the fore with a nice dribble, the ball going into touch in goal, and play ensued in neutral ground. Barnes, Davies, and Boardman having been instrumental in registering a touch down, half time was called. J. Pownall re-started the ball from centre, and fast play followed. Home team played well. The ball, however, was propelled over the Runcorn line, and was touched down by Speakman. Following the drop out, Boardman made s fine run in the home 25, from which Larkin and Potinall advanced into Wanderers' 25, Cox grounding the ball over the line. The point was, however, disputed, on plea of the home umpire ruling offside, which proved incorrect. Scrimmage being formed in the Wanderers' 25, play lasted some time here, and Wm. Pownall dribbled the ball over the line, Jones falling on it. Pownall then took the place but failed to add the premier point. No 'other matter of importance being registered to call of no side, Runcorn won a strongly contested match. Score: 1 try, two minor points, to Wanderers' three minor points. :roams :-Runcarn : Whinvates, full back ; Speakman, Larkin, and J. Pownall (captain), three-quarter back§. W,Focnall and Hankinson half-backs. Dunbavand, Jones, Cox, Gittins, Burrows, Clarke, Stubbs, Ford and Andrews for- wards. Wanderers: Helsby, back. Matthews and Board- man three-quarter backs, Maywell, and Bolton (captain), half-backs. Barnes, Speakman; Davies, liumphries, Foster, Gilbert, Garretty, Sudlow, and Ussworth, forwards.

It is stated in the annual report of the Altrincham Wes- leyan Sunday School Band of Rope that the society was never more flourishing than at the present. The total num- ber of members is 813, and of these 127 are scholars in the Sunday schoel. INQUEST.—An inquest was held at the Woolpack Inn, on Saturday, by Mr. Yates, coroner, touching the death of Patrick Skell, aged two years and ten months. Bridget Skell, wife of a labourer in Cimpel-street, stated that the deceased, who up to that time had never had a day's illness, was taken ill on Thursday about noon. About fire o'clock he appeared much worse, but they did not think a great deal of it. A neighbour named Lan Muloney came in about nine o'clock, and said the child was dying. She went to Mr. Broadbent, relieving officer, for a medical order, and on returning home found the child was dead. All the jury agreed that the child had been well cared for, and a verdict of "Death from natural causes " was returned. KNUTSFORD.

The Middievrich magistrates have committed a man named Ralph Percival to the Knutsford Sessions on a charge of geese stealing. The owner of the geese was awakened in the night by a noise which proceeded from his pen. He went down to examine the cause, and found two of them gone and an cid clog left in exchagge. A clograaker des- cribes the clog as one similar to a pair ho made for the prisoner a short time ago, and other incriminating evidence •was supplied ky the police, who found a blood-stained Ee in his possession and in h;.O h.,ase some

A gentleman 'travelling in a sleeping car from Nice to Marseilles was strangled at St. Thomas. His pocket was emptied by the murderer, who has got away. His watch and a valuable diamond ring have also disappeared. On Tuesday evening, in the Reichsallon Theatre, Berlin —a sort of music hall—the eldest of three young French acrobats, named Forbee, suddenly expired on the stage, having exerted himself too violently during his gymnastic performance. It is semi-officially announced that there is no intention on the part of Earl Spencer to abandon his post. The special resident magistrates had an interview with His Excellency at the Viceregal Lodge on Thursday, in reference to the state of the country. Two Liverpool pawnbrokers were on Thursday convicted and fined for doing business en Sundays, and the magistrates remar'ked that if further cases were brought before them, a line of £5 would be inflicted. This announcement will probably la.rgeiy Cenirlbute,to the suppression of the illegal and mischievous practice. The adjourned annual sessions of Lancashire County Justices was held at Preston on Thursday. The County Treasurer's estimate of the funds iequired for the business of the county from November 30, 1882, to the end of August, 1883, showed a decrease of between £17,000 and £lB,OOO on the preceding year's figures. A committee was appointed to prepare a new basis for fair and equal county rates. AN UNREHEARSED SCENE.—At the Plymouth Theatre Royal, the other afternoon, an accident ccuurred which was very near causing the postponement of the pantomime. The borough surveyor had been inspecting the water service of the building, when, through a defect in the valve, the "water curtain" suddenly rained down its flood upon the stage. A rehearsal was in progress at the time, and the effect of the unexpected deluge upon the actors and actresses may be imagined. The "water curtain" is an arrangement of pipes in front of the drop." by means of which an immense quantity of water can be poured, so as to place a liquid barrier between the stage and the audience in case of an outbreak of fire. When this immense fountain threw its " damper " upon the proceedings there was a general stampede; actors and actresses were scattered in all directions, many of them wet to the skin, and the majority of the ladies greatly alarmed. Fortunately, however, there was very little of the new and costly scenery within reach of injury, though one or two of the scenes were wetted. Had the accident occurred when scenery was in course of pre- paration on the stage the production of the pantomime must have been delayed. As it was the water was quickly turned Off, and the only serious inconvenience was the postpone- ment of a " scene " rehearsal which had been arranged for the evening. div.head: NANTWICFI.
div.p: NANTWICFI.

At a meeting of the Nantwich Local Board, a proposition was made by Mr. Pierce with a view to prevent the fire- engine of the Board going more than two miles out of the town. The Board, however, decided to abide by the existing arrangement, whereby the services of the engine and brigade might attend fires in the country whenever a request of the kind was made, a charge of one guinea being made for the use of the engine, and the payment of the firemen according to a scale of charges which has been in force for some time. NORTH WICH.

A carrier of Hartford, named John Sutton, was charged, on Tuesday, before the Northwich magistrates, with cruelty to a pony. It appeared that the inspectors of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals had previously sum- moned two men at Warrington ix respect of the same animal. The defendant promised to destroy the pony, and the case was adjourned. A man, named George Booth, has been remanded, at Northwich, on a charge of stealing a number of turkeys and geese from farmhouses. None of the birds have been found, but when the prisoner was apprehended, a constable found a quantity of newly-washed bed tick, which had been taken away along with the turkeys and geese.

div.head: ORMSKIRK.
div.p: ORMSKIRK.

At Ormskirk, on Tuesday, Caleb S. Hilton, M.D., of Soutbport, was committed for trial on a charge of having stolen a watch from the house of a Scarisbrick farmer whose children he bad been attending professionally.

RAINFORD. ASSAULTING A POLICEMAN AT RAINFORD.—Wm. Fair- hurst was on Friday charged, on remand, at the St. Helens Police Court, with having assaulted P.C. Ratcliffe, at Rain- ford, on the Oth August. 1881.—Mr. Swift defended.—The particulars of the charge in this case appeared in our last week's issue. On the present occasion it was urged in de- fence that the constable- had used unnecessary violence, having used his staff pretty freely against the prisoner.— The Mayor, who presided, said the bench had no doubt an assault had been committed on the officer, and if the pri- soner had received severe usage he had thmself to blame. Ile was fined 20s, and costs.

div.head: WIN WICK.
div.p: WIN WICK.

LEIGH PARISH CHURCH.—A Cross has been placed in the Leigh Parish Church, defrayed by su'Jscriptions collected by Mr. J E. Worsley, F.S.A., Winwick, historian of the church, in memory of Sir Thomas Tyldesley, "the hero of Wigan-lane." The inscription runs thus: "At the east end of the north aisle, formerly the Tyldesley Chantry of Saint Nicholas, within this ancient parish church, resteth the body of Sir Thomas Tyldesley, of Tyldesley, Morleys, Myerscough, in this county, Knight, a General in His Majesty's Army, and Governor of Lichfield, who was slain figLting pliantly for his Royal Master, under James, Seventh Earl of Derby, in the battle of Wigan Lane, near this place, on the twenty-fifth dny of August, 1651." With this are engraved the arms of Sir Thomas.

WINSFORD. TAQUIDATION.—A statutory meeting of the creditors of Charles Lee, draper, High-street, Winsford, was held at the Home Trade Association Rooms, York-street, Manchester, on Friday last. The statement of affairs presented showed liabilities secured, £449 ; liabilities unsecured, 959 ; and assets, estimated at £307. Liquidation was unanimously resolved upon, and Mr. George Mountain, of 39, York-street, Manchester, was appointed trustee. Messrs. Juhn Cooke and Sons, solicitors, Winsford, were entrusted with the re- gistration of the resolutions. CM2IfinIAS AT Wll-tP6ll.ls.—The usual attractions of this season of the year were somewhat minimised. Either the weather, or greater home attractions, or something prevailed. Early in the morning certain chapel and church choirs went round to leading houses to carol, and when the day turned out wet the four churches held out their attraction and re- ceived fairly goodicongregations. The chapels later on pro- vided; and the " Army " did its share. Station-road Pri- mitive and Mission Room (Free Church) had entertainments for their Sunday schools, and by speech or song endeavoured to enlist the sympathies of their peoples. One may fairly judge how a place will keep its Christmastide by the market preparations. The way the butchers, grocers, &c., set off their respective stores, the arnottas of Christmas beef, &c., displayed, was a test of the thrift, good management, and providence of a town. Winsford was no exception. De- spite the number out of work, the hope arises that many were able to avail themselves of good Christmas cheer. CHRISTMAS DINNER TO AGED PEOPLE.—The design which entered the minds of one or two gentlemen of Wins- ford some months ago to provide a good dinner for the poor and old people of Winsford at Christmas time took a definite form when they began the pleassnt evenings.' The concerts, so-called, produced about £7. and this was supple- mented by generous dosations of various ladies and gentle- men in the vicinity, whose subscriptions—when 103 or above—we append :—Messrs. Stubbs Brothers, £5; Messrs. J. Verdin and Sons, £5, and their employes £4 10s; Mr. T. Knowles, MP., £2; Mr. J. D. Kay, J.P., £3 Sc; Lord Delamere, £2; Mr. J. H. Cooke, £1; Mr. James Stubbs, £1 ; Mr. J. R. Armstrong, £1; Mr. T. W. Johnson, 11; Rev. Canon France-Hayhurst, £1; Mrs. A. Dudley, £1 ; Mrs. Captain Turner, £1; Hon. W. F. Tollomache, £1; Hr. T.

Beatley, SI ; Rev. C. Cay, LL.B., 10.5; Mr. C. Kay, J.P.. 103 ; Mr. R. G. Cross, 10s; Mr. E. Leigh, lOs ; Mr. Joseph Slater (Mayor of Over), 105 Oh; Mr. J. H. Billington, 10s; Mr. H. Barnett, 15s; to which must be added small sums amounting to £39 us 6i, and the proceeds of the concert& This formed the fund for this benevolent project. The committee invited 300 persons above 55 years of age to come to the Town Hall on Tuesday at one o'clock, when a sub- stantial dinner of roast beef and vegetables, followed by plum pudding and coffee or tea ad lib, was provided, to which it need not be added the old people did ample justice. During the dinner, Mr. F. Vernon's string band played selections of music with considerable effect. With such proficiency did these musicians perform their share of the entertainment, that the waiters—consisting of many of the sprightliest young ladies of the town, with a sprinkling of their mammas—almost carried the plates of roast beef and plum pudding to the inspiriting strains of the band. After all had satisfied themselves, the tables were cleared for a concert. Here Mr. Jos. Slater (Mayor) occupied the chair. In the course of a few remarks he said he felt pleased to see so many old people in full course of enjoyment at this time when they were reminded of the coming of a Saviour to save our race.—Mr. Eilisor, the treasurer, read the report,. which showed that after all expenses had been cleared there would be a balance in hand, so they proposed to add a soup kitchen arid coal gifts to needy persons in the town during the slack time of this winter. This is the more welcome news since there are a great number at present out of work in Winsford owing to the depression in the salt trade.—Mr. Dunn read "Christmas in a London attic," which proved very accept- able. Miss Woodyatt sang "Darby and Joan " very tel- lingly. One of the diners—John McDean, gave a song, and was followed by Mr. Cromack, whose song so amused the audience that he received an encore, when he gave " Three little pigs." Mr. Kennerley, one of the " string band," gave a cornet solo, variations on "In my cottage near the wood!! The song of the "Deaf women," by Miss Ninis, was warmly received, so she repeated part as an encore. A duet, " The wrens," by Misses Greenhalgh, was sweetly rendered. The Rev. W. T. Symons gave a recitation of his own composi- tion, "The gentleman," which was followed by votes of thanks to Mr. Ellison, the treasurer, and Mr. F. B. Cooke, the honorary secretary, by the Rev. E. Woodyatt. To Mayor, musicians, waiters, and carvers, which Mr. E. Leigh proposed very warmly, and Mr. H. Barnett seconded. The most aged invited was upwards of 90, but his infirmity pre- vented his being present. It was hoped the three old women of Whitegate would have been present, but death snatched them off two weeks ago. Their united ages was nearly 280 years. ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.

A marriage is arranged, and will take place in January, between Mr. W. Rovlance Court, the Manor, Middlewich, Cheshire, barrister-at-law (Inner Temple), and Miss Mary C. Walker, eldest daughter of Sir Andrew Barclay Walker, Gateacre Grange, Lancashire. The marriage is announced to take place on January 16th, between Mr. Richard Marcus Brooke, eldest son of Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., of Norton Priory, Cheshire. and Alice, eldest daughter of John Sambrooke, Crawley, Esq., of Stockwood-Laton, Beds. It is generally understood that the West Cheshire Liberals will adopt Mr. Davie Duncan, Gayton Hall, Neston, as the second Liberal candidate for West Cheshire. Mr. Duncan recently announced that if invited he would be prepared to contest the constituency along with Mr. Tomkinson, who has already unsuccessfully fought West Cheshire against his cousin, Mr. Tollemache, M.P. A meeting of delegates from various parts of the division will shortly be held to consider Mr. Duncan's candidature. _

_ -Camas DISEASE IN CHESHIRE.—The Chief Constable of Cheshire (Lieut.-Colonel Hamersley) reports that during; the past week there have been no fresh outbreaks of pleuro- pneumonia. A farm in the township of Bridge Trafford is still infected with the disease. The county remains free from foot and mouth disease. There have been no fresh cases of swine fever; but four farms in the townships of Altrincham, Clifton, Weaverham, and Whitley Superior remain infected. Sheep scab exists on twelve farms in the townships of Acton, Adlington, Alpraham, Brereton, Beeston, Bigley-cum-Gatehouse, Bromborough, Norton. Newton-by-Frodsham, Tarporley, Ridley, and Rushton, 83 sheep being under treatment. CHESTER SAY/NGS BANK.—The annual meeting of this trustees and managers of the Chester Savings Bank was held on Wednesday, the Venerable Archdeacon Darby pre- siding. It appealed from the statement of accounts that: the total amount deposited during the 65 years of the bauk's existence had been £1,728,883, and the aggregate repay- ments during the same period £1,545,681, leaving £183,202 due to 3,983 depositors. Assets of the bank on the 20th November last: amount in the hands of the Commissioners for the rtduction of the national debt, £182,932; amount of separate surplus fund, £380; amount in the old bank in the name of the treasurer, £974 15s 10d; total cash assets, £184,287; deducting £183,202, there remains a cash sur- plus of £1,084.. INCREASE OF PAUPERISM IN CHESHIRE.—At the meeting of the Chester Board of Guardians on Wednesday, the Chairman (Mr. Henry Davies) said that, notwithstanding all their exertions for the past seven or eight years, they had not, he thought, discovered the right way of working. Every year hiought an increase of pauperism, and for this there was some cause which they could not fathom. Mr. Essrey attributed the increase of pauperism to the nature of the weather which ha s prevailed for the past few years, and to the fact that the agriculturists of this country were now working not only on the cheapest but the most expe- ditious system. Less manual labour was required, and the thousands of Irish labourers who used to come ever 'were not wanted now. Wort( bAa in proportion to the increase or population, and the question of improving the emigration system would have to be considered. . _ _

At the Eddislinry Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Lord Tollemache (in the chair) and other magistrates, Peter Booth, a labourer, of Northwich, was charged with night poaching in Vale Royal Park, on the 21st inst., and taking rabbits, the property of Lord Delamere. It appeared that William Arnold, gamekeeper, John Dickinson, a farmer, with assistants, where watching about two o'clock on the morning in question at Morton, in Lord Delamere's park at Vale Royal, when they suddenly came across a gang of nine men. Most of the men had bags apparently full of game on their backs. They were walking along the park itt the direction of the Greenbank failway station. Hear Arnold and his assistants subsequently met them. The keepers made a rush on the poachers, and a desperate tight ensued, sticks and stones being freely used. The keepers being out- numbered they could only secure the prisoner, the other men decamped, leaving behind the a number of stakes, nets, and bags, in addition to four formidable-bludgeons. In the bags were a long gauze net and stakes for setting it to- gether. with 21 rabbits freshly killed. Booth now said ,that that was the first time in his life that be had been up for poaching, and he hoped the Bench would deal leniently with him.—The magistrates committal him to take his trial at the assizes.

div.head: APPALLING DISASTER AT BRADFORD
div.p: APPALLING DISASTER AT BRADFORD

FALL OF A MILL CHIMNEY. NEARLY THIRTY LIVES LOST. On Thursday morning, a horrible accident occurred at Sir Henry Ripley's mill, in Spring Mill-street, Bradford, which has resulted in the death, it is feared, of at least thirty people, whilst the number injured cannot be estimated. At eight o'clock on Thursday morning, the majority of the workpeople in the spinning and drawing-rooms left the works to partake of breakfast, but in ten minutes afterwards the whole neighbourhood was startled by hearing a rumbling noise-as if there was thunder in the distance, and immediately afterwards there was a terrific crash, and the rooms named above were completely demolished, doing thousands of pounds worth of damage. The moaning, shrieking, and crying of the helpless and of the injured was something horrible, and it is feared that there is a larger number underneath the debris than was at first anticipated. During the morning the police, assisted by a large number of workpeople, were continually conveying the injured from the rubbish and placing them in cabs and other conveyances, so that they could be removed to the infirmary. Information was sent to a large number of medical gentlemen, and about a dozen were soon on the spot. At 11 o'clock the sight was a most sickly and horrible one, as what the workpeople, consisting of about IGO, were removing the debris, little girls and young women could be heard crying for water and their parents. At the base of the building it was known that a man, an overlook-er, in company with giree others were in the ruins, but it was a hopeless case as no one could get to them. The cravings for water were horrible, and many a man there with a stout heart was willing to rush into any danger so that they could give a helping band, but it was of no use, as the weight that was upon these poor creatures was so large. Chief , Constable Withers, Superintendent Layeock. and Inspector Dobson, with a large number of polide officers were present to keep back the crowd which was an orderly one. The police were very assiduous in their endeavours to render what assistance they possibly could. Cabs and carts wer4ll continually running to and from the Infirmary -with those that were extricated. In one instance a mother of two girls who were engaged in the fatal rooms upen hearing that her children were under the debris, rushed about the yard, and then into the street like one mad and then prayed to God that He would spare her "bairns.' At the Infirmary the scene was also one of great grief, for there was a large crowd of people anxiously waiting to see ' the injured, in many cases those that had been conveyed there could not be identified, nor could they g'ir° anY in- formation. We understand that the chimney stack was erected some twenty years ago, and since that time it has been lowered, and on Thursday, it-was stated by marl"' that the chimney was seen to sway- when the wind was b owbeen ing persona, mainly young girls, have ' hard. Dear Sir,—From a feeling of deep gratitude to you, and a desire to benefit those who suffer, I beg to inform yoa of the great benefit I have derived from wearing your " Magnetaire " Appliances. When I came to consult you I was suffering much from indigestion and nervous action, so much so that I feared an attack of epilepsy or St. Vitus Dance. I was, indeed, distressed ; now, thank God, the nervous action has greatly subsided. I attend to my duties with more ease and comfort, the digestive organs have con- siderably improved, and I look forward to a return of health and vigour. I would strongly reccommend your Appliances to all who suffer, as I am quite convinced of their efficacy in the treatment of all nervous complaints and of diseases in general. With very kind regards,—l remain, my dear sir, yours sincerely, ROBI. HAYDON DIGNUM, Mr. R. Lonsdale.

51, Legh-street, Ifair:iTi-gio-n., October, 25th, 1882. Dear Sir,—After wearing the Magnetic Belt, for pains in the body, I am pleased to 3ay I am considerably better, and so far can recommend it to my friends. Believe me to be—Yours truly, Mr. R. Lonsdale ALFRED PERRIS.

div.p: ACUTE PAINS_ IN THE BACK.

64, Priestly-street, Warrington, Oct. 20th, 1882. Dear am very glad to say that I have in a very short time received a great amount of relief from wearing your "Magnetaire " Belt. .1 was at the time of visiting you suffering acute pains in the back, so much so, that I was afraid I should have to leave my work ; but thanks to your appliance, I have not done so, and my back is se much better that I shall always recomment it, and be pleased to answer inquiries.—Yours faithfully, Mr. R. Lonsdale. THOMAS GAUNT.

WEAR SPINE. 6, Atherton's Quay, Warrington, Oct. 19th, 1882. Dear Sir,—You will be pleased to her that my son has quite recovered from weakness of the spine since wearing your " Magnetaire " Appliances. He gradually began to improve from the first day of wearing them, and now gets about comfortably. Wishing you succes—l am, yours truly, Mr. R. Lonsdale. LEVI JAMES.

SCIATICA AND RHEUMATISM. 22, Ludlow-street, Lower Grangetown Cardiff, Ist December, 1882. Dear Sir —I wish to express my great satisfaction, and to testify to the benefit I have derived from the" Magnetaire " Appliances I purchased of you a fortnight since. After a day's trial I felt a glow throughout my whole system, and commenced to lose the pain, in my hip and knee, from which I had suffered acutely for three years, and had tried all sorts of temedies, and speni many pounds, without re- ceiving the least benefit; but I can safely say, after wearing the "Magnetaire " a few days, I have since been entirely free from pain. I shall spare no trouble in recommending your Appliances to anyone I may know suffering.—l remain, yours very truly, DAVID WILLIAMS. Mr. R. Lonsdale.

• PARALYSIS. • Rodney Wharf, Newport, Dear Sir,—l have worn one of your " Magnetaire " Appliances with the following satisfactory results. For over four years I had been paralysegi partly down one side. My arm and band I could scarcely raise, losing nearly all power, and the circulation throughout my system was very poor, my spirits were much depressed, and my nerves being completely prostrated, my life at times seemed a burden to me. I began to despair of ever getting better. I can scarcely express how thankful I am for the marvellous change your Appliances have effected in me. My arm and hand I can now use freely. My appetite is good, can sleep well and rise early in the morning to do my duties. I had tried other appliances with no beneficial results. Should anyperson inquire of me, I shall be happy to recommend your " Magnetaire."—Yours gratefully, Mr. R. Lonsdale. W. THOMAS.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, DECEMBER 30, liB2.

As this is the last Examiner which will be published this year, it may not be unprofitable to bring before our readers a few of the leading events of the past twelve months, which, not Only. in England, but in other countries, have been marked by considerable unrest. Trade, on the whole, has everywhere been good, and the prospects are bright for the coming' year; but in political matters there has been much uneasiness, not only here but elsewhere, though at the present time all is perfectly quiet. The legislation of the past session has not been prolific in many measures, but what have been entered on the statute book may be fairly trusted to produce good fruit. Par- liament opened in February, and a number of bills were promised from the Throne, including one relating to county government, another to rivers conservancy, a third to bank- ruptcy and patent law reform, a fourth to ' Criminal code reform, a fifth to educational reform, and so on; whilst it was further pro- posed to reform the rules of Parliamentary Procedure. The Procedure Rules have been Passed, but the measures promised in the Queen's Speech have had to give place to Other and more urgent matters relating to Ireland. At the beginning of the session a good deal of time was needlessly wasted. For instance, the debate on the Address occupied no less than seven days, and a very much Shorter period should have sufficed. Again, the OPposition caused unnecessary delay in the transaction of the business set before. Parlia- . hient by refusing to allow the duly-elected them.ber for Northampton (Mr. BRIDLAUGH) to take the oath and his seat, thereby depriving the constituency of a representative. These matters disposed of, the House at once turned its attention to the reform of the Pro- cedure Rules, from which, however, it was nioved by an unexpected circumstance "t he House of Lords, by a substantial ~./hajority, passed a resolution submitted by Lord DONOUGHMORE, declaring it desirable that a Select Committee should be appointed to inquire into the working of the Irish Land .i.ket of the previous year, and the PREMIER • It necessary to counteract this; hence 'lle House of Commons passed a motion itlractically censuring the Lords, and declaring zue appointment of a Select Committee flexpethent. Many important personages have been removed by death during the year just closing. Churchmen have to lament the loss of the Archbishop of CANTERBURY and Dr. PUSEY ; the Wesleyan community has lcst one of its brightest ornaments in Dr. GERVASE SMITH ; and by other Dissenters Dr.. HANNA will be missed. Of our legis- lators the most notable death is that oF Mr. ! ON SLOW, of Tichborne Claimant notoriety. From the English Bench, Sir JOHN HOLKER has been taken away after enjoying but a short spell of promotion; and from the Irish I Bar, the familiar form of Mr. IT DONOUGH, who played an important part in many State prosecutions, has been removed. Naturalists must all regret the death of Dr. DARWIN, and the Medical Profession that of Sir R. CIIRISTISON. The ranks of the poets have I been thinned by LONGFELLOW and DANTE GABRIEL ROSSETTI ; novelists, by HA.RRISON AINSWORTH ; artists, by JOHN LINNEL ; sculptors, by Senor DUPE; and warriors, by Generals KAUFMANN and SKOBELEFF. This brief record would be incomplete without mentiop of the name of General GARIBALDI, whose death all lovers of freedom deplore.

Closure debate resumed in the Commons, .111. d a second time was it interrupted, on this occasion by the dreadful murders of Lord FREDERICKeCAVENDISH and Mr. BURKE in Phcenix Park, Ireland. These assassinations caused such a deep sensation throughout the country, that the Government was compelled to at once introduce a Bill for the repression of ,crime in Ireland, followed by another dealing with arrears of rent, which was a source of trouble to the tenant farmers. Both measures passed the Commons. The Lords passed the Crimes Bill without a murmur ; but the Arrears Pill was vehemently opposed on account of its alleged confiscatory character. The leader of the Opposition, Lord SALISBURY, would, indeed, have thrown out the measure altogether, but he was deserted by his followers. It seemed at one time as if there would be a conflict between the two Houses over this bill, but the PREMIER showed a spirit of conciliation, and the difficulties were satisfactorily bridgecl. over. The Irish legilation led to the retire- ment from the Government of Earl COWPER (Lord Lieutenant of Ireland) and of Mr. FORSTER (Chief Secretary), the latter de- claring he would be no party to the release from Kilmainham prison, in which they had for some months been incarcerated, of Messrs. i PARNELL, DILLON, and O'KELL).-, though j they had promised to exert their influence on ' the side of law and order. The places of the Lord Lieutenant and Chief Secretary are now filled by Lord SPENCER and Mr. TREVELYAN, ' the latter succeeding Lord F. CAVENDISH. The chief measures passed during the present i session were an Electric Lighting Bill, a I settled Land Bill, a Married Women's Property I Bill, and Scotch Educational Endowment: Bill. The Procedure Rules were reformed I during the autumn. Whilst Parliament was 1 sitting, Mr. BRADLAUGH was returned a' third time for Northampton ; and MICHAEL 1 DAVITT was elected fof Meath, but being a I convict he was unable to sit in the House. j A large number of Irish members, it should 1 he stated, were suspended for obstruction during the session, which leads us to remark that the greatest troubles England has experienced during the year have been in Ireland, where a series of horrible crimes must for ever darken the pages of its history. Notable amongst these are the murders in Phcenix Park, already alluded to, and the murder of the Joyce family at Maamtrasna These were evidently the outcome of secret societies ; and that the ramifications of these societies extended to England was, we think, shown by the seizure of arms at Clerkenwell, pointing to Fenian plots on an extensive scale. SUDDEN DELTII AT WIDNES.—On. Tuesday Mr. Price held an inquest at Widnes on the body of Richard Bibby, a child sixteen months old, son of Edward Bibby, labourer, living at 25, Ann-street West. It appeared that about four o'llock on Saturday afternoon the child, apparently in its usual health, was put to bed, but four hours later the mother found it dead and cold. A verdict to the effect that death resulted from natural causes, probably convulsion!, was recorded.

A RUNAWAY PAUPER. AND THE GUALDIANS' CLOTHES. —Before Mr. James Reynolds and Mr. James Brundrit, at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, Mary Jane Ann Gallagher, a pauper, was charged with running away from the Workhouse On the 3rd October, and taking With her clothes to the value of LI. It seemed the prisoner received leave of absence for a certain period, and she did not return. She had with her clothing belonging to the Guardians of the Runcorn Union. She was apprehended at Northwich, and was now sentenced to two months hard labour. •
