A HALTON CHARITY.—On St. Thomas's Day,, the usual charities, in connection with Halton parish, amcfrwting to £2l, were distributed at the Norton Arms. The Rev. J. Lockwood, the vicar, occupied the chaiT, and he was ported by Messrs. C. L. Evans (agent to Sir Richd Brooke), John Smith (one of the surviving trustees of Mrs. Easton's charity), Hugh Rowe and W. Nixon. The vicar's and churchwarden's "coal charity" will be dispensed during January. ASSAULT ON A CONSTABLE AT DlTTON.—Patrick Brody- was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Johnson- street, Ditton, on Saturday night, and also with assaulting P.C. Coutts. The prisoner, who was drunk, was creating a disturbance, and the officer forcibly placed him in his own house. Whilst there he remeved his coat, and, again issu- ing forth, he attacked the officer, kicking him severely on the legs. The prisoner was sent to gaol for a month. THE RATES OF LANCASHIRE TONV.N.S.—At the monthly meeting of the Michiletcn and Tonge Improvement Commis- ' sioners, held on Tuesday night, Mr. R. Robinson presiding, Mr. A. Mills submitted a statement showing the rates levied in 15 Lancashire towns, as compared with the rate of 2s. CI in'the pound for Middleton, on the basis of a two-thirds assessment Accrington, 3s. ; Ashton, 23. 81.; Bury, 4.3.; Blackburn (including poor rate), 53. 101.; Bolton, 3.3. ; Burnley, 33.; Chorley, 43. 21.; Heywood, 45.; Old- ham, 35.; Over Darwen, 3e. Oct.; Preston, 3. 21.; Rochdale, ss. Td.; St. Helenis, 2s. 91.; Stalybridge, 23. 101.; and Sri- ford, 43. 2d.

CIIRISTSIA.S DRINKING AT AUNCOR I.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Thomas Butters was fined 10s. and costs for beiog drt;nk and disorderly in PQnketh-lane, on Sunday night. The case was proved by P.C. Davenport.— For a similar offence committed in Church-street, on Satur- day night, and proved by P.S. Whalley, Daniel Donevan, a Cornish sailor, was fined 103. and Ns. 101 costs.—A like penalty was imposed on Mary Ann Jones, who was con- victed of being drunk and disorderly in Penketh-lano, on Christmas Eve, on the evidence of LS. Whalley. EXCITING STRUGGLE IN HALTON-LoAD.—Oa Tues- day, at Runcorn Petry Sessions, Thomas Eaton Fowler was charged in custody with being drunk and disorderly in Wood-row, on Christmas Day; and also with assaulting P.C. Noden.—About twenty minutes past ten on the night of the day named, P.C. Noden went to the Half-way House, Halton-road, where he found the prisoner knocking with violence at the back door. When his pleasant occupation was interfered with he struck two men, and seizing hold of Noden, swung him round and rolled him on the ground. An exciting struggle of ten minutes' duration ensued. At the end of that period Noden mastered his opponent, and placed the " snaps " upon his wrists. He was then conveyed to the police station.—The prisoner was fined 53. and costs on the first charge, and 10s. and costs on the second.

A FILTHY LODGING DEN AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Tette- Sessions on Tuesday, before Mr. William Benkes and Mr. :Tohn Brundrit, Luke Cavanagh, of Back Cooper-street, was brought up under a warrant, charging him with keeping an unregistered lodging-house on the 12:h November. He was also charged with committing a similar offence on the 3rd December. Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared on behalf of the Commissioners.—lnspector Dutton depos,:d to visiting the prisoner's house on the 12th November, when he found two men and two women, lodgers, upstairs; and again on the 3rd December, when three men and three women and a child were in the house.—Prisoner asked the inspector if there was not a partition in the room. Inspector Hatton replied that there was a "kind of pig cote partition." He must say it was the most dirty •house he had ever entered in his life.—The prisoner, who pleaded not guilty to both charges, was fined 40s and at in each case; total, £6 is 4.(1. A BEGGAR IN THE TRIES: ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN POLICEMAN.—A young fellow, named Edwin Porter, was charged at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Tuesday, with beg- ging in Church-street, and also with assaultitg P.C. Wal- lace whilst in the execution of his duty, on Sunday night. —P.C. Wallace said on Sunday night, shortly after six &a ck, he saw the prisoner begging front several people in Church-street, as they went to the Parish Church. He followed him, and saw him receive 2d. from a young man. Near the church gate, he (the officer) -overtook the prisoner, who asked him for a copper. Witness replied that he would lock him up if he liked, when the prisoner struck him on the eye with his fist. He made known to him that he was a police-csmstable, and the prisoner became very violent, struck him several times, and also kicked him. The assistance. of P.C. Thompson was obtained, and tke prisoner was locked up.—The prisoner made a plausible statement, to the effect that he was a compositor just arrived from Dublin, and bore the best of characters. He alleged that an officer struck him in the face as he was being taken to the cells, tut it transpired that his violence was so great that it required two officers to hold him.—Superintendent William- son produced a list of convictions against the prisoner, which showed that he had served seven years' penal servi- tude, and many long terms of imprisonment.—He was committed to gaol for a month's hard labour on each eharge. RWNCORN BOARD OF• GUARDIANS. —The Rev. Car.oll Barclay presided over the meeting held at Dutton Work- house on Tuesday. There were also present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, Messrs. Mclntyre, 'l'. Norman, J. Weir, R. Ashton, J. Highfield, J. Darbyshire, E. A. Andrews, T. Smith, Peter Hall, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). The Rev. J. Lockwood read the report of the Finance Committee, which stated that the com- tnittee had passed accounts amounting to £1,031 Ils. 3d., including the precept for the county rate. The following letter was read from Dr. Robinson, of Frodsharn :—" I beg to call the attention of the Board to the increase in my duties as medical officer to your Workhouse. When I was appointed .13 gyears ago there were only 30 beds in the hospital, and there are now 70. In justice to myself I can- not longer discharge the duties of the office I hold at the present remuneration, and I must ask you to consider what (looking at the additional work devolving upon me).should be the amount of my salary for the future."—Mr. R. Ashton remarked that it did not follow because there were 70 beds they were all occupied.—The letter was referred to a com- mittee consisting of Messrs. T. Norman, Robert Ashton, John Weir, J. Mclntyre, and J. Derbyshire. A report on the subject will be presented at the next meeting. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITT.—The fort- nightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tues- day, under the presidency of the chairman, the Rev. Callen Barclay. There were also present the Revs. J. W. N. Tan- ner, J. Lockwood, Messrs. Mclntyre, R. Ashton, J. High- field, J. Derbyshire, J. Weir, E. A. Wallington, T. Andrews, T. Smith, Henry Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).—An application was read from Messrs. Muir and Massey, of Frodsham Bridge asking for permis- sion to carry on the trade of soap makers at that place.—lt was stated that the works were already in operation, and a member of the Authority said a fortnight or three weeks ago smells were observed in Frodsham 'when the wind blew from from the north-east, hut no clue as to whence they proceeded had been obtained.--It was suggested that the consideration of the application should be postponed for a month, so that the matter might be properly investigated. —lt was resolved that the attention of Messrs. Muir and Massey be called to the fact that they were infringing the law in carrying on the trade without permission of the Authority, and requesting them to discontinue carrying on the business under the 112th section of the Public Health Act.—A letter was read from Mr. ThomSs Rigby, pf Prod- sham Bridge, drawing the attention of the Authority to the deficiency of the supply of water to his house in Sutton.— The letter was referred to Mr. Bancroft, the engineer, to re- port thereon. ALLEGED UNLAWFUL WOUNDING WITH A BOTTLE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. John Brock, a married woman, named Mary Grayson, was charged with wounding Margaret McCann, at Widnes, on the previous night,—The prosecutrix said she was a single woman, residing in Davis-street, Moss Bank, and the priso- ner lived in the same neighbourhood. On the previous night she was passing the prisoner's house, between 10 and 11 o'clock, when the prisoner emerged from the doorway, and made use of some filthy expressions to her. The pro- secutrix, indignant at the abuse heaped upon her, told the prisoner she would" make her pay for it," when the priso- ner struck her three blows on the head with a bottle and once in the mouth, loosening two of her teeth. The wounds she had received bled very much. She gave the prisoner no provocation. Site still felt the effects of the blows. Dr. O'Keeffe dressed her wounds.—ln answer to the prisoner, the prosecutrix denied that she created a disturbance at her door.—Mary Daly, wife of John Daly, stated she saw the prisoner strike the prosecutrix three times on the head.—Dr. 'O'Keeffe deposed to examining the prosecutrix, who when she arrived at his surgery was bleeding, her neck, hair, and clothes being covered with blood. She was suffering from a contused lacerated wound about an inch long on the left side of the forehead. To inflict such wounds with a glass bottle considerable force would be requiled.--e?.S. Strickland, who apprehended the prisoner, stated that the prisoner's reply to the charge was as follows: " Mrs. McCann chucked a bottle into my house, and I threw it out again." She now stated the prosecuteix , threw a pop bottle into her yard, and she threw it back, whereupon the disturbaece arose.—She was cemmitted to the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial, bail being allowed, herself in £2O, and two sureties of £lO each. CHARGE AGAINST A WIDNES PUBLICAN. —Andrew Carragher, landlord of the Arch Hotel, Widnes, was charged with having, on the 9th December, unlawfully allowed gambling for money or money's worth to take place in his ' house.—Mr. swift, of St. Helens, appeared for the defen- dant.—P.S. Robinson said he and P.C. Irving were standing near the Arch Hotel about a quarter to eleven on the day in question. He could hear persons talking in a loud voice in the side room of the defendant's house, and the subject of their conversation was dominoes, one stating, "Let's have ' another game; first four out, the last out pay for drinks. One of the company then said to the defendant, "We have time for another game, have we not, Andrew ? " Defendant replied, "Yes,it wants seven minutes." Witness waited until the game had commenced, and then he went into the room where the playing was taking place. ' The defendant was sitting at the table with other persons with the dominoes in his hand. In answer to a remark by the officer, the defend- ant seid, "Well, you know what sort of a house it is. lam compelled to allow some sort of game, and it is a Thing which is allowed in all houses." There were glasses con- taining liquor on the tahle.—P.C. Irving corroborated, and Mr. Swift addressed the Bench for the defence. He called the defendant, who stated that he had always permitted dotninoe playing, and had done since he received this sum- mons; but he had never permitted betting to take place. ' No gambling took place.—Thomas Lowe, a chemical labourer, also denied that any gambling took place. "Glasses round" were stood by several persons in the house, but their doing so was not dependent upon the game of dominoes.—James Roscoe, Thomas Jolley, Wm. Roscoe, 1 Samuel Pemberton, and Cafferty were ca!led, and gave evidence of a similar nature. They all adMitted that several rounds of beer were paid for.—The magistrates retired to I consider their decision, and on returning into court Mr. " Hall said there was considerable doubt about the case, and 1 they would not therefore inflict a penalty. They advised the defendant to be careful how he conducted his house in f entre.

ATTEMPTED 'RESCUE OF A PRISONER AT WIDNES.—On Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, James Carr, a young; man, was charged with resisting. P.C. Savory in the execu- tion of his duty. On Tuesday night P.C. Savory and another constable took a man in custody. - -As they wtre bringing him along the street the prisoner met them, and seizing Savory by the arm, declared that the officers should not take the prisoner to the police station. A disturbance took place, and had it not been for two other constables arriving on the scene, the prisoner would have succeeded in making his escape. . Stones were freely thrown, and the constables were struck in various parts of• the body.—The prisoner was committed to gaol for seven days as a general watning against such conduct.

TEMPERANCE ENTERTAINMENT A.T DITTON.—OR Tues- day evening last, a very interesting entertainment was given in the Wesleyan school-room, Ditton, by tha members of the Cronton Blue Ribbon Army. A tea had been pro- vided, at which about 70 sat down, and who appeared to greatly enjoy themselves. At 7-15 the meeting commenced, Mr. John Hewson being in the chair. On the platform were Mews. Houghton, Cook, Mather, Sparks, Brimelow, Clark, and several lagies, all of whom wore medals. Addresses were delivered by Mr. Hewson, Mr. James Glover, Mr. John Brimilow, and Mr. Ephraim Brirnilow, the last gentleman making a most impassioned speech to those who had not signed the pledge. Songs were given by the Misses Glover, B. Cook, and Mather; a" trio "song by J. Stott. E. Brimi- low, and W. Stott, entitled "The social glass," received a hearty encore. The proceedings concluded by Mr. Hunt proposing a vote of thanks to the chairman and company, which was carried unanimously.

DISTURBING WAIT SINGERS AT WIDNES. —Two boys named Samuel Harper and Patrick McCreece were brought up on remand at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, to answer a charge of wilfully damaging Lacey-street school- room. It seemed that on Christmas Eve the choir of the Primitive Methodist Chapel were " wait singing " bef,re the residence of Mr. Bray, in Lac?y-street, when the prisoners, one of whom it was stated was drunk, endeavoured to create a disturbance. Several men, however, frustrated their design, and administered to them a little corporal punishment. Boy-like they seized a few stones and sent them crashing through the windows of the Lacey-street schoolroom, doing damage, Mr. Brown stated, to the extent Of 30s. The trustees of the school had suffered considerably threugh the wilful breakage of windows.—Superintendent Barker said McCreece had served five years in a reformatory school and had only recently been released.—Each prisoner was fined Is and costs, 83 6,1, and pay half the damage, or in default 21 days' imprisonment.

ATTEMPT. TO BREAK INTO A WIDNES PAWNBROKER'S SHoP.—Stephen Scallv, a young fellow, was brought up on remand, charged with attempting to break into the lock-up shop of Horatio Syred, pawnbroker, Marsh-street, Widnes ; and also with doing wilful damage to the extent of £s. The manager of Mr. Syred's shop stated he saw everything safe at half past seven on Wednesday evening. The shut- ters were up, the doors locked, and the window intact. About midnight he found the shutters had been removed, and a large plate-glass window in Marsh-street broken, which would cost £5 103. to replace.—P.C. Barker deposed that about half-past eleven on the night in in question he was walking along Waterloo-road, when he heard a crash of glass breaking. He went into Marsh-street, where be found the prisoner standing near a broken N:indew in Mr. Syredas shop. He walked away, but the officer followed him, and arrested him. Prisoner denied that he had brokeu the glass —He was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. BANK HOLIDAY AT WIDNES AND BTINCORN.—Bank Holiday was pretty generally observed in both Runcorn and Widnes, and each town assumed a more bustling aspect than on the previous day. The railway station bad a consider- able amount of traffic to deal with; but the accident at the Central Station, Liverpool, seriously interfered with that from the Sheffield and Midland Statlon at Widnes. Trains arrived in many instances five hours late, and others never put in an appearance at all. For hours passengers waited on the platform to he taken to their des- tination, and Mr. Patten (the stationmaster) and Mr. I Beacham (the inspector) were fully occupied in answering I their questions, and as far as possible, keeping them in a good humour. Many persons had their fares returned to II them, and either went home again or travelled by the London I and North-Western Railway. On Wednesday matters were I very little improved, and contract ticket holders WAS put to much inconvenience. Many of them travelled by tl e London and North-Western line, protesting that they would claim their fares from the Cheshire Lines Committee. Matters were made worse by the fact that the tele2raphic communi- cation was stopped, adding greatly to the nrtcertainty of the arrival and departure of trains. THE VICAR OF RUNCORN ON HIS MlNlSTHX.—Preaelling at Runcorn Parish Church on Sunday front the text "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, make straight the way of the Lord," the Rev. Canon Barclay, the vicar, I referred to the fact that that day was the 37th anniversary of his ministry at Runcorn. He thanked the congregation for the liberal support given during the year to the paro- chial charities and institutions, for the kindly sympathy shown to himself and his fellow labourers in the ministry, and the generous forbearance extended to their faults and failings. He dwelt with satisfaction upon the uninterrupted harmony which .for a period of 37 years had characterised the relations between pastor and people, in which their own pirish presented such a Witting contrast to many others of which they often heard and read, where disputes between the minister and congregation, or differences between the people themselves, were a sad hindrance to the work of the ministry. He fervently hoped that such a kindly feeling. might continue to the end, and solicited their prayers for their pastors that they might with God's help open their mouths boldly, and order their plans discreetly, and perform their duties faithfully; yea, that they might so discharge their ministry as to make ready an acceptable people for the Lord at His coming.—The church bells were. rung in honour of the anniversary at the conclu- sion of the service.

A VIOLENT YOUNG PRIFIONER AT WIDNES; ROBBERY OF InoN.—At Widnes Poiice Court, yesterday, before Mr. John Brock. John Power and Steven Power, brothers, were charged with having, on Thursday, stolen 451bs of scrap iron, the property of the Widnes Metal Company. Owing to the extreme youth of Stephen, who was only eight years of age, Inspector Barker said he would offer no evidence against him, and asked for his discharge, which was granted. From the evidence of Wm. Moss, a labourer at the metal works, and of Wm. Harper, the foreman, it ap- peared that whilst the former was on his way home, at noon, on Thursday, he saw the prisoner and two other boys assisting each other over the fence which surrounds the works. On seeing him they ran away, one of them carry- ing a big bag on his back. He followed them and caught the prisoner, who struggled violently, and struck Moss with a long stick, which he used as a crutch. He released him, when Mr. Harper seized him. He bit the latter's hand, and tore his coat, and then finding his struggling of no avail, he pretended to be in a fit. He was allowed to go, but was afterwards apprehended by P.C. Laing. The bag of iron was afterwards found at a corner of the street, and an examination of the works showed that the prisoner had been amongst the scrap iron, the marks made by his cratch being visible. Tbe iron produced was the property of the Metal Company.—The prisoner, who had previously been convicted, was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial.

TRESPASSING ON THE RAILWAY AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. H. S. Hall and Mr. John Brock, nine persons named Charles Baxter, Francis Dean, Owen Price, Charles Bunn, Isaac Sankey, Thomas Roberts, Charles Upworth, John Melia, and John Hunt were summoned on a charge of having on the 10th November trespassed on the London and North-Western railway at Widnes. Mr. Ferrand, who represented the com- pany, stated that it was twelve months ago sinca a batch of persons were brought up on a similar charge. With the ex- ception of Dean and Upworth, all the defendants were em- ployed at the Tharsis Copperworks,and by trespassing on the lino they saved themselves the trouble of traversing a quar- ter or half a mile in going to and from their homes. It was a very dangerous practice, and two or three lives had been lost at that part of the line sometime ago. The company were once in twelve months compelled to station an officer ' to watch the line, and this was done on the 9th and 10th inst. On the 10th he saw the defendants walking up the line, and as he had cautioned them on the day Previous, he took their names and summoned them. Evidence in support of this statement was given, and the defendants were each fined 5.3. and costs, with the exception of Dean and Roberts, who were each ordered to pay the cips:s.

div.head: VIOLENT ASSAULT WITII A POKER AT WIDNES.
div.p: VIOLENT ASSAULT WITII A POKER AT WIDNES.

Yesterday, before Mr. John Brock, at Whines Police , Court, Michael Grogan, a young feilow, was charged, on remand, with unlawfully wounding Michael Mannion, with intent to do bins grievous bodily karm. The prosecutor, , who is a tine-looking young fellow, was in se weak a cc/3. dition that he witS aeeOinnt °Li e(.l with a seat ai lit"! solicitors table, from where he gave his evidence.—Mr. IL L. Riley, of St. Helens, appeared to defend the prisoner. —The prosecutor said he was a chemical labourer, residing , 22 Hutchinson-street, Widucs. On Saturday .night last, company of John Develin, went to the house of John grocer, Victoria-rod, Widnes. The prisoner lived with le.itzpatricle. Shortly after entering, the prosecu- tor had supper .with Fitzpatrick, and whilst the meal was being consumed, tho prisoner went in. Afterwards the party commei7cal to play cards. They were engalsed in Ois , game from about half past eleeen until fonr o'clock the following morning, and during that time they were drialsivg whiskey. They were all more or less under the influence pf liquor. A dispute arose about tour o'clock between Devlin and the prisoner, and some angry words p-Assed. The prosecutor endeavoured to pacify theta, but not accomplishing his intent, Fitz- patrick told them if they cpuld not agree, they must leave the house. They did so, waking out through a back pas- sage or entry, and whilst there, the prosecutor received a blow on one side of his head. lie was stunned,but turning round, he saw the prisoner with a pair of torgs in his hand. They were raised in a threatening position, and the prose- cutor raised his arm to ward off tlee-blow, which be received upon his right arm. Blood was theta streaming from his bead over his face, and upon his shoulders. The prosecutor ran up the entry, and made a complaint to a constable, whom he showed where the attack took place. He then went to the police station, but remembered nothing more until - his wounds were dressed by Dr. O'Keeffe. He had eiuce then suffered much pain, and until Wednesday was unable to leave the house. The prisoner was a comparative stranger to him, and .he had had no quarrel with him. In cross-examination by Mr. Riley, the prisoner said he should not be surprised to hear that lie fell asleep in Fitz- patrick's house shortly after he arrived, but he had no recollection of being awakened by a quantity of water being , emptied over him twice from his own hat. The dispute through which-Me curd party broke up was one )ut six-

aboe peace- between the prisoner' and Develin, and he (the prosecutor) said he would fight the former for the sixpence. The prisoner replied, "I have won the sixpence. I will either have blood or money." Witness remembered saying that the prisoner was much bigger than Develin, and that though he was much bigger than him he thought he would be a match for him. He did not remember saying that he would not leave the house unless put out by Fitzpatrick. Before reaching Fitzpatrick's house on the night in ques- tion, be remembered calling in four public-heuses. He did not consider that he was drunk, but he was "pretty full." There were two quarts of whiskey in the house, and be said he drank one, afterwards, however, qualifying this state- ment by saying he "did not drink it all."—By Inspector Barnett: They were playing "nap."—John Develin, of 15, Elliott-street, Widnes, said lee was a foreman at a chemical works. He deposed to accompanying the prosecutor to Fitzpatrick's hones, and stated that after sup- per they were playing cards until five o'clock on Sunday morning, when a dispute arose. He asked Fitzpatrick to open the back door, and let them out, and he did so. Wit- ness went outside first and stayed in the yard. Whilst there he heard the noise of a struggle, and some person shouting. He ran out and saw the prosecutor running away, with the prisoner after him, holding in his uplifted hand a. pair of tongs. He then lost sight of them- and went into Lacey- street, where he met the prieoner, who ran against him with such violence, that he was knocked to the ground. He afterwards found the prosecutor with a police-constable in the street. The prosecutor's face was covered with blood. He accompanied bins to the surgery of Dr. O'Keeffe, who dressed his wounds. He then took him to his (the wit- ness's) own house, where he had since remained. Having been cross,examined by Mr. Riley, who failed to extract any new facts from the witness.---John Fitzpatrick, grocer ! and provisicn dealer, Vicoria-road, was called. Referring ' to the departure of prosecutor and Develin from his house, he said he saw them go from the yard into the entry. He did not use any force to get Mannion out, but whilst he had hold of him at the yard door he heard someone run past him into the passage, and the next thing he saw was Develin lying in tilts passage. He asked the prisoner what he had done that for, and he replied that he could not stand it any longer. He asked Develin where Mannion had gone, and the former stated he had gone home. He (witness) did not see any weapon in the prisoner's hands.—ln cross-examination by Mr. Riley, witness said he could see that the prosecutor and• Develin had had some drink. He twice put about half a wine glass of water into prosecutor's hat, and poured it on his face to waken hirn.—P.S. MacGregor deposed to being in the police station, where, although cautioned, persisted in snak- ing a statement. He said he had the tongs in his hind to stir up the fire in order to malre some tea for Fitzpatrick and himself, when he sew Fitzpatrick putting out the prosecutor and Develin, and he went to aid him. He had soma words with thesis, and he struck Mannion once. He did not iuteud to hint him much. It was "drink " tliat had done it.—Dr. O'Keeffe said he examined the prosecutor at the house of Develin about seven o'clock on Sunday morn- ing. He was not properly conscious, and his hair and clothes were saturated with blood. He was suffering from a contused lacerated wound on the right side of the ton of the head. It was a ragged wound, going in different directions, and was an inch and a (pester in length. There was an artery wounded, and when he saw him he was bleeding profusely. He must have lost an immense quantity of blood. He was in such a weak state Vett he (the doctor) could hardly feel the pulsation of the wrist. The wound might have been caused by tile pair of tongs. The prosecutcr might have bled to death if assistance had not been cslled in. He did not think he would be able to follow his usual employment for some weeks.—P.C. Timperley deposed to apprehending the prisoner.—ln answer to the usual questions prisoner said "I am very sorry for what has occurred, and he would never do it again."—The prisoner was committed to the sessions for trial.—Mr. Riley applied for bail, but Inspector Barnett objected.—Mr. Brock refused the application.

LANCASHIRE ENGINEERING, IRON, AND COAL TRADES DURING 1882. The year now closing has been one of considerable activity in the iron trade and the various allied branches of industry in this district, and although it is not leaving be- hind it the same activity with which it began, there appears to be no reason at present for any feeling of serious anxiety with reward to the future. The activity in trade has, how- ever, not been accompanied by a corresponding improvement in prica, and although wages have advanced generally throughout the coal, iron, and engineering trades of the district, this can scarcely be said to have been the outcome of the higher profits realised on business operations. A large output of both coal and iron has maintained produc- tion ahead of requiremerlt;, and with an undoubtedly large trade doing priceltoav tieeti kept at a comparatively low point. In the engineering trades the year opened Well, auti although subsequent operations hava not realised all that was looked forward to from the weight of the original inquiries, still the results have been sufficient to give full employment generally. Locomotive building has been exceptionally busy all through the year. Rolling stocks abroad had been allowed to work down, and almost simul- taneously nearly every railway company on the Continent seems to have decided upon replacing worn-out plant. From India, the colonies, and South America good orders have been received, and a considerable amount of work has also been given out by home railways. Manufacturers of railway car- riage and other rolling stock have shared in the activity, and have had good orders in hand. Cotton machinists have been moderately employed, but with the latter portion of the year there has been a slackening off in orders, which is leaving some of the works only partially employed. In the iron ship-building trade the activity has been quite abnormal, and so far as booked orders are concerned the various ship yards are still full of work, but the higher prices ship- builders are now compelled to quote as one result of the great spring which has taken place in wages are checking the placing out of further contracts. For both light and heavy tools there has been a demand which has kept works fully employed, and boiler makers have experienced no'scarcity of orders during the year. Stationary engine builders have not been quite so busy as other branches of the trade, but there has been a good deal of heavy work in hand both for home and abroad, and in connection with the ligher class of work the manufacture of gas engines is a branch of industry which has undergone considerable development in this district during the year. So far as the workmen are concerned the year has been one of prosperity, and they at least have secured a full share of any advantages which have been derived from the activity of trade. Early in the year they secured a return of the rate of wages lost during the period of depression following 1878, which in the general engineering trades represented an advance of 2s per week, whilst considerably more than this has been secured in some branches of the shipbuilding trade. With higher' wages they have also bad full work all throught the twelve months, and probably during no previous period have the trade union societies been called upon to pay less out of their funds in the shape of "out of work" donations. This has enabled the trade union organisations to considerably strengthen their position, which in many cases had been very seriously weakened during the strain of bad trade, and it is estimated that the accumulation of funds in connection with the Amalgamated Society of Engineers during the past year will amount to upwards of £30,000. The year also commenced very hopefully as regards the iron trade, but it has since been a period of expectation rather than of actual realisation of better trade. January opened with an active demand in the market, and as this had been going on during the preceding November and December, makers had their hocks already so full of orders that they were indifferent about entering into further en- gagements, especially as an upward movement in prices" confidently looked forward to. Large sales were made at advancing prices, and before the close of the month Lanca- shire pig iron got up to 523. 6d., Lincolnshire to 535. to 543 , and some brands of Derbyshire to as high as 555. " 565. per ton, less 21.., delivered equal to Manchester ; whilst quotations for finished iron following the quarterly meetings got up to .£ss. ss. per ton, and subsequently the wages of the finished ironworkers were advanced 7A- per cent. This was the highest point touched during the year, but it represented little more th In a teml.,:aars- fictitious basis of values. Con- sumers by this time were so fully covered by the purchases

made during the preceding two months that they were un- der no necessity of placing out further orders, and were cer- tainly not inclined to buy in anticipation at the advanced rates. For the ensuing two or three months makers were kept going with their contracts, and consum era were able to meet their requirements with deliveries on account of iron already bought, but very little new buying went on Gradually, as makers found their order-beoks getting bare ,• prices began to recede,and a keen competition commenced to dtire beeiness which mlit geese into the market. District bands of pig iron were pushed in the marke t at very low figures, • and LincOlnehire and Derbyshire makers, who were underselling tio local iron, got down to as low as 44s 6.1 and 453, less 4, delivered. These low figures again temnted buyers into the market, but the bulk of the orders passed into the hands of the district makers, who were able to do a large business during May and June, when prices again began to advance. Lancashire makers of pig iron, whose prices had got down to 45s to 465, , less 2?-e, only very closely recovered the lost ground, but gradually they were able to fel ate their order books, and ul- timately to follow the upward mevernent in prices. During the second half of the year district brands by gradual advances of is and is 6d per ton got up to 49s and 51s for Lincolnshire and 52s and 633 for Derbyshire, Put it was not until about the commencement of November fleet local makers by one advance of between 4s and 5s per ton put up their list rates to 50.3 to 503 61 per ton, less 4., delivered. Te advance again put a step to buying; November found makers easier in their prices, and in:December a renewal of the down-ward mevement was inaugurated by the district makers, Lincolnshire brags being reduced to 47s 4d to 48s 41, vehith was ultimately followed by local makers coming down to 49. s and 495, less 21, delivered. With the close o the year district makers were able to secure orders to a moderate extent at their reduced rates, but the con- cernions in loca brands ware apparently not sufficient tc: satisfy buyers, and local makers fiaish the year open to offers, but with little or no business corning forward. The mandactured iron, trade has followed mach the same couree as pig iron, but if anything finished iron makers have been in a relatively better position as regards the margie of pro fit on the prices realised. During the first half year prices gradually gave way until bars teuched as low as .f.. 6 2s 6.1 per ton, delivered into the Manchester district ; then fol- lowed a gradual stiffening in valves, uutil the September quarterly meetings got quotations up to ec's6s ids.; but this figure was found too high to be maintained, and during November and December makers as a•rule fell back to about £6 10s., at which the year closes, with, however, very Hal* doing. Although makers of iron have not bees able to maintain any material advance in prices during the year, the results of the twelve months' operations have not on the whole been unsatisfactory. Even with an increased outputs Lincashire makers of pig iron have been enabled to find a. market for their productions, and the forges throughout the district have been kept fully employed. A. better average of prices has also been realised than during 1881, and a large business has been done, one satisfactory feature of which has been a marked absence of the speculative eleenent Business in the coal trade commenced under less favour- able conditions than in the other branches of industry. Daring the urecetting autumn consumers had laid in large stocks in anticipation of wage difficulties with the men, and the subsequent exceptional mildness of the winter enabled them in many cases to work on with these until well into the spring. -Notwithstanding a large consumption going on in common &asses of coal for iron making and steam pur- poses, the limited requirements for house-fire purposes caused supplies to be abundant in the market. During the winter months the house-fire coal trade scarcely reached the level of an ordinary summer demand, and colliery proprie- tors entered upon the summer season with large stocks on their bands and pits in most cases already working short time. The pressure of excessive supplies upon the market and the competition of Yorkshire and Derbyshire coal forced prices steadily downwerds, until best coal, which commenced the year at about 9s 61 to 103, could be bought as low as Bs, seconds had dropped from is 61 and 83 to 6s and 6s 6d, common house coals from 63 31 and Gs 9d to 5s 6,1 and 6.5, steam and forge coals from 53 Gd and 63 to 43 91 and 5a 3d, burg,y from 43 91 and 53 3d to 4s 3d and 4s 91 and good slack from 33 91 and 41 31 to 33 6.1 and 33 91 per ton at the pit. All through the summer trade continued in a very depressed condition, and although the North Wales strike tended somewhat to relieve the pressure of stocks, colliery proprieters were not able to com- mand any better prices, which had got to so low a point that the necessity of a reduction in wages was strongly urged in many quarters. The only attempt, however, which was made in this direction by Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., of St. Helens, resulted in a protracted strike of about 4.000 men. The men were successful in resisting the reduc- tion, and in the autumn followed a general agitation for an advance. The movement was stimulated by conferences of miners' delegates held in Manchester, and upon the refusal of the employers to concede the demands of the men, con- sumers took alarm at the prospect of a threatened general strike. Orders were rushed in for supplies to cover forward requirements, and, the men at the same time restricting the output, so much pressure was brought upon the market that an upward moverneat in prices at once commenced. This went en during September and October, and in.some Cases advances of 3s. to 3s. Gd. per ton upon the lowest summer rates bad been secured by the commence- ment of Nevember, whilst the general advance averaged from is. 61. te 2s. per ton. With this an advance of 10 per cent. in wages was conceded to the men. It was, how- ever, soon apparent that the basis of the upward movement had been a temporary inflation of the market, and not a legitimate improvement in trade. The fears of a strike at an end, the pressure for supplies ceased, and during Novem- ber stocks began to accumulate. Colliery proprietors had to surrender a good. deal of the highest advances which had been made, and although an advance of from is. to is. ad. per ton is still generally being maintained upon the lowest rates, the year closes with a good deal of strain upon prices, whilst the enormous means of production, which have throuehout the year exerted so depressing an influence upon the market, seem likely to operate still in the same direction.

NATIONAL REFUGE HARBOURS.

Sir,—The following facts are almost unknown—we have it on authority of the Board of Trade returns—that in the official year 1881-82, the loss of life by shipwreck on our coasts was 984; in the list 27 yeiirs no fewer than 19,531 lives were sacrificed, and 55,410 vessels. We have now a most powerful organisation composed of a very great number of our nobility, naval authorities,:and leading public spirited people of the greatest capacity and highest influ- ence, who at the beginning of the. new year will make united effort for the protection and safety of our fishermen and mariners, and which effort if supported by the many who care for the welfare and safety of our seafaring popu- lation must command success. The general aim of the society is the prevention of loss by shipwreck of life and property on the coasts of the British Islands, and the improvement of harbour accommodation. Each locality will be treated with strict impartiality on its merits alone as a purely national matter. Such an or- ganisation can never be too strong, aid I shall be glad to hear from all volunteers desirous of working with us to miti- gate these most serious losses of life and property, and be pleased to forward to them a list of the names of those by whom the movement is supported. The society's head quar- ters will shortly be in London, and it is desired to establish branches throughout the provinces, in the same manner as the Royal National Life Boat Institution, and the Ship- wrecked Mariners' Society. Thanking you for granting a little space for me to plead the cause of seafaring men who perish in such large numbers annually from causes which are in great measure preventable.—l remain, your obedient Servant; F. JOHNSON,
Hon. Managing Site. Norman-road, St. Leonards-on-Sea. December, 1882. A YULETIDE GREETING FROM "ANGLO-SCOTUS " TO "NEWTONIAN."

Sir,—Although I have wandered a bit in my time, I cannot consent to follow "Newtonian" all over the world, or "all over the shop." Will you allow me to say in answer to him—First; As regards the "smoking rabbit," I can assure " Newtonian " that I did not cross the " silver streak" to study sign boards, or to flirt with French or Belgian landladies. I should not be suprisal to hear that he Wat ofte of the party that were sO elated after viewing the rather indelicate •sign that used to hang outside a mustard shop in the Rue du Chatel, Beauvais, but which is now exhibited ia the Muses d'Antiquites of that town. It represents a fool stirring mustard in a barrel with a large stick, whilst a tall grinning monkey stands just opposite, assisting him in a way we need not describe. lam afraid "Newtonian," when he is on his walks abroad, makes so- called study of antiqui;ies, stained glass, tapestry, &c., veil in an ingenious manner the pursuit of "fugitive studies" of a different kind, just as his ancestor used bay to cover the retreat of a hunted man. "Oh, those men, those men, when they get out of sight of their wives and sweethearts there is no telling what they get up to." I hope the land- lady, after disappointing "Newtonian" and his friend in the matter of dinne-, did not befool them further by direct- ing them back to the Green Monkey (le singe veil) at Paris. I would remind "Newtonian" that " kliping " is an awkward habit, especially if he has a wife or a sweetheart. A man of his varied experiences and curious discoveries should bear in mind the fate of the Irish fairy. In case he has not heard it, I will quote briefly from the record : _ _
An Iri:h fairy lost her way ; Of course she could not find it. Ehe was so debonnair and gay, _ She vow'd she did not mind it.

Like "Newtonian," she stumb!ed over a Variety of things she had always taken to be or mean something else; hut she is bent on reaching the horizon, and so She murmued. "Oh, if on I go, Unheeding gates and hedges; I'm sure that I must touch the sky, And giant, upon the ed4es," And then we learn bow the little creature, discarding her shoes and stockings, just as "Newtonian "at times over- looks the reverse or obverse side. So we are further told that--

She went so far, that alt the trees Were made of isu4ar candy; And all the little pods of peas Held drops of .cherry-brandy ; And every well contained Morelle, And all the rivers sherry,.. And effszs were made of marma!ade,— A charming country, very Eh e came to where the sky rains cats And dogs, to drown the mlller ; And in their mouths- the little rats • Are born with spoons of shier.

And on she goes through lands and lands,— Till she reaches the horizon! She's there at last! Her heart beats fast,— Oh, what will she discover? She's on the ledge,—the very edge: And then she tumbles over! Nov:, I should not like to see " Newtonian " " tumble. over," —either into a barrel of muQtard, or on the prongs of that fork; but he must really be careful. Such curioua things do happen. If he will make due inquiry he willlind that a certain individual once involuntarily gauged the depth of an old cesspool. ' S3cond : I think if "Newtonian " will pay another visit to St. Helens, and make due inquiries about that signboard, he will find that " Pig _and Whistle " is a corruption of pige-washail, Our Lady's Salutation. That is according to Danish-Saxon. The Scotch have it that as pig means pot, and whistle small change, the sign of the "Pig and Whistle " is a sarcastic way of symbolising the fact that he who spends too tunch•time and money in the alehouse will "go to pot." I incline to the religious , derivation myself, seeing that in an old book of accounts belonging to Warrington parish the following minute oc- curs :—" Nov. 5, 1888. Paid for drink at the church steele {stile] ;" and again in 1732, "It is ordered that hereafter no money be spent on ye sth of November or any cther State day on the parish account, either at the church stile or any other place." The Chapel Bell, the Church Stile, and the Church 'Gates used to be, and possibly are now, common signs. Let my friend tike a trot round the streets of Chester, Macclesfield, and Coventry, in addition to those of Warrington. Third: He had better be reverent in the matter of Castle Hill, or he will have that ghost about his ears or his bed- side. Fourth and last: The mountain in labour is said to have brought forth a mouse. May I ask "Newtonian" what inlubatory results will spring from the bridge which is "sitting" on the Sankey? " Plim "is the word that will apply beyond that superstructure he alludes to. Capital P's are plentiful just now—plays, pantomimes, puddings, printingolic ,to wit. And so possibly a sitting attitude is the 'natural result of a plim condition. I always thought bridges spanned rivers. But the sitting position may be another Newton peculiarity. Once more I insist that "Newtonian" must be a wag. With the compliments of the season to yourself, Mr. Editor, and to your readers, I remain, airricc. ANGLO-SCOTUS. Newington, London, Christmas morning, 1882.

OATH TAKING. Sir,—So long as the question of oath taking remains in its present unsatisfactory state, all who care for the world's progress mustbe up and doing. With the commencement of the New Year we shall again have the thrice-elected mem- ber for Northampton to the front, respectfully. but most determinedly insisting upon his right to sit in the people's Howe of Commons. Men whose minds are clear of the taießof bigotry and fanaticism have long been satisfied about the ultimate result of this war betwixt intellectual capability andpious stupidity. The oaths question three years since was asa small acorn, it is now a mighty tree spreading its branch.% wherever the fungus—superstition—exists, and in goocltimas will " certainly be consigned to the limbo of all burning questions. "Let your speech be, yea, yea; nay, nay," are words given to Christians for their conduct of lire's business. Hew .do they act up to it? The pulpit record gives the following for answer, ' The gabbling over of a form of words, the touching with our lips of a delapi- dated book, which we strpposs to be a New Testament, will scarcely, we think, give additional krce to what we may have to say or sign." The real truth is that we are living in an age of shams, pretending to be good and pious, while at the same time proof is being daily given by the Press that AIt:TR with all this pretence goes hand in hand a distrustfulness of one another that keeps the various classes of society in a state of chronic antagonism towards each other. Hem, we take no man's word, but in each act of life's drama we Insist upon an oath, nay, we go further than this, and deny a man of irreproachable character and proven truthfulness, the right to either swear according to law, or to affirm in accor- dance with his conscience ; and, as there are always deeper depths, we see this surpassed by the Bishop of Manchester, who in exercise of his legal authority refuses to institute the Rev. tlarry Cowgill to the benefice of St. John's, Miles Platting, because he, the bishop, thinks the Reverend Harry intends to perjure himself—" the eath would be administered in one sense, but taken in another." If common report , speaks the truth, the thirty-nine articles are always swal- lowed along with 3 doze of mental rezervation, Obedience I

to the laws of the country, and respect for the oath taken before God, have been two of the most remarkable features in the lives of our clergy during the past few years. On every occasion where such clashed with individual likes and dislikes, obedience and the oath must go to the wall. The prestige of the Establithment must be upheld, even to insulting the dead. Witness the base and inhuman conduct of the Rev. C. E. Taunton, vicar of St. John's, Harlow. It may be said these are exceptional cases. I say the public Press teems with them. Were I not afraid of trespassing on your space I could, from the "Life of Bishop Wilberforce," call such splendid specimevs of greed and grab, as would prove to your readers that their interests would he served by helping Mr. Bradlaugh to uproot the cursed upas tree of trade unionism that shelters the horse leeches clothed in purple and fine linen. That it is desirable a guarantee should accompany all public duties, I am aware; but I ask what binding effect has the oath taken by the Hone Rulers had upon their patriotic pledges? Why, none whatever. They have sworn to uphold the Queen and Constitution, yet are every day trying to uproot the whole thing. Mr. Bradlaugh has re- peatedly in public declared that ho has no sympathy with violent revolutions of any kind. I have myself heard him say that he would net, at present, vote for a republic, so lone as good intentions carry with them active work. He would leave the rest to be done by the moral power that is contained in our educational •code. 'lime will work wonders, and we may even live to see our teachers and preachers act- ing out in purity and truth the duties of the good steward.— Yours, HENRY WHITHAM. Warrington, December 26th, 1882.

div.head: FUNERAL OF MR. E. BILLINGSLEY, OF RUNCORN.
div.p: FUNERAL OF MR. E. BILLINGSLEY, OF RUNCORN.

The funeral of Mr. E. Billingsley, of Runcorn, whose death we recorded in our last issue, took place on Christmas Day, in very gloomy and wet weather- Tokens of the respect in which the deceased was held were to be seen on every hand, and at two o'clock, the time fixed for the cortege to start, Ashbridge-street, where the deceased had resided, was crowded with a concourse of sympathetic observers. At various points on the route which the pro- cession bad to traverse—along lir:nand-street, High-street,

and Greenway-road--large crowds of people had also col- lected to testify their respect to the deceased. The cortege, which was composed of upwards of 200 people, halted at Greenway-road chapel, where the deceased for many years had been the organist, and the body was taken from the hearse and borne to the communion by members of the choir. The sacred edifice was filled by a mournful congre- gation, which was visibly affected as the selemn service proceeded. 'During the service "The Orphan's Prayer," composed by the deceased, and included in the service of song "The Basket of Flowers," was sung by the choir with much feeling. Prayers were offered by the Revs. Joseph Morton (of Warrington) and Mr Wm. Shaw (sea- men's Missionary). The Rev. J. Pickwell, the pastor, de- livered a short address, in which he said that daring his ministerial life he had witnessed death in all its aspects, but he never spent such a night of grief as last Thursday night, when their dear friend was battling with death. The earnest prayers which were offered up in his behalf not only in his own house, but in the houses of others who knew him, showed how deeply he hal laid hold upon the affec- tions of all who were connected with him. If prayer could have saved the life of their friend they would not have been there that afternoon under such distressing circum- stances. God's providence had removed him, and they bowed in submission to the will of the Almighty. Never be- fore had he witnessed so sorrowful a service as that held in the chapel on the previous morning, when the tones of the organ were hushed, and the orchestra was deserted, and there was hardly a dry eye in the whole congregation. In the prayers which had been offered hope had been expressEd in the death of their brotner, and he felt that even under such sorrowful circumstances they could rejoice.l A loving Saviour in his dying moments was presented to him; and although speech bad for some time before his death been denied him, he (the speaker) heard him before the last distinctly say "The angles are coming." It did seem strange that a young man of "31 years of age, highly respected and beloved by all, should have been taken away; yet it was the work of God, which was right. Addressing the choir, Mr. Pickwell said, let the decease of their brother draw them nearer to one another and nearer to God, and exhorted them that as God had removed their leader' to try to fill his place by working harder in the cause of Christ. The body was again placed inside the hearse. The proces- sion was re-formed, headed by Mr. E. Timmins (of the Bridgewater Foundry), Mr. Thomas Timmins, Mr. Charles Timmins, and Mr. Walter Timmins, the Revs. J. Pickwell, J. Morton, and Dr. Mouritz. Following were the workmen employed at the foundry, the superintendents of the-Sun- day school, several local preachere 'and class-leaders, and a large number of teachers and scholars of the school. Pre- ceding the hearse were the members of the choir, and be- hind walked three young children •i the deceased, his father, Mr. Wm. Billingsley, Mr. John Peacock, Mr. Isaac Broad- hurst, Mr. Joseph Stubbs, a number of friends and relatives, and several tradesmen in the town. At the cemetery, the body was borne to the grave by eight members of the choir, and the burial service was concluded amid a drenching rain. many beautiful wreathes being placed upon the coffin.

div.head: ALLEGED EXTRAORDINARY ROBBERY AT GOLBORNE.
div.p: ALLEGED EXTRAORDINARY ROB- BERY AT GOLBORNE.

LEAVING A MAN PENNILESS AND NAKED. During the week a report of a serious robbery at Grolhorne, under circumstances of a most unusual and extraordinary character, has gained credence, though enquiries which have been made have not tended to a confirmation of the story. It is stated that at the end of last week—Saturday or Sun- day—a young man, residing at Rochdale, visited Earlestown for the purpose of spending Christmas week with a friend, residing in a pirticular district of Earlestown. These two friends visited Golborne on the Sunday, and after " enjoy- ing " themselves to their hearts content, returned home, the Rochdaleian spending thenight at Newton. On the following day (Christmas Day) the latter again went to Golborne and spent another " enjoyable " afternoon and evening. He ultimately secured "lodgings" there, and was shown to the room in which he had to sleep during the night. On the following morning, when the Rochdale young man awoke, he found himself in a sorry plight, for not only had his silver watch, guard, money, &c., been taken, but the whole of his clothing had by some means disappeared. Enquiries and searches did not give any satisfaction, and the young man was thus left quite penniless and devoid of clothing. He succeeded in borrowing another suit of clothes, attired in which he resembled a navvy more than a merchant, and in these he has been enabled te prosecute his search for the missing articles. It is, however, added that no definite information as to their disappearance has been
