div.head: 17_,'XAMINE-11; SATURDAY, DECEMBER 30, 1882.
div.p: THE 17_,'XAMINE-11; SATURDAY, DECEMBER 30, 1882.

ST. ALBAN'S CATHOLIC CHURCH, WARRINGTON. The annual service was held in this church at midnight en Christmas Eve. The altar was suitably decorated for the festival, but greater attention had evidently been given to the "crib," which was the chief feature in the adorn- ment of the church, presenting a very striking and pleasing appearance. Long before the appointed hour the sacred edifice was quite full, every available seat being occupied. Solemn mass was sung by the priests of the mission, and during the ceremony a short sermon, pleasing and instructive, was preached by the Rev. Father Beauvoisin on the text "I bring you tidings of great joy." He showed how the human hearts can only be satisfied by some manifestation of a personal God, and after instancing various manifestations in the old law, he dwelt in detail on the great miracle of the birth of Christ. Mozart's N 0.12 Mass was rendered by St. Alban's choir with very pleasing effects. The "Gloria in Excalsis "and the " Et Incarnatus Est" were remarkably well sung—indeed, the mass throughout was given with great spirit and taste, and must have afforded the utmost satisfaction to all present. The most perfect order and quiet prevailed during the whole time of the impressive ceremony.

div.head: CHRISTMAS FESTIV. 'TIES.
div.p: CHRISTMAS FESTIV. 'TIES.
W ARRINI:(TON.

Since our last issue another Christmas has been added to the long roll of past events. The great festival was cele- brated in Warrington in the conventional manner, and the general rejoicings were unaffected by the depressing and exceptional weather that prevailed throughout the day. Instead of the mantle of snow, and the clear, frosty atmos- phere associated with a good old-fashioned Christm is, there was a drizzling rain and a heavy mist that rendered it ex- , ceedingly disagreeable out of doors. As a consequence few persons were to be seen in the streets, ad the town all through the day bad a deserted appearance. The rain com- menced to fall on the previous day, and continued to do so at intervals on Christmas Eve, but this did not deter the numerous choirs, choral singers, and musicians from paying their annual visits. It was noticeable, however, that the vocalists were considerably outnumbered by the instrumen- talists. The latter were chiefly youths, who had formed themsAves into bands of half-a-dozen, and para- ded the streets for a full week previously, making the townspeople only too familiar with the dole- ful pieces of their limited repertoire. Occasion- ally there were heard strains more in consonance with the joyous character of the fast approaching festival, but on the whole the tunes were most melancholy, and, doubtless, sounded all the more dismal by reason of the de- pressing state of the weather. But the absence of frost and snow has not been without its advantages, for it has enabled those that follow out-door occupations to join in the festivi- ties with higher hearts than usual, from the fact that em- ployment is good, and the sympathetic people were not troubled with the thought of the existence of destitution similar to that of previous years, when work was scarce and the weather severe. The way piles of currant bread, rows of poultry, circ., and quarters of -beef disappeared from provision, poulterers', and butchers' shops on Saturday, testified in an unmistakable manner to the general prosperity of the towns- people, a condition of things essential for spending a merry Christmas. In the morning service was held in the Episcopal Churches, but the congregations were by no means large; and in the evening several Nonconformist congregational tea meetings were held, at which there were only moderate attendances. People naturally preferred to remain indoors, and the wretched atmospheric conditions tended to bring into closer sympathy those long absent them- hers who had been enabled by the unusually long heliday to join in the family gatherings which the many lighted parlours indicated were being held. Below will b.: found an account of the fostivities. THE CHURCHES.

As already stated services were held on Christmas Day in the episcopal churches of the town which had been specially decorated. At the Parish church, where a ser- mon was preached by the Rev. F. W. Cory, the ornamenta- tion was on a more extensive scale and had a more finished appearance than usual. Below the east window were the words, in neatly executed letters, " Unto you is born this day a Saviour," and the ledges of the chancel windows were covered with cotton woot, bordered with holly, two of which bore in large red characters the words " 34viont'i" Ptl " siestts," tw9 9ttlerq haying representations of snow flakes, while the windows within the CoMmunion rails were decorated with moss and evergreens. The clergy and choir stalls were adorned with holly, and the prayer desk, which was embellished with holly and chrysanthe- mums, bore the words "Lord, hear my praper," neatly worked in holly on a white ground. A very pretty ap- pearance had been imparted to the pulpit. Round the top was a fringe of yew, and holly and everlasting flowers entwined the rails. The panels were bordered with holly and filled in with cotton wool, and in the centre were blue monograms formed of the letters A. 0., 1.H.5., and A.O. The windows on the south side were ornamented with evergreens, and on the ledges, on a white ground fringed with moss and evergreens, was the text " Glory to God in the highest," Skilfully formed of bolly leaves. On the south gallery were the texts, executei in Ornamental characters, "Wonderful, Counsellor, the Mighty God, the Everlasting rather, the Prince of Peace ;" and on the north," Behold 1 bring you good tidings of great joy. Unto you is both A Etivionr, Christ the Lord. Glory to the newhoiia King-. On earth peace, goodwill to men." Other texts were placed in various parts of the edifice, the pillars of which were entwined with evergreens, as also were the gas standards. Choice maids bait ferns,chrysanthemums and other flowers were effectively Used in the decoration of the font, the general effect of the embellishment of the church being very pretty.—St. James's Church, Latchford, had been most tastefully and effectively decorated. The panels of the pulpit were filled in with a blue and White ground alternately, and bordered with evergreens, a croSs of white everlasting flowers being placed in the centre. The reading desk had been treated in a like manner, and much time had been spent on the font, which was nicely decorated with everlasting flowers, ferns, ct c. The window ledges were tet off with holly and cotton wool, and the words "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will towards men," numerous ecclesiastical emblems being displayed in various parts of the -church.—At Holy Trinity Church, Sankey-street, the decorations were confined to the altar, pulpit, font, and readisg desk, which were ornamented with evergreens. In a very conspicuous position over the attar was the text on a white ground, bordered with holly, "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners."—Though not very extensive, the ornamentation of St. Paul's Church was very effective, and evinced the possession of considerable

had been used to adorn the pulpit, which had a wreath of holly, and in the centre a cross composed of white ehrysan- thetnums. Four vases containing 'chrysanthemums and a -cross were placed on the re-table and above this were the words '"Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will towards men." The communion rails and choir stalls were decorated with evergreens, as was the font, and in the window ledges round the church were the words "Be- hold I bring you good tidings of great joy," .Ic., in white letters on a crimson ground.—Much care had been bestowed in the decoration of St. Barnabas Chnrch, Lovely-lane, On'the wall near the entrance door was the text," Unto us a child is bern' unto us a son is given," the window ledge above being adorned witt ivy. Eung,'lrom the wall on -each side of the window were two bannerets, one bearing the text, "Fight the good fight of faith," and the other, "Lay hold on eternal life." Over the altar was a cross formed of flowers, and the text, "'Glory to God in the highest, on earth peace, goodwill to men," while on the ledges of the windows were the words " Ueto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour which is Christ the Lord." The pulpit, font, and reading desk were also adorned with evergreens, &c. Although the,aeeorations at St. Anne's Church, in Winwick-road, were of a meagre character, the effect was on the whole very pretty. The pulpit, reading desk, and prayer desk were trimmed with evergreens. on the altar table stood a number of vases containing choice flowers, while on the wall above was the text, "All Thy works, 0 Lord, shall praise Thee." SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN CHAPEL. On Tuesday, the annual tea meeting was held. The chapel presented a gay appearance, being profusely decorated with flowers, evergreens, and mottoes. Several mottoes deserve special notice, "Glory to God in the highest," lettered in variegated holly ; "God is our refuge and strength," on blue sateen in ivy; "Lo, I am with you always," on brewn sateen, in white wool; and "Success to our chapel." The committee provided an ample supply of him and tongue sandwiches, bun loaf, seed bread, mince pies, and tarts. A much larger number than on any former occasion was present, rendering it diffi- cult to find accommodation. The following ladies presided at the tables: Mrs. Surnmerfield, Mrs. George, Mrs. Tonge, Mrs. Snoddy, Mrs. &rough, Mrs. Gillman, and Miss Webb, assisted by Misses Williamson, Sum- mersgill, George, L. George, Tonge, Woolley, and Webb. After tea, the evening's entertainment commenced, with the Rev. T. Eippon in the chair. The choir did excellent service under the leadership of Mr. Bough, assisted by the following instrumentalists : Harmonium, Mr. Tomkinson ; violin, Mr. Ball; violoncello, Mr. George. The Chairman called upon the secretary, Mr. Snoddy to read his report, which was of the most satisfac- tory character. Overture, "Choral march," by the instru- mentalists. Then followed on the chairman, and in his address referred to the many pointe of interest in the report, and spoke of the advantage of social gatherings and the work belonging to the Christian Church, to labour for the salvation of the world to Christ. ETe made a brief reference to its multiplied agency and wide Celd of operation, urging those whose services had been hitherto so graciously blessed by God at Sankey Bridges to expect greater things than these. Anthem, "I will lift mine eyes," by the Choir. Addresses were given by Messrs. C. George, Sumrnerfield, and S. Blythe on Sunday school work, followed by a song, "Orphan's prayer," Miss Sparks; "Lead -thou me," by the Choir. Further addresses by Mews. T. Woolley, J. Corrodine, and F. Lloyd on the Blue Ribbon movement. Overture, "The promenade," by the Instrumental iste. Mr. Summeregill next spoke on the position of the church, its finances, etc. He referred to the many expenses of late, and said that notwithstanding a heavy item in substituting slates for the old iron roof a small balance remained in hand. A few remarks were solicited from the speakereby the chairman, on the prospect of a new chapel for Sankey Bridges, which were not of a very encouraging character for the present owing to an important building scheme new before the circuit, viz., "Wesleyan Sunday schools for 'Warrington," a want, the speaker said, which had been felt for more than 11 a quarter of a century. Duet, "Gently lead us," by Misses George and Sparks. Addresses by Messrs. Tomkhason and George,on "Congregational singing." The old Methodist tuner were greatly approved of in preference to the more :modern. "How sweet, how heavenly," by the choir ; song," I chasten those I lave," by Miss George. At the conclusion of the programme, Mr. Savage moved the thanks of the meeting be given to the decorators and ladies who had presided at the tea-tables, which was seconded by the Rev. T. Rippon, supported by Mr. Webb, and received with a burst of applause. It was moved by Mr. Hough that the best thanks of the meeting be given to the chairman for his able services. This was seconded by Mr. Grice, and it was carried with acclamation. The chairman having briefly responded, the concluding hymn, commencing " We are travelling home to heaven above," followed by the benedic- tion, lerought this happy and interesting meeting to a close. —The day following (Wednesday) the Sunday school child- ren's tea party was held. The room was inconveniently crowded. After tea Mr. Summerse;ll occupied the chair. An interesting entertainment followed, consisting of tengs and recitations, also addresses to the chilcieen and their parents, I by Messrs. Webb, legmmers4eld, aud C. Pritchard,

div.head: ST. ALBAN'S TEA PARTY.
div.p: ST. ALBAN'S TEA PARTY.

About 200 persons attended the tea party and ball, held on Thursday evening, in the Public Hall, in aid of the new presbytery at St. Alban's Catholic Church. After tea the Rev. Father Feeney ascended the platform, and explained the object of the gathering. The exterNion of the presbytery in Bewsey•street had, he said, cost about £5OO, and he wished to correct a rumour that the debt had been paid. There had been nearly £2OO paid, through the all of generous b.anefac- tors in and eut of town, but there still remained a debt of about £3OO which they would have to clear off as best they could. He announced that the list of subscriptions would be kept open until Sunday week, and stated that that morn- ing he received a cheque from a person who had always been a friend. He did not ask for it, and he did not look for it, but he thought it was only fair to mention his name—their worthy member, Mr. McMinnies,had sent him £5. (Applause.) He concluded by thanking the officials who were helping to make the party a success, and by wishing all the compli• ments of the season. Dancing then commenced to the music of Mr. Stirrup's band, and was kept up for several hours. Mr. James Boyle was the general manager of the party, and Mr. T. Connolly Brookes officiated as M.C. Trays for the tea were given by the following: Mr. Thos. Shepherd, Mrs. E. Fox. Mrs. L. Voisey, Mrs. R. Hind, Mrs. Mrs. John Dolan, Mrs. J. Fleming, Mrs. Connor; Mrs. Jas. Marsh, Mrs. J. Eckersley, Mrs. Lythgoe, Mrs. Dillon, Mrs. Unsworth, Mrs. Hellian, Mrs. Kavanagh, Mrs. J. Green, Mrs. McCiew.

METHODIST FREE CHURCH, BUCKLEY-STREET. The schoolroom, in connection with this church, was very tistefully adorned with evergreens and mottoes, suit• able for the present season of the year, much credit being due to Miss Hindley, the day school mistress, and Mr. Geo. Woodward, for the manner in which they carried out the decorations. There was a public tea meeting held on Tues- day evening, there bang a very large attendance, and a second sitting had to be arranged. After tea a very interest- ing programme was gone through, consisting.: 9f songs, recitations, &c., conducted by Mr. Edward Plinston, secre- tary, after which the remainder of the evening was spent in various amusements, which were much enjoyed by all present.

div.head: WARRINGTON WORKHOUSE.
div.p: WARRINGTON WORKHOUSE.

The genial influence of Christmastide was more or less felt by the inmates of Warrington Workhouse in their being served one day in the year with an unlimited supply of creature comforts. All had bread and butter, tea or coffee for breakfast. Over 300 sat down to dinner is the large dining hallovhieh was tastefully decorated for the occasion by the schoolmasters and inmates under the direction of the matron with evergreens, shields, scrolls, mottoes, ezc., the evergreens having been kindly sent by Sir Giltkrt Greenall and Thomas Lyon, Esq. The dinner consisted of prime roast joints of beef and ptum pudding, with which all were served ad libitum. After ample justice had been done, Major Cartwright,- who had come specially from Liverpool, addressed those present in a few appropriate words, which was much appreciated. Mr. Burn also addressed the assembly. As there were a great many old people unable to come to the dining hall, the Major and Mr. Burn went round the rooms to see them, and the old folks were much pleased to find that some one took an intetest in them, And that they were not altogether forgotten by the world. Mrs. Lawless and Mr. Robert Heaton each sent a box of oranges for the children, and Mr. Heaton offered to send two barrels of best beer for the old people, as did Mr. Wm. Bolton, and Mr. J. Barlow half a barrel, but the offers were respectfully declined by the master, as the Guardians had decided there was to be no beer on that day. THE WORKHOUSE SCHOOLS.

Yr. IT. M. Mines, superintendent of the Workhouse Schools, reported to the Board of Guardians, on Wedbesday, that ha had pleasure in stating that everything in connec- tion with their Christmas festivities had passed off satisfac- torily. The children's dinner, which consisted of a bounti- ful supply of roast beef, potatoes, and plum pudding, was served up in the Assembly-room, which had been tastefully decorated for the occasion. The hand was in attendance 'during the dinner hour, snot played a selection of good old English melodies. After dinner oranges, nuts, and sweets were distributed among the children. He was much grati- fied on seeing between twenty and thirty apprentices and hired servants (formerly 'pupils in the schools) who had come to spend Christmas Day with them. In the evening a round of amusements was got up, consisting of selections of dance music from the band, songs, recitatio-ns &c. At nine o'clock all retired to rest well satisEed with the day's pleasure. Their especial acknowledgments were due to the chairman of the Board (Mr. Blackhurst), also to-the chairman of the om- mittee (Rev. J. Yonge), -and to Mr. Lawless, each of whom sent them a large box of oranges; to Mr. Bonnet!, for his present of a large box of nuts; and Mr. Lythgoe, for a bag of sweets. He had also on behalf of the children to thank the numerous -subscribers to the Christmas tree fund. Daring the dinner hour the Rev. J. Yonge„ and Mr. W. Blackhurst T'ere present and addressed' the children. The band was Ender the leadership of Mr. Mines, who with Mrs. Mines, had executed the decorations. HILL CLIFFE BAPTIST CHAPEL.

A most-successful tea meeting was held in connection j with the above chapel on Christmas Day. Notwithstand- ing the unfavourable weather a goodly number assembled at the tea,Tor providing for the expenses of which trays had been given by the ladies and friends. After tea recitations were given by scholars of the Sunday school, and pieces of music rendered by the choir, one of which, "Consider the lilies," was much appreciated. The meeting was opened by the pastor, the Rev. Win. Pilling, who called upon Mr. W. Davidson, of Little Leigh, to prnide, in the enforced absence of Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P., who was suffering from a sevete cold. The CHAIRmAN expressed his pleasure in`being with them on -that occasion, and said what need there was of earnest effort and united co-operation on the part of Christians when we glanced at the great ungodliness to b 3 seen on every hand. London itself, with its great wealth, was very inefficiently supplied religiously, and the same was true in degree of the provinces. If they were Christians let them live for the glory of Christ, and the well- being of their fellow men. (Applause.)—Rev. R. YEAT- KAN, of. Liverpool, urged them to earnest effort, for that was the true condition of Chrietian life, and to be con- tent with doing that which was next to them. (Applause.) —Rev, G. HARVEY, of Thiry, then addressed the meeting, and spoke of the great importance of the temperance move- ment in connectioa with the churches. This stumbling block would never be removed until the Church took up the work. The ministers of all denominations were taking it up, for the best of them were teetotallers, and it remained for the churches to follow. (Applause.)—Mr. JOHN LONG- RIDGE, of Manchester, then delivered a short address ex- pressive of his obligation to the Sunday school in days past. —Mr. JAMES KENNVORTRY urged them to greater individual 1-effort. All could do something. -Let them look about, and having found thcir work go and do it irrespective of others. They should think of the past history of Hill Cliffe, and let that encourage them. (Applause.)—Mr. E. FORD, of Warrington, referring to the past history of the chapel, urged them to be worthy of their noble ancestors who had sacrificed much for the liberties we now enjoyed. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. T. GoontEß and Mr. W. BOOTH seconded a <vote of thanks to those who had taken part in the proceed- ings.—Rey. W. PILLING moved, and Mr. E. Faun seconded a vote of thanks to the chairman, which was accorded, and concluded a most successful gathering. CAIRO7STREET, WARLINGTON.- -

The annual children's party was held in these schools •on Christmas Day, when upwards of -260 guests assembled. The entertainment consisted of hymns, tic., sung by the children, and choruses sung by a selected chair trained by Mr. J. Owen. These choruses were so arranged as to illus- trate the four scenes of "Alfred, a drama for young people," which, we hear, is composed by a teacher in the school. This last was excellently performed by Messrs. F. Turner, Charles Travers, F. B. Mellor, Alfred Mellor, Thomas Knowles, S. Wellings, Thomas Monks, Josh. Monks, Wm. Monks, and John Dunbobin. The •" Cake" scene and the "Surprise of the Danish camp" were especially well done. A capital piece "Miss Spriggin's work," was capitally given by Miss Annie Wytch, Martha Worrall, and Margaret Medli- cott. Miss Chamberlain recited "A good old fashioned Christmas" with excellent effect. The younger children were sent home at 8-30, an orange being given to each ; whilst the elder scholars, teachers, and friends enjoyed various games, dancing, &c., till about eleven, There are now 220 -scholars on the books, and the sahool ie., we under- stand in a very healthy condition. A word of especial praise isdue to Messrs. A. Pemliertorb T. Pemberton and J. Danbobin far their really artietic decoration of the room. They added immensely to the pleasure of all.

div.head: ORFORD BARRACKS.
div.p: ORFORD BARRACKS.

The annual Christmas festivities of the South Laneas'aire Regiment took place at Orford Barracks, on Monday and Tuesday. The men proved themselves as zealous in their endeavours to outvie each other in the matter of decoration as in former years, and the prize given by Colonel H. J. Bell, was carried off by K Company of the 40th Depot. On Monday, by permission of the same officer, the whole of the men and their civilian friends had a ball at the Barracks, which passed off most successfully. A surprise was pro- vided for the children in the shape of a Christmas tree, con- taining a number of presents which were given to them during the evening, much to their delight and satisfaction. Captain Manse], in conjunction with Colour-Sergeants Connor, acted as masters of ceremonies. On Tuesday, the sergeants, with their wives and families, had a re-union. After partaking of an excellent repast. the evening was spent in a very enjoyable manner' the usual toasts - being given, interspersed with songs, re- citations, &c. Mr. Praeger gave several soles on the piano and violin with his accustomed ability

in addition to which he acted as accompanist. The annual dance in commemoration of the battle of Maharajpore was held last evening. It may ha interesting to mention that the battle was fought on the 29th December, 1843, and the 40th Regiment, which took part in it, and captured a gun, a copper drum, and a set of colours, has celebrated its an- niversary ever since. The decoration of the bronze star which the regiment received was manufactuied from the captured gun. The room in which the festivities were held was very tastefully decorated with evergreens, and pre- sented a very pleasing and attractive appearance. Oa the wall immediately opposite the entrance was fixed a glitter- ing star of bayonets, and round the room were hung several mottoes, and the many honours which the regiment had won. There are also representations in water colours of Father Christmas, itc., which, though presenting rather an unfinished appearance, reflects credit upon the artists, and the embellishments generally are such as call for a word of praise for the decorators.

div.head: HALTON PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: HALTON PARISH CHURCH.

The Christmas decorations in this Church were really beautiful, having been carried out by the following Chancel: Sir Richard and Lady Brooke and the Misses Brooke. Nave: Mrs. W. Stokes, Misses Short, Wright, Nannerley, Greswell, L. and J. Woodier, M. J. Wilson, A. Jeacock, S. Ackerley, Pollard, C. Lambert, J. Potter, M. Rogerson, M. Diwson, A. Percival, J. Dearden, A. and E. Acton; Messrs. D. T. Baguley (churchwarden), J. S. Jea- cock (organist), A. Povey, J. Poyey, J. Chrimes, W. Leath- wood, T. Pollard, and the choir boys. The evergreens were kindly supplied by Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., Messrs. T. F. Acton and D. T. Baguley (churchwardens), W. Baker and J. Stokes (R)ck Savage), W. Stokes (Prospect Farm), and Leather (Norton). The whole of the Christmas berries were the gift of Mrs. William Stokes, sent to her from Shropshire for the purpose. The chancel text, "Glory to the new-born King," was the work of Miss Short, the school- mistress. At the west end was the word "Alleluia." The choir sang a special Christmas anthem, entitled " Unto us a Child is born."

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

The announcement of the railway company that trains would run on Christmas Day as on Sunday, meant the isolation to a great extent, of Runcorn from the rest of the world on that day, for the Sabbath in Runcorn is undis- turbed by the roar of the trains as they cross the iron bridge which spans the Mersey. With no railway communication —except at Widnes, of course—a foggy atmosphere and drenching rain; Runcorn was dull and quiet. True, many of the places of worship held services of some kind ol another, but there were no other signs of life in the place. In the afternoon, whilst the funeral of Mr. E. Billingsley was passing along, the main thoroughfares were crowded with parsons, who regarded it with a melancholy interest, but immediately after the streets resumed their wonted ap- pearance. As in Widnes, "the happy morn" was ushered in with the ringing of bells and the singing of choirs, who moved about from place to place daring the night. The various works in the neighbourhood were closed.

div.head: WIDNES.
div.p: WIDNES.

Christmas Day was as unlike what fancy pictures that joyous time as it possibly could be. Instead of frost and snow, there was a dense humid atmosphere, and a persistent down-pour of rain all day. These were conditions which it can be well imagined did not add to the attractiveness of the centre of the chemical trade, on all occasions presenting a dull and dirty appearalce. Fortunately for the wait singers, Christmas Eve was bright and fine, and from mid- night until an early hour next morning the still silent air was resonant with their melodies. The treets on Christmas Day presented a deserted appearance for the most part, and only occasionally, when people were traversing the muddy streets to attend Divine service, or when the Salvation Army, who held one of their characteris/ic "demonstra- tions," marched along to their usual noisy accompaniment, did they present any signs of animation. Trams on both railway systems ran as on Sundays, and numbers of people "on pleasure bent" left by the early morning trains, returning in the evening. As an evidence of the quietness of the town, we may state that the number of " drunks " at the police court on Friday morning were comparatively few.

EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON. The weather on Christmas Day (Monday last) was far from being cheering or pleasant. From an early hour in the morning rain commenced to fall, and its miserable drizzling aspect greatly interfered with the comfort and enjoyment of pleasureleakers, and those who wished or those who were in any way compelled to remain outside. The advent of the day was celebrated in many ways—the well-trained choirs from several places of worship, and other carol singers visiting the residences of members of the various congregations and friends; whilst the band of the Viaduct Institute, the Ilaydock Brass Band also gave selections in the streets. The day was observed as a general holi- day—all the places of business, wonts, &c., being closed and stopped. As a consequence business was at an entire standstill, and this was almost the case on the following day, Tuesday (Bank Holiday)—as the principal places of business were closed--and scarcely anyone, except those in holiday attire, were to be seen in the streets. Many persons visited Liverpool and Manchester for the purpose of enjoy- ing an out to those places, witnessing the pantomimes, .Szc. The work of the officials at the Post-offices was greatly increased, and an exceedingly large number of letters, com- munications, and Christmas cards passed through the post. The letter carriers had additional labour thrown upon them, and as could only be expected the deliveries were not com- pleted quite as soon as is usually the else.

CHRISTMAS AT WHISTON WORKHOUSIL Christmas was made as pleasant to the inmates of Prescot Union Workhouse as the good will of the Guardians and the philanthropy of ladies and gentlemen resident in the district comprised in the 'Mien, could make it. On Christ- mas Day 550 inmates sat down to an instituted dinner of roast beef and plum pudding, with the accompaniment of a pint of ale for each inmate, followed by a dessert of oranges. Nor were the after dinner proceedings less agree- able. Some Guardians kad provided a plentiful supply of tobacco and snuff for such of the old folks as desired such luxuries; and this supply was supplemented by a liberal present of tobacco from Mr. Nuttall, of Nutgrove Hall. For the children Miss Ada Harrison, St. Mary's Villa, Huyton, sent a number of picture books, and Mr. W. Blinkhorn, of Sutton Grange, a large box of toys. Lady Stapleton- Brethertort made a donation of £3 towards the festivities, and large parcels of mufflers and shawls were contributed by Mrs. jowatt and Mrs. Boyd, Huyton. To each of the inmates a Christmas greeting, in the shape of a letter and card, was sent by Mrs. Webster, Abbotsfield, St. Helens. At the conclusion of the dinner three cheers were given for the Guardians, and also for the master and matron (Mr. and Mrs. Bicknell) and the medical 'officer (Mr. Hall). Later in the evening the agreeable quadrille band of Mr. Welsby, Praseor, attended and played a selection of mu4ic, and the hours up to twelve o'clock were pleasantly spent in sipging and -dancing. During the day Mr. J. T. Hall, chairman of the House Committee, Mr. Newsome, Mr. Leatherbarrow, and the clerk (Mr. Hartley) joined in the festivities.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

The Christmas that 13. s just passed has not been marked by anything of a very stirring or notable character at St. Helene; and here, as elsewhere, the unseasonable kind of weather which has prevailed has to some extent deprived the great festival, which is associated in people's minds, with frost and show and blazing gule-logs, of a good deal of its distinctive character. The happy morn was, however, as usual, ushered in by a considerable number of waits and carol-singers, both male and female, who paraded the streets and made night melodious. The fact that Christmas had once more arrived would also be less pleasantly impressed on the minds of many a household by the numberless urchins who, in groups of from two to in soma instanc-s neatly a dozen, went from door to door in the most respectable streets singing dissonantly scraps of songs more or less appropriate to the season. In many of these cases it can easily be imagined the gratuity sought for would be bestowed with more than usual alacrity on the youthful songsters, more however to bribe their absence than to encourage their pre- sence. ,Christmas being by many looked upon as a sort of carnival, is often the occasion of a good deal of drunken- ness, but it must be confessed that to an ordinary observer this does not seem to have been so much the case at St. Helens on this occasion, a pleasing circumstance which may in some degree, perhaps, be accounted for by the recent Blue Ribbon crusade—a not improbable explanation when we consider the number of blue ribbons which seem to be sported—or it may be accounted for by other influences or several combinec, As is customary, ser- vices were held in many of the, places of worship in The town, and the Parish Church, St. Helens, and St. Peter's, Parr, were tastefully and suitablydecorated. As might have been •expected, the post-office officials again found Christmas a-busy epoch in their particular department. The extra inflow of Christmas cards, presents, &c., was fully as large as on former occasions, but the influx was more dis- persed, owing,to Christmas Dv being on a Monday, which of course conelderably relieved the strain on the officials. At the railway,station the traffic in parcels and seasonable presents was very large, and as usual the passenger department was kept busy on Christ- mas Day, and still more so on the Bank Holiday following, when large numbers of people passed to and fro between St. Helens and Liverpool, and other adjacent places. 'Tuesday was very generally observed as a holiday at the works and manufactories in and around St. Helens, and also by the principal tradeamen and shop- keepers. Diversiont of a special nature were likewise provided for those in aearch of amusement at the circus and theatre, both of which places, particularly the former, were well patronised.

Twelve inclAs of snow fell cu Wednesday at Banar Bridge, Caithnesshire, while in some pa •ts of Perthshire the depth was six inches. Over Banff and Aberdeenshire the fall was very heavy. Keen frost set in at night, and flockmasters are again apprehensive for the safety of their sheep. Dur- ing the night a gale from the north-west raged with extreme violence, causing the snow to form drifts of great depth. aus RIBBON Anew MEETING.—A public meeting and entertainment in connection with the Blue Ribbon Army was held in the Mission Tent, Legh-street, on Wed- nesday evening. There was a moderate attendance, and Mr. E. J. Weaver presided. During the evening capital recitations were given by Miss Alice Marsh, Miss Maggie Norris, Miss Sarah Ann Lackland, and Mr. John Wadding- ton; a reading entitled "Bargain with a pump," by Mr. Boughton, and a song "Nobody cares for me," was given by Mrs. Whittey. Interesting addresses were given by the Chairman, and Messrs. Adamson and Boughton. The meeting was a very enjoyable one.

WESLEYAN SALE OF- WORK AT 'WIDNES. A sale of work and Christmas tree, the proceeds of which will be devoted to liquidating the debt on Lacey-street school, Widnes, was held in that building on Tuesday after- noon. The school was erected at a cost of £3,000, of which £1,300 remains unpaid. Of this amount, however, i'3oo has been promised, making the total amount to be raised £l,OOO. The liquidation of the debt was not, however, the only object of the sale, for it was intended to use any surn obtained over £5O, for the ordinary purposes of the Sandal school. Mr. T. Robinson, who performed the opening ceremony, was introduced by the Rev. 4t. Harper, the super- ' intendent minister, who made a few appropriate remarks. He congratulated the decorators upon the prettiness of the adornments of the room, observing that he knew of nothing which brought together so much youthful beauty and matronly grace as a bazaar. Mr. Robinson who was warmly received, remarked that the object of the sale was to assist the greatest movement of modern times; for be did not hesitate to apply that term to Sunday schools. (Applause.) Board schools, and other educational institutions taught outward things, but the labours of Sun- day schools had a higher aim —they gave religious educa- tion, which was most essential to the well-being of everybody. The decoration of the room had been carried out with great taste and effectiveness. Mottoes and suitable emblems adorned the wall, while from the ceiling depended the handsome banners of the school. The one stall, which occupied the centre of the room, represented one of those quaint black-timbered shops of three centuries ago, and from which some of our ancient villages and towns aro in- debted for much of their picturesqueness and attractive beauty. Its construction reflected the highest credit upon the amateur builders. The " shop " was stockedwith an infinite variety of articles, and was under the superintendence of Mesdames Harper, Tessyman, Robinson, Stringer Fogg, J. Robinson. But the aye of the juvenile wandered from the quaint gables and overhanging eaves of the " old shop" to the attractions of the Christmas tree, occupying a position near by. From its branches depended almost every toy and fancy '• nicknack " which youthful fancy could wish for, and the dispensers of these treasures were Mrs. Thomas Sadler and Mrs. T. S. Swale (the wives of the superintendents of the Sunday school), assisted by Mrs. Cooper Miss M. J. Sadler, MiSB Gillon, Miss Evans, and the teachers and members of the • select classes. A refreshment stall, stocked with good things, was in charge of Mrs. T. Sadler, who was assisted by Mes- dames Lawrenson, Duxbury, Spencer, Seed, J. Robinson, J. Sadler, Forshaw, and Miss Jane Sadler. Endless diver- sion was afforded by a variety of entertainments which had been arranged. Under the direction of Messrs. R. Fogg and J. Robinson a number of concerts were given; while the Revs. R. Harper and J. Tessyman judged the eforts of the would-be orators in the speaking bee, over which Mr. T. Sadler presided. A ventriloquial entertainment and wax- work exhibition were in charge of Messrs. S. B. Stringer, Peat, and Booth; and the microscope, sterescope, and zoo- trope were in care of Messrs. J. Hargreaves, Robinson, and Sepliton. The shocks from a galvanic battery were admin- istered by Messrs. W. Rigby and D. Taylor, and Messrs. A. Powlson and R. C. Taylor presided over the weighing machine, while Mr. John Sadler acted as curator to the museum. The general arrangements had been carried out by Mr. T. Robinson, secretary, and Mr. T. Sadler, treasurer. The attendance at the opening ceremony was only moderate, but towards evening the room filled rapidly, and the sale was a successful enterprise. The sale was continued on Weenesday and Thursday evenings, and was very successful, the amount realised being about £lOO.

French ships will take posseseion of their ports, and will then, by right of conqaest, .claim the sovereignty of the island. Will Englial statesmen alrow suck tlrnauda to be enforced oi,on a people who owe largely their position to our help, and with whom, we have had friendly relations for so long a period, without friendly intervention and firm protest against such gross injustice? It will perhaps he asked by some, "On what grounds can England claim a right to interfere in this question ?" It ma Y suffice to say here, briefly, that during the reign of Rada.ma 1., we largely aided the Malagasy Government to establish the central authority over other portions of the island; and to put down the export slave trade in former times, and more recently the import slave-trade ; that we have done very much, and have expended large sums of money, to enlighten and civilise and christianise the Mala- gasy people ; that we have in Madagascar about five times as many English subjects as there are French citizens ; that our valuable colony. of Mauritius derives almost all its food supply, from Madagascar; that we have a considerable and increasing trade with the coun- try, four times as large as that carried en by France ; that the acquisition by France of the north-west provinces will inevita,)ly lead to a revival of the slave trade on that coast, from which, in a modified form, it has already been largely going on for some time past by French vessels to supply coolies for Reunion; that in such cases our cruisers' right of search of ports and harbours would cease ; and finally, that for several years past there has been a distinct under- standing between England and France that each nation -shall respect the independence of Madagascar. On these grounds we submit that the Madagascar committee have ample reason for asking that the British Government will use its friendly offices with the French Government, so that the Malagasy people may be preserved in possession of their rights, and that, freed from foreign aggression, they may be allowed still to pursue that path of progress and enlightenment, in which they have made such remarkable advances for the last twenty years.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS The fortnightly meeting of the Board was held on Wed- nesday at the Workhouse. Present—Mr. G. Blackhurst (chairman), Mtn. J. Yonge, Alajor Cartwright, Messrs. Greening, Longshaw, Darbyshire, Appleton, Greenall, Hunt, Fairhurst, Woolfall, Burn, Cooper, Houghton, Bonnell, Gibson, Owen, and J. C. Sutton (clerk). THE MEDICAL OFFICER AND THE DRUG SUPPLY. The House Committee on the 22nd instant recommended an extra quantity of tobacco and snuff for Christmas. They also recommended that a few illustrated papers be bought second-hand. The following letter was received from Dr. Spinks : "Gentlemen,—Mr. Sutton, the clerk to the Board, has been urging me to sign a con'..-act for the supply of drugs, Sze., to this Workhouse, allow- ing only four of the most expensive medicines. May I ask you to supply all the drugs, as is done now in nearly all the workhouses, and in all hospitals? The number of patients have more than doubled during the past ten years, and now the consumption of drugs almost consumes one-half of my salary. Trusting that you will receive this application favourably."—The committee recommended unanimously that the application was a reasonable one.— Major CAnTwutonT moved the adoption of the minutes of the House Committee, and gave notice of his intention to mgye the consideration of Dr. Spinks's letter that day fortnight. —Mr. BuRN seconded the motion, which was carried.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Thursday, the members present being Mr. S. Marsh, (chair- man), Rev. J. Barnacle, Messrs. Fisher, Jackson, Buckley, Penketh, Hall, Tyrer, Matthews, Birchall, Dobell, Newsome, Swift,Gilbody, Syder, Kenwright, Gerrard, Fidler, Meadows, and Hartley (clerk). A REPUDIATED SET OFF. The CLERK asked for instructions as to recovering from Mr. Dennett, a local tradesman, the sum of £6 is. for Indian meal supplied to him. Mr. INIEADOWS remarked that pro- bably Mr. Dennett intended his account to be a set off against the amount he alleged the Guardians owed him for dinners —The CIIAIRMAN said Mr. Dennett believed he had a claim against the Board. The CLERK, in answer to a Guardian, stated that Mr. Dennett had no legal claim against the Board. On the motion of Mr. DOBELL, seconded by Mr. GERRARD, the clerk was instructed to pro- ceed against Mr. Dennett for the amount owing by him.

div.head: TRAMPS.
div.p: TRAMPS.

The CLERK produced a circular from the Local Govern- ment Board with reference to the new regulations to come in force at the beginning of the new year, as to the relief of "casuals." The circular was referred to a committee. It was remarked by the Clerk that the carrying out of the new regulations might involve the establishment of vagrant wards in St. Helens.—Mr. NEWSOME inquired whether the labour of the " casuals " could not be employed in the utilisation of the rain water caught in a cistern whibh had been erected by the Gnardians at a cost of £2,000, and which was capable of holding 28.000 gallons of water. He was under the impression that this water was not used.—lt was explained that the water was utilised for the purposes of the Workhouse by means of pipes, and under the direc- tion of the officers of the House. MEDICAL APPOINTMENTS.—AN EXPLANATION. _ _ .

The Local dovernimt Board wrote, appreving of the ap- pointinent of Dr. Thomas Arthur Wood as medical officer for Woolton district. With reference to the proposal of the Guardians to appoint Dr. Wood medical officer for Hale, the Board inquired, reverting to previous correspondence, whe- ther the Guardians, although unable to obtain the services of a medical practitioner resident within the Hale district, had it not in their power to elect one who lived nearer the district than Dr. Wood.—Mr. GILBODY stated that Dr. Wood lived five :nilea frcin Ille, but there was no medical gentle- an nearer.—The Clerk was instructed to reply to the Local GoVernment Board that Dr. Wood was the only qualified medical gentleman eligible for the office.—Mr. JACKSON, re- verting to a discussion which took place at last meetiug as to the appointment of a medical officer for Sutton district stated that he had received two letters complaining of what had been said by Mr. Hall and himself with regard to the letters from clergymen read on that occasion. While still holding that the wire pullers had been at work on behalf of the late medical officer, he disclaimed ant insinua- ticn that the clergymen in question had been influenced by other than proper motives; but urged that when questions affecting a particular township arose they should address themselves to the Guardians of that township before writing to the Guardians or to an outsider. He complained that in the else in point clergymen had written to Mr. Cham- bers who lived so far distant as Halewood, instead of the Guardians at Parr and Sutton. The only exception in the case was afforded by the Rev. Father O'Sullivan, of Black- brook.—Mr. HALL supported Mr. Jackson's remarks.—The Rev. J. BARNACLE defended the conduct of the clergymen mentioned, affirming that they had no intention of ignoring ' the Guardians of Parr and Sutton, and had only adopted what they thought, although perhaps erroneously, was the , proper course.—The subject then dropped. THE EXPENSES OF GUARDIANS..
a - , Tht. `-er. Board

_ne CLEM( read a letter from the Local Government eoard stating that they had had under their consideration the representations made by the deputation which waited on the President of the Local Government relative to the ex- penses of the Guardians in visiting lunatic asylums, the provision of hay and provender for the Guardians' horses, and the allowance of some payment of those members of the board who attended the periodical revision of the relief cases to enable them to provide refreshments on those occasions. The Board bad also considered the letter which the clerk bad addressed to them on the subject. As regards the first point, they were of opinion that the Guardians were em- powered to appoint a deputation to visit asylums provided the number of members constituting the deputation was restricted within moderate limits. It was requisite that the total expenditure should not exceed a reasonable amount for each member, But the Board thought it might properly include not only the necessary travelling expenses, but a reasonable sum for refreshments required. What that RUM should be must, it appeared to the Board, depend on the circumstances of the particular case, as it was evident the refreshments needed would vary according to the distance of the asylum and the time occwpied in the visit. It did not seem to the Board, therefore, that a fixed sum could be determined upon which could be allo,sed in any case. As to the second point, the Board did not find any legal author- ity empowering the Guardians to supply hay and provender for the horses of members attending their meetings and to charge the cost to the rates. With respect to the question whether some allowance for refreshments could be made to those Guardians who attended the revision of the relief lists the Board fully appreciated the benefits derived from those revisions, but they were unable to satisfy themselves that the services rendered by the Guardians in making them could be regarded as " extraordinary " duties. In the absence of the Rev. T. Chambers, who had brought the , subject forward, the consideration of the matter was deferred.

div.head: VISIT OF THE MALAGASY ENVOYS TO WARRINGTON.
div.p: VISIT OF THE MALAGASY ENVOYS TO WARRINGTON.

The Malagasy Envoys have now been in England fully a month, the object ef their visit being to awaken the sym- pathy of this country with them in their troubles with the French Government, That they have been successfulla doing this is shown by the fact that the committee which has been formed in England in support of the cause of the Madagascar people comprises more than sixty M.P.'s, many high colonial officials, several directors of the London Mis- sionary and other missionary societies, members of the Society of Friends, and supporters of philanthropic agencies. The members of the embassy are His Excellency Ravioninahitriniarivo, 15th Honour, Officer of the Palace, Chief Minister for Foreign Affairs, and His Excellency Ratnaniraka, 14th Honour, Officer of the Palace, Queen's Counsellor, with Mr. Moses Andrianisa, French and English secretary and interpreter, and Mr. Anthony Tacchi, secretary and law translator, and Rabibisoa and Ranjalahy in their suite. Mr. Tacchi is accompanied by his wife, the only lady with the Embassy. During their stay in England they hate visited many important centres, and on Thursday next they are to visit Warrington. They will arrive here, we understand, about two o'clock in the afternoon when they will be met by his Worship the Mayor (John C, ostield, Esq.) and the Town Clerk (Mr. W. H. Brook). His Worship will entertain the Envoys at a luncheon in the Town Hall, a select company having been invited to meet them. The reception wfiich the Envoys will receive will no doubt be a very cordial one. It might be profitable to here point out the .origin of the extraordinary claims which are made by the French on Madagascar, and which have given rise to so much controversy. These claims, as summarised by the Madagascar Committee, are said to rest on the following grounds:— 1. The forcible seizure in the 17th century of several military posts on the east coast, from which, after having been held only thirty years, they were at length driven off by the people, the positions being abandoned altogether for seventy years. 2. The resumption of some of these places in the middle of the 18th century, and their final abandon- ment towards the commencement of this century, soon after , which time the conquest of the Mascarene Islands by the British, transferred all their dependencies in Madagascar-if any such existed, to England. And these rights were ior- mally restored by us to the Malagasy Govsrnment in 1817. 3. The cession in 1840 by a north-west tribe, ,then in rebellion, of a portion of their territory to France ; a cession never recognised by the central government; never claimed by the French in their treaty of 1856; and never brought forward at all until the present year. 4. A treaty made by the Hove king on his own sole authority,in 1862, against all Malagasy usage, with a French trading company <often known as the "Lambert Company "), but which was speedily repudiated by the Malagasy Government, and all claims discharged by payment of a large sum to the company. Thess are, we the committee) believe, in brief, all the grounds on which large demands are now being made upon the Mala- gasy by the French authorities; demands which, if ac- ceded to, will virtually band over the island to French rule, and which the Malagasy ambassadors are now being pressed 1 to Agree to, while they remoin in some amount of constraint

MORE BODIES' RECOVERED. The Central News Bradford correspondent telegraphed yesterday morning :—The work of removing the rubbish and extricating the dead was continued up to three o'clock this morning, at which time 30 dead bodies had been recovered, but a large number are still believed to be buried amongst the ruins. Numerous fresh inquiries have been made during the past few hours. Crowds of people assembled round the demolished mill watching the proceed- ings with great anxiety. From 200 to 300 men are still at work disengaging huge pieces of timber and im- mense stones, and placing them in waggons to be conveyed away. There are still several mutilated bodies lying in the temporary deadhouse unidentified, and the friends of a young gentleman named Webster, who is known to be under the debris, have anxiously waited upon the scene all night. THE PREMIER'S BIRTHDAY. Yesterday being Mr. Gladstone's seventy-third birthday, he received a large number of congratulations by letters and telegrams from all parts of the country, and also from the colonies, a telegram from Australia reaching him as early as half-past seven. Amongst the communications re- ceived were telegrams from the Prince and Princess of of Wales. The bells of Hawarden Parish Church rang throughout the morning; and Mr. Gladstone's health has so much improved that he was able to attend divine service.

A SUGAR REFINERY BURNT DOWN. THREE HUNDRED -MEN THROWN OUT OF EMPLOYMENT. A large suzar refinery in Greenock, belonging to Messrs. M.Cachran, Adam, and Co., was destroyed by fire yesterday morning. The fire broke out in the upper storey, and, fanned by a strong wind, spread with such alarming rapidity that it was with the utmost difficulty the workmen escaped. In an hour the building of nine storeys, was gutted. The surrounding houses caught fire several times, but the firemen managed to extinguish the flames. The darnige is estimated at between £30,000 and £40,000, wb is believed to be covered by insarance. Three hundred people have been thrown out of employment.

SHOCKING FATAL CRANE ACCIDENT. On Thursday night, a shocking fatal crane accident oc- curred at a quarry near Messrs. Rylands and Codd's glass works, Stairfoot„ near Barnsley. Whilst eight men were engaged in raising a large stone with a crane, it broke. John Elvidge, aged 38, married, falling 14 feet, was so seriously injured that he died shortly aftc.rwards. Thomas Bunk lies at Beckett's Hospital in a critical state, whilst Richard Watson was injured on the head; the others narrowly escaped. DISASTROUS FIRE AT BELFAST.—A FIREMAN KILLED. Yesterday morning, shortly before one o'clock, a fire broke out in the extensive flour mills of Messrs. Hughes, Belfast. In half an hour the whole building was enveloped in flames. At five o'clock the main wall fell, burying four firemen, one of whom, named Samuel Patterson, was killed. The other three, whose names are James Patterson (brother to the deceased), Robert Magee, and James Doherty, are seriously injured, and lie in a critical condition. The fire raged with unusual fury, and a number of workmen who were on the premises at the time had narrow escapes. The whole of the valuable machinery and stock is destroyed. - The damage is estimated at L 40,003. BIRTHS. DISTRESS IN THE CHESHIRE SALT DISTRICTS. STOCK AND SHARE. MARKET.

Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share I.;rokers, 13, Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write Dec,k 28th) : The days on which business has been attended to daring the past week have been employed either in preparation for or the artangement of the account which cominenced yesterday. On the whole though very little has been doing in fresh open 3.- tions, a steady tone pervades the markets, the new year being looked forward to with confidence. What changes in quotations have occurred are in no ease of moment, and the alterations are fairly balanced as regards rise and fall in prices ; the changes being apparently more the result Of individual influences than of any decided ge.:eral tende.acy. BANES. on the whole, are firm. COAL, IRON, &C , AND MINING are inactive, and movements irregular. COTTON SPINNING, &C., very little doing, and prices tending in buyers' favour. TELEPHONES : Irregular. Uniteds show an advance of to ' whilst Lmcashire and Cheshires are 1-16 down. CORPORATION STOCKS, &.—Several quoted ex-dividend, hpt ot her wise no change to report. f, MISCELLANEOUS —Movements contradictory. Ryiands and eons are up.

THE LAND AGITATION £EN SHYE.-With reference to the land agitation in the North of Scotland, it is said that an agreement has been concluded between Lord Macdonald and the Braes crofters respecting Ben Lee. The interdict pre- ceedings will now be stopped, and the request for police assistance has now been withdrawn. The proprietors of Glendale have petitioned the Court of Session to take measures against the refractory tenants in the matter of the Waterstein grazings. Mr. Wood, of :Radsay, has informed his tenants that he will make a reduction of a third of the year's rent due last Martinmas. Sr]i HERBERT riTACPHERSOM-SIT Herbert Macpherson was on Tuesday presented with a Highland claymore, and entertained by the Town Council and citizens of Inverness. Sir Herbert, replying to a statement published in a Scotch magazine that the 72nd Regiment were so done up before reaching Zagazig that they had to be conveyed thither by train, said there was not the slightest foundation for such a statement. He explained that when he reached Zagazig he was informed that an Egyptian division.was coming from Salahnh. He had only 20 ;horsemen, and a train was despatched for reinforce,nente. As it happened, the 721c1 were brought in, but they were •quite fresh and ready for anythina. Michael Burns, a private in the Cameronian Highlanders, who was-engaged at Tel-el-Kebir, was charged at Altrin- cham Police Court, on Tiaursday morning, with assaulting a police-oLgcer. There was a country ball at the Unicorn Inn Hall.rand prisoner and some companions went to create a disturbance, and the police-o-Mcer was knocked down by the prisonu and another man, named ]Bird, and severely kicked. A farmer's son, named Wood, was also seriously assaulted, and in the general ilLgee, in which a dozen men tock part, the,policeman was pitched across the road. Burns and Bird were sent to gaol for two months' hard labonr.

This has been promised him. Shipbuilding is so brisk on the Clyde that the New Year holidays are likely to be limited to two or three days. An idea of the activity and extent of the work gone through may be gathered from the fact that in Messrs. Elder's yard alone a sum of £23,000 is required for workmen's weekly wages alone. Not the faintest clue has yet been obtained as to the fate or whereabouts of Thayer, the Cardiff cabman, whose horse and hansom were found wandering at Pontypridd-street on Wednesday morning. The strictest and most unflagging search is kept up, at in many quarters it is feared Thayer has been murdered. • A Tralee correspondent telegraphs that about midnight a a police patrol from Tralee was attacked by Moonlighters between that town and Castlemaine, who took from them their horse and car and threatened to assassinate them if they offered the least resistance. The police returned to Tralee without having made any arrests. Turkey red dyeing at the Tale of Leven, the centre of the industry in Scotland, continues dull, and at present there is no hope of a speedy revival. Works have for months been only on three-quarters time, and the loss to the district is serious. It is cheering, however, that calico printing is brisk, and that the prospects for next year are good. Upwards of one hundred colliers refused to go to work yesterday at Messrs. Collis and Co.'s colliery, Rowley, in consequence, it is alleged, of the proprietors refusing to give tbe usual Christmas feast or money in lieu of it. It is stated to have been customary for fifty years at all collieries in. Staffordshire and Worcestershire for employers to give the miners a treat at Christmas either in money or kind.
